Promise.allSettled always completes faster because it does not wait for rejected promises to settle
They both return the same array shape containing only the successfully fulfilled promise values
explanation: Use Promise.all when all must succeed; use Promise.allSettled when you need results regardless of success or failure.

text: What does the async/await syntax do?
options: Creates a dedicated OS thread for each asynchronous operation
Makes Promise-based asynchronous code readable as if synchronous
Blocks the event loop until every pending Promise has completed
Automatically replaces all callbacks with native synchronous function calls
explanation: async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises, improving readability without changing the underlying async model.

text: What is a WeakMap in JavaScript?
options: A collection where keys may be duplicated and each key stores multiple independent values
A collection where keys must be objects and are held weakly, allowing garbage collection
A collection that prevents all entries from being changed after they are inserted
A collection whose lookups block until garbage collection has completed
explanation: WeakMaps are useful for storing metadata about objects without preventing their garbage collection.

text: What does Object.freeze() do?
options: Creates a fully independent deep copy of the object and all nested references
Prevents properties from being added, removed, or modified (shallow freeze)
Serializes the entire object into a JSON string while preserving every property
Combines properties from two source objects into one newly created object
explanation: Object.freeze() is a shallow freeze — nested objects can still be mutated unless also frozen.

text: What is a generator function?
options: A function that schedules its body to run repeatedly, returning each result through a timer callback
A function that can pause with yield and resume later, returning an iterator
A function that performs asynchronous work with await, returning a Promise for its eventual result
A function that creates an object from a class, returning a configured instance when called
explanation: Generators are useful for lazy sequences, async iteration, and cooperative multitasking patterns.

text: What does the optional chaining operator (?.) do?
options: Safely converts a value to a boolean, returning false instead of throwing when the value is null or undefined
Safely accesses a property, returning undefined instead of throwing if the object is null or undefined
Safely creates a missing property on an object, returning null instead of throwing when the base is null or undefined
Safely accesses a property, throwing a TypeError instead of returning undefined when the object is null or undefined
explanation: obj?.prop short-circuits to undefined if obj is null or undefined rather than throwing a TypeError.

text: How does JavaScript garbage collection work?
options: By reference counting — objects are collected when no references remain, but cycles are not reclaimed
Primarily via mark-and-sweep — objects unreachable from the root are collected
By object age — only long-lived objects are collected after surviving several allocation cycles
When the heap reaches its limit — execution pauses and all allocated objects are scanned for collection
explanation: V8 uses generational GC: a scavenger for short-lived objects and a mark-sweep-compact cycle for long-lived ones.

text: What does Symbol.iterator enable?
options: Automatic asynchronous iteration — objects implementing it work only with for await...of and async generators
Custom iteration — objects implementing it work with for...of, spread, and destructuring
Runtime type conversion — objects implementing it control concatenation, numeric coercion, and template-string interpolation
Class-based enumeration — objects implementing it expose inherited properties through for...in and Object.keys
explanation: Built-in iterables (Array, String, Map, Set) implement Symbol.iterator. Any object can be made iterable by defining it.

text: What is the purpose of Proxy in JavaScript?
options: Routing outbound network requests through an intermediary server that forwards HTTP traffic and filters remote responses
Defining custom behaviour for fundamental object operations like get, set, has, and deleteProperty
Encrypting object properties automatically so intercepted values remain unreadable without a private key
Resolving and executing imported files before evaluation, including dependency paths and package metadata
explanation: Proxies enable reactive state, validation, logging, and default values without modifying the target object.

text: What is tail call optimisation (TCO)?
options: An array optimisation that compacts packed elements and replaces sparse indexing with contiguous storage during repeated loops
When the last action is a function call, the engine reuses the current stack frame, preventing stack overflow in deep recursion
A memory-cache technique that stores recently returned function values so later recursive calls avoid recomputing them
An event-loop feature that schedules the final recursive call as a microtask, allowing the current call stack to unwind
explanation: TCO is in the ES2015 spec but only Safari implements it reliably as of 2024.

text: What is Vault's Secrets Sync feature?
options: Replicating secrets between separate Vault clusters so that identical paths and values remain synchronized across primary and disaster-recovery environments
Syncing secrets from Vault to external destinations (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, GitHub Actions) automatically
A backup feature that periodically exports encrypted Vault data to a durable storage location so operators can restore deleted secrets later
A secret-versioning feature that records every previous value in Vault and lets applications select an earlier version when reading a secret
explanation: Vault Secrets Sync (Enterprise/1.16+) propagates Vault secrets to external platforms, bridging Vault with platform-native secret stores.

text: What commonly causes memory leaks in JavaScript?
options: Declaring variables with let automatically prevents garbage collection, causing their bindings to remain alive after the function returns
Unintentionally retained references — forgotten event listeners, closures capturing large objects, detached DOM nodes
Declaring const values makes referenced objects permanently reachable, even when no event listeners or closures retain them
Returning undefined from a function causes the runtime to retain its local variables and objects for later garbage collection
explanation: Common patterns: event listeners not removed on component teardown, variables in setInterval closures, DOM references after removal.

text: What is V8 hidden class optimisation?
options: It compresses each object's properties into a smaller representation, reducing memory use without changing how access is compiled
V8 assigns hidden classes to objects with the same property layout enabling JIT-compiled direct property access
It stores every object property in a hash table, making access speed independent of insertion order or shared layouts
It builds hidden classes from prototype chains and serializes objects before each property lookup to improve consistency
explanation: Adding properties in inconsistent order triggers hidden class transitions and de-optimises JIT-compiled hot paths.

text: What does HTTPS provide that HTTP does not?
options: Automatic response caching by browsers and intermediary servers to reduce repeated requests to the origin
Encrypted communication via TLS between client and server
Reduced page-load latency through mandatory connection optimization and lower server processing overhead
Lossless compression of all request and response bodies before transmission across the network
explanation: TLS encrypts data in transit, preventing eavesdropping and tampering by intermediaries.

text: What is a firewall?
options: A malware detection service that scans files for suspicious code and removes infected programs
A network security system that monitors and controls traffic based on predefined rules
A cryptographic method that transforms readable data into protected ciphertext using a secret key
A remote-access service that encrypts a user's connection to another network through a secure tunnel
explanation: Firewalls operate at network or application layer, allowing or blocking traffic based on rules.

text: What is malware?
options: Software that has become outdated because its vendor no longer provides security updates
Any software intentionally designed to harm, exploit, or gain unauthorised access to systems
A set of communication rules that controls how devices exchange data across a network
A browser add-on that changes website features or manages online content for the user
explanation: Malware includes viruses, ransomware, spyware, trojans, and worms.

text: What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Using the smallest available encryption key or algorithm to protect information efficiently
Granting users only the permissions they need for their role and nothing more
Preventing every connection from outside the organisation, regardless of its purpose or trust level
Choosing simple passwords that are easy to remember so employees can work more quickly
explanation: Least privilege limits the blast radius of compromised accounts and insider threats.

text: What is a DDoS attack?
options: Overwhelming a target with legitimate traffic from one source to slow or interrupt its service
Overwhelming a target with traffic from multiple sources to disrupt availability
Blocking traffic from multiple sources by filtering requests at the network perimeter
Stealing data from multiple systems by coordinating malware across a connected network
explanation: Distributed Denial of Service attacks use botnets or amplification to exhaust target resources.

text: What is a security patch?
options: A network design that separates systems into isolated security zones
A software update that fixes a known vulnerability or bug
A firewall rule that permits or blocks traffic by port and address
An encryption key used by authorised systems to protect data
explanation: Patching known vulnerabilities quickly is one of the most effective defences against exploitation.

text: What is SQL injection?
options: A database backup technique that copies selected tables for recovery after corruption or data loss
An attack inserting malicious SQL into user input to manipulate or extract database data
A stored procedure type that executes predefined database operations when called by an application
A data type that controls how values are stored and validated within a relational database
explanation: SQL injection is mitigated by parameterised queries and prepared statements — never by string concatenation.

text: What is a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack?
options: An attacker impersonating one party while communicating separately with the other
An attacker secretly intercepting and potentially altering communication between two parties
An attacker repeatedly guessing credentials against multiple accounts without intercepting traffic
An attacker overwhelming a service with requests until legitimate users cannot connect
explanation: MITM is mitigated by TLS certificate validation, HSTS, and certificate pinning.

text: What is Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)?
options: Embedding malicious script in a trusted page so it executes in another user's browser
Tricking a users browser into making an unwanted authenticated request to a site they are logged into
Stealing an authenticated session cookie and reusing it to access the user's account from another device
Redirecting a domain's name resolution to a fraudulent server that copies the legitimate website
explanation: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and checking the Origin/Referer header are common defences.

text: What does a cryptographic hash function guarantee?
options: A reversible transformation that lets anyone recover the original message from the digest using the same algorithm
A fixed-size one-way output — the same input always yields the same hash, but the hash cannot reveal the input
An encryption mechanism that stores data securely by allowing authorized recipients to decrypt the hash with a secret key
A guaranteed unique identifier in which every different input produces a distinct digest with no possible collisions
explanation: Collisions (two inputs producing the same hash) must be computationally infeasible for a secure hash like SHA-256.

text: How do you balance Agile flexibility with compliance and regulatory requirements?
options: Keep compliance outside the delivery workflow by completing a separate approval phase after development, testing, and release work are finished by the Agile team
Integrate compliance tasks into the definition of done, use acceptance criteria for regulatory requirements, and involve compliance stakeholders in sprint reviews
Adopt a Waterfall process for regulated products, using sequential requirements, implementation, validation, and sign-off stages instead of incremental Agile delivery
Collect design evidence, test records, and regulatory approvals in one comprehensive package at project close, rather than maintaining traceability and review activities throughout delivery
explanation: Agile can incorporate compliance (GDPR, SOC2, HIPAA) by treating compliance requirements as non-functional requirements and adding them to DoD.

text: Which SQL clause filters rows?
options: ORDER BY
GROUP BY
WHERE
HAVING
explanation: WHERE is evaluated before grouping; HAVING is evaluated after aggregation.

text: What does COUNT(*) return?
options: The sum of all values
The total number of rows including those with NULL values
The number of non-null values in a column
Distinct row count only
explanation: COUNT(column) excludes NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs.

text: Which JOIN type returns only rows with matches in both tables?
options: LEFT JOIN
RIGHT JOIN
FULL OUTER JOIN
INNER JOIN
explanation: INNER JOIN is the default join type and returns the intersection of the two tables.

text: What does ORDER BY name DESC do?
options: Orders alphabetically A to Z
Orders results from Z to A in descending order
Groups rows by name
Filters rows by name
explanation: ASC is the default direction; DESC reverses the sort order.

text: What is threat modelling?
options: A visual or computational model that renders attackers, assets, and possible attack paths as diagrams for review
A structured process for identifying, ranking, and mitigating security threats to a system before or during development
An authorized process of probing a running application to discover and demonstrate exploitable security weaknesses
A post-compromise process for coordinating containment, eradication, recovery, and communications after a security incident
explanation: Common frameworks include STRIDE (Microsoft), PASTA, and LINDDUN. Output is a prioritised list of threats and mitigations.

text: What is the zero-trust security model?
options: Assume internal users and devices are trustworthy after they connect through the corporate network or VPN
Never trust always verify — no user, device, or network segment is trusted by default regardless of location
Protect information primarily by encrypting databases, backups, and files while they remain stored on disk
Require multifactor authentication for privileged administrators while leaving ordinary user accounts unchanged
explanation: Zero trust assumes breach and enforces continuous verification, least privilege, and micro-segmentation everywhere.

text: What distinguishes a vulnerability from an exploit?
options: They are two names for the same security condition, with no meaningful distinction between a weakness and an attack method
A vulnerability is a weakness in a system; an exploit is code or a technique that actively takes advantage of that weakness
An exploit is a hypothetical weakness description, while a vulnerability is the working code used to trigger it
A vulnerability is generally a successful attack that has already been used, whereas an exploit is a weakness awaiting discovery
explanation: A vulnerability with a public exploit has a much higher risk score and demands immediate patching.

text: What does SELECT * FROM users do?
options: Deletes all rows in the users table but keeps the table structure
Retrieves all columns and rows from the users table
Changes every users row to the same specified values
Creates a saved view named users from another query
explanation: SELECT * is convenient but listing specific columns is better practice to avoid fetching unnecessary data.

text: What does a PRIMARY KEY enforce?
options: Sorts key values alphabetically whenever rows are inserted or retrieved
Uniqueness and a NOT NULL constraint on one or more columns
Generates sequential numeric values automatically for each inserted row
Requires matching values in another table through a foreign key relationship
explanation: A table can have only one primary key, but it can span multiple columns as a composite key.

text: What is a NULL value in SQL?
options: A zero-valued numeric entry indicating that no quantity is present
An empty text value stored when a column contains no characters
The absence of any value — unknown or inapplicable
A Boolean false value used to represent an absent or negative condition
explanation: NULL is not equal to anything, including itself. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to check for it.

text: What is the OWASP Top 10?
options: A ranking of popular programming languages and web frameworks used to build current web applications
A regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks
A baseline for firewall segmentation and inbound filtering rules protecting public web servers
A set of formatting conventions for writing consistent, readable application source code
explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is a widely used awareness document for web application security risk prioritisation.

text: What is certificate pinning?
options: An operating-system control that restricts which physical machines may connect to a protected server
Hardcoding a servers expected certificate or public key in a client app to prevent MITM attacks
A TLS configuration that selects cipher suites and protocol versions for encrypted client connections
A browser security policy that limits which domains may load scripts, frames, or other web resources
explanation: Pinning prevents accepting rogue certificates signed by a compromised CA, but complicates certificate rotation.

text: What is the difference between IDS and IPS?
options: IDS records events on hosts; IPS reports network anomalies without blocking suspicious traffic
IDS detects and alerts; IPS also actively blocks threats inline
IDS blocks suspicious packets at the perimeter; IPS only generates alerts for later review
IDS and IPS are identical tools, differing only in vendor terminology and dashboard design
explanation: IPS sits inline in network traffic; IDS is typically passive and monitors a copy of traffic.

text: What is OAuth 2.0?
options: An encryption protocol that protects application data in transit by negotiating keys between communicating endpoints
An authorisation framework allowing third-party apps limited access to resources without exposing user credentials
A session management standard that issues cookies and refresh tokens to maintain a user's logged-in state
An authentication protocol that verifies user identity and returns identity claims, without separating it from OpenID Connect
explanation: OAuth 2.0 is for authorisation (delegated access); OpenID Connect is the identity layer on top for authentication.

text: A company wants to store session data with millisecond latency. Which service should they use?
options: RDS
DynamoDB
S3
CloudFront
explanation: Automates infrastructure deployment via templates.

text: Which SQL statement adds new rows to a table?
options: UPDATE
CREATE
INSERT
SELECT
explanation: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values) adds one or more rows.

text: Which Go keyword is used to initialize packages before main()?
options: init
start
setup
pre
explanation: Terminates Goroutine.

text: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE)?
options: A permanent table created by a query and retained in the database for later sessions
A named temporary result set defined with WITH that can be referenced within a single query
A materialised view that is automatically stored and refreshed independently of the query that defines it
A schema object declared with WITH that remains available to other queries after execution
explanation: CTEs improve readability and can be recursive for hierarchical data queries.

text: What is a window function in SQL?
options: A function that opens a user-interface window for each returned row and displays interactive results
A function computing values across related rows without collapsing them, like ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and LAG
A cursor that iterates through query results one record at a time while maintaining its current position
A stored function that executes server-side logic and returns a reusable scalar or table result
explanation: Unlike GROUP BY aggregates, window functions preserve individual rows in the result set.

text: What does an EXPLAIN plan show?
options: Column definitions, including names, data types, constraints, and default values
The query optimisers execution plan — access paths, join methods, and estimated costs
Table relationships, including foreign keys, cardinality, and logical connections among entities
Index definitions, including indexed columns, uniqueness settings, and storage options
explanation: Reading EXPLAIN output is essential for diagnosing slow queries. Look for sequential scans on large tables.

text: What does COALESCE do?
options: Joins multiple text arguments into one string value
Returns the first non-NULL value from a list of arguments
Rounds a numeric expression to a specified decimal precision
Converts an expression from one data type to another
explanation: COALESCE(a, b, c) returns a if not null, else b, else c. Useful for providing default values.

text: What is database normalisation?
options: Assigning predefined values to columns when an INSERT statement omits those columns during row creation
Organising data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity by applying normal forms (1NF through BCNF)
Creating indexes on every column to accelerate lookups and enforce efficient access paths
Dividing large tables into separate physical pieces based on ranges, lists, or hash values
explanation: Over-normalisation hurts read performance; denormalisation trades redundancy for query speed.

text: What does a UNIQUE constraint enforce?
options: That values are returned in alphabetical or numeric order whenever rows are read from the table
That all values in a column or set of columns are distinct across the table
That every row supplies a non-NULL value for the constrained column or column set
That new rows receive sequential numeric identifiers automatically when they are inserted
explanation: Unlike PRIMARY KEY, a UNIQUE column can contain multiple NULLs in most databases.

text: What are the ACID properties?
options: Automated, Consistent, Integrated, Distributed — design goals for coordinating data across services
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — guarantees for reliable transaction processing
Atomic, Cached, Indexed, Durable — characteristics describing how database pages are stored and retrieved
Available, Consistent, Isolated, Distributed — guarantees that every replicated system should provide
explanation: Isolation levels from READ UNCOMMITTED to SERIALIZABLE trade performance for consistency guarantees.

text: What is a deadlock in a database?
options: A condition where a query exceeds its permitted execution time and the database cancels it
Two or more transactions each holding locks the other needs, causing them to wait indefinitely
A condition where two transactions attempt to insert the same primary key and one operation is rejected
A condition where the optimizer reads every row because no suitable index exists for the requested predicate
explanation: DBMSs detect deadlocks and roll back one victim. Design to acquire locks in a consistent order to avoid them.

text: What is a materialised view?
options: A materialised view is a logical query definition evaluated whenever rows are selected, without storing its result persistently
A database object storing a querys result physically on disk, refreshed periodically, unlike a regular view computed on access
A materialised view is an automatically indexed table that updates immediately after every change to its underlying relations
A materialised view is a temporary result set held in memory for one transaction and discarded when that transaction ends
explanation: Materialised views speed up expensive aggregation queries but introduce staleness and refresh overhead.

text: What is the N+1 query problem?
options: Fetching one record and then issuing a single additional query for every unrelated table, regardless of how many records exist
Fetching N records then issuing N additional queries for related data — solved with eager loading or JOINs
The N+1 problem occurs when N separate transactions each retrieve one row, followed by one query that combines their results
Running one query per field of a record and then N more queries to validate the resulting schema
explanation: ORMs make N+1 easy to introduce accidentally. Use query profiling or logging to detect it in development.

text: What does MVCC provide?
options: MVCC maintains several synchronized database replicas so every transaction can read from a different server without waiting
Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot allowing reads and writes to proceed without blocking each other
MVCC allows multiple primary nodes to accept conflicting writes and resolves them later through replication
MVCC provides a single current row image protected by exclusive locks, forcing readers to wait for writers
explanation: PostgreSQL uses MVCC natively. Dead tuples accumulate and must be reclaimed by the VACUUM process.

text: What is query plan caching and how can it cause problems?
options: The database caches result sets rather than execution plans, so repeated queries can skip execution but may return stale rows
The database caches compiled execution plans for reuse; stale plans become suboptimal when data distributions change
Plan caching stores only parsed SQL text and never compiled strategies, causing syntax checks to be repeated for every execution
Cached plans are rebuilt for every execution and therefore cannot become inefficient when parameter values or distributions change
explanation: Force a recompile or use query hints when a cached plan causes regressions after statistics update.

text: What is a query parameter in FastAPI?
options: A value stored in the request body and mapped to a Pydantic field before the endpoint function is called
A parameter passed in the URL query string (?key=value) declared as function arguments not present in the path
A metadata option on a route that changes how FastAPI constructs the URL and matches incoming paths
A value extracted from HTTP headers and passed to the endpoint as authentication or content-negotiation data
explanation: FastAPI automatically reads function parameters not in the path as query parameters, with optional defaults.

text: What does DNS stand for and what is its purpose?
options: Domain Name System — translates domain names to IP addresses
Dynamic Network Service — assigns IPs
Data Node Selector — routes packets
Distributed Name Server — encrypts traffic
explanation: DNS is often called the phone book of the internet, mapping human-readable names like google.com to IP addresses.

text: Which AWS service automates infrastructure provisioning using templates?
options: CloudFormation
CloudWatch
IAM
Lambda
explanation: Runs containers without managing servers.

text: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
explanation: Port 80 is HTTP, port 443 is HTTPS, port 22 is SSH, and port 21 is FTP.

text: Which device connects different networks and directs traffic between them?
options: Switch
Hub
Router
Repeater
explanation: Routers operate at Layer 3, forwarding packets based on IP routing tables between different networks.

text: What does DHCP do?
options: Encrypts packets and connection metadata before transmission, preventing unauthorized devices from inspecting network traffic
Automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways, and DNS servers to devices on a network
Translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses by querying authoritative and recursive DNS servers
Selects next-hop routes and forwards packets between separate networks according to destination address information
explanation: Without DHCP, each device would need a manually configured static IP address.

text: What does the OSI model describe?
options: A physical networking specification defining cable types, signaling methods, connectors, and transmission characteristics
A seven-layer conceptual framework for network communication from Physical to Application
A set of algorithms for exchanging reachability information and selecting paths between independent networks
A software development architecture organizing programs into reusable modules, interfaces, and execution components
explanation: The layers from bottom to top: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

text: What is bandwidth?
options: The propagation velocity of an electrical or optical signal through a cable, typically expressed as a fraction of light speed
The maximum rate of data transfer across a network path measured in bits per second
The elapsed delay required for a packet to travel across a network path and return a response to the sender
The largest amount of data that a single network packet can carry without being fragmented during transmission
explanation: Bandwidth determines throughput capacity; latency determines delay. High bandwidth does not mean low latency.

text: What is ARP?
options: Domain Name System — resolves hostnames into IP addresses by querying recursive resolvers and authoritative name servers
Address Resolution Protocol — maps an IP address to a MAC address on a local network
Border Gateway Protocol — exchanges route advertisements between autonomous systems and selects paths using policy attributes
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — automatically provides address configuration and other network parameters to requesting clients
explanation: ARP broadcasts a query asking who has a target IP; the owner responds with its MAC address.

text: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
options: TCP is connectionless and best-effort, while UDP establishes sessions with acknowledgments, ordering, and retransmission for reliable delivery
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable with ordering and retransmission; UDP is connectionless and faster with no delivery guarantee
TCP and UDP both guarantee ordered delivery, but TCP uses datagrams while UDP maintains a persistent connection for flow control
UDP is connection-oriented and reliable with congestion control; TCP is connectionless and faster, without retransmission guarantees
explanation: TCP suits reliable applications like HTTP and email; UDP suits latency-sensitive ones like DNS, VoIP, and video streaming.

text: What is the difference between a hub and a switch?
options: A hub and a switch are equivalent devices that forward every received frame to all connected ports
A hub broadcasts frames to all ports; a switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the correct port
A switch broadcasts every frame to all ports, while a hub uses learned MAC-address tables to choose destinations
Hubs are always faster because they forward traffic immediately without spending time learning MAC addresses
explanation: Switches operate at Layer 2 and build a MAC address table; hubs are purely Layer 1 repeaters.

text: What is the purpose of TTL in an IP packet?
options: To specify the maximum packet size carried across a network path, allowing routers to fragment oversized packets
To limit packet lifetime by decrementing at each router hop; packets are dropped when TTL reaches zero preventing routing loops
To indicate packet priority for congestion handling, causing routers to forward high-TTL traffic before other packets
To store timestamps at each router hop so receivers can calculate the total transit time through the network
explanation: traceroute exploits TTL expiry to map network hops by sending probes with incrementing TTL values.

text: What is a VLAN?
options: A type of VPN that creates an encrypted virtual connection between devices located on separate physical networks
A logical partition of a physical network at Layer 2, grouping devices into separate broadcast domains regardless of physical location
A virtual network interface card that provides a software-based Ethernet adapter for an operating system
A wireless network type that separates radio clients into independent channels using different access-point identifiers
explanation: VLANs are configured on managed switches using IEEE 802.1Q tagging and improve security and traffic management.

text: What is OSPF?
options: An exterior routing protocol that exchanges reachability information between separate autonomous systems across the internet
An interior gateway protocol using Dijkstra shortest-path-first algorithm for routing within an autonomous system
A DNS protocol that discovers authoritative name servers and distributes domain records between network resolvers
A tunnelling protocol that encapsulates packets inside another protocol to connect remote networks over an IP link
explanation: OSPF converges quickly after topology changes and supports variable-length subnet masking.

text: What is FastAPI's dependency injection system?
options: A package-management feature that installs shared database, authentication, and configuration components for routes
A mechanism using Depends() to inject reusable logic (DB sessions, auth, config) into route handlers
A class-based view pattern that creates reusable controller objects and dispatches requests to their methods
A middleware layer that wraps every request globally and supplies shared services before route processing begins
explanation: Depends() injects dependencies declared as function parameters, supporting nested dependencies, shared state, and lifespan management.

text: What is anycast addressing?
options: A broadcast type that delivers one packet to every host on a subnet, regardless of topology or the host's network distance
Routing traffic to the topologically nearest node sharing the same IP address, used by DNS roots and CDNs
IPv6-only multicast that sends traffic to a subscribed group of interfaces, with routers replicating packets along the delivery tree
DHCP addressing that assigns temporary IP configurations to clients based on lease duration, relay information, and address availability
explanation: Anycast improves performance and resilience — if one anycast node fails, traffic automatically routes to the next nearest.

text: What is the QUIC protocol?
options: A DNS protocol that runs name resolution over UDP, compresses recursive queries, and uses multiplexed responses to reduce lookup latency
A UDP-based transport used in HTTP/3 that reduces connection latency and eliminates TCP head-of-line blocking
An improved TCP transport that preserves TCP's packet-ordering behavior while adding encrypted headers and a faster three-way connection handshake
An application-layer protocol that replaces HTTP by defining request methods, resource formats, and browser semantics directly over ordinary UDP datagrams
explanation: QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 into the handshake, reducing connection setup from 2 RTT (TCP+TLS) to 1 or 0 RTT.

text: What is a CDN?
options: A type of DNS that stores replicated domain records at regional resolvers and selects the fastest authoritative response for each requesting client
A geographically distributed network of servers caching content close to users, reducing latency and origin server load
A VPN service that establishes encrypted tunnels between users and regional gateways, concealing source addresses and improving access to distant websites
A load balancer type that distributes live application sessions among backend servers but does not cache static objects or serve content from edge locations
explanation: CDNs also provide DDoS mitigation, TLS termination, and WAF capabilities at the network edge.

text: What is a GRE tunnel?
options: A VPN encryption standard — applying cryptographic protection to IP payloads and negotiating secure tunnels between remote networks
Generic Routing Encapsulation — encapsulating packets inside IP packets to create a virtual point-to-point link between networks
An MPLS variant — assigning provider labels to forwarded packets so separate customer sites share a virtual routed path
A BGP extension — advertising tunnel endpoints and encapsulation attributes so an autonomous system can exchange routes across providers
explanation: GRE itself is not encrypted. It is commonly combined with IPsec to create encrypted VPN tunnels.

text: What is Microsoft Azure?
options: An operating system — managing local hardware, applications, accounts, and system services on a computer or server
A cloud computing platform providing IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS services globally
An on-premises data center product — combining server, storage, and networking hardware into a privately operated facility
A programming language — providing syntax, libraries, and runtime tools for building applications across supported operating systems
explanation: Azure is Microsofts public cloud, competing with AWS and GCP, offering 200+ services across compute, storage, AI, and more.

text: What is an Azure Virtual Machine?
options: A container service — packaging an application and its dependencies into an isolated environment that shares the host kernel
An on-demand scalable compute resource providing a virtualised OS environment in Azure
A serverless function — executing short event-driven code without exposing a persistent virtualised operating system to the user
A managed database service — providing hosted relational storage, automated backups, and query processing without a customer-managed OS
explanation: Azure VMs support Windows and Linux. You choose the size and OS image and are responsible for patching.

text: What is an Azure Resource Group?
options: A billing tier — defining included quotas, pricing discounts, and service limits applied to a customer’s Azure consumption
A logical container holding related Azure resources for unified management, deployment, and lifecycle control
A virtual network segment — isolating subnets, routes, and private addresses so selected Azure resources can communicate securely
A subscription type — determining service eligibility, geographic availability, and administrative permissions for an Azure account
explanation: Deleting a resource group deletes all resources within it — useful for tearing down environments cleanly.

text: What is an Azure Subscription?
options: An email newsletter service — delivering periodic product announcements, service updates, and promotional messages to registered recipients
A billing container granting access to Azure services and tracking resource usage and costs
A VM disk image — containing an operating system and applications that can be copied onto virtual machine storage during deployment
A virtual network — defining subnets, address spaces, routing rules, and private connectivity for resources within an Azure environment
explanation: Organisations use management groups to apply governance policies across multiple subscriptions.

text: What is the purpose of Azure Monitor?
options: Provisioning and configuring virtual machines, including image selection, sizing, networking, and automated deployment workflows
Collecting, analysing, and acting on telemetry from Azure and on-premises environments for monitoring and alerting
Managing identities, authentication policies, and access permissions for users, applications, and administrators across tenants
Designing and routing private virtual networks, subnets, gateways, and traffic rules for Azure-hosted workloads
explanation: Azure Monitor feeds data into Log Analytics workspaces and can trigger alerts or auto-remediation via Action Groups.

text: What is an Availability Zone in Azure?
options: A broad geographic area containing multiple Azure regions and providing a boundary for data residency and service availability
A physically separate data center within an Azure region with independent power, cooling, and networking for high availability
A commercial subscription level that determines quotas, billing rates, support options, and access to selected Azure services
A logical container for grouping related Azure resources, applying tags, and controlling role-based access permissions
explanation: Deploying across zones protects against single data center failure. Not all Azure regions have availability zones.

text: What is a FastAPI middleware and how is it used?
options: A route decorator that maps an HTTP method and URL path to the function handling a request
Code that runs before and after each request (timing, CORS, logging) added with @app.middleware('http') or add_middleware()
A Pydantic validator that checks incoming fields and transforms their values before the endpoint executes
A background task runner that defers application work until after the HTTP response has been returned
explanation: Middleware wraps all requests. Common uses: request timing, adding CORS headers, logging, and exception handling.

text: What is the purpose of Terraform state?
options: Track resources managed by Terraform
Encrypt secrets
Backup data
Monitor logs
explanation: Multiple backends supported.

text: What is an Azure Function?
options: A configurable virtual machine size providing a selected number of CPU cores, memory, disks, and network interfaces
A serverless compute service running event-triggered code without managing infrastructure, scaling to zero when idle
A managed repository for storing, scanning, and distributing container images to deployment tools and compute services
A database-side routine that executes predefined SQL logic when called by an application or database event
explanation: Azure Functions support HTTP triggers, timer triggers, queue triggers, and blob triggers among others.

text: What is Azure ExpressRoute?
options: A globally distributed content delivery service that caches static files at edge locations to reduce download latency for internet users
A dedicated private connection between on-premises networks and Azure, bypassing the public internet for lower latency and higher reliability
A managed VPN endpoint that encrypts site-to-site or point-to-site tunnels over the public internet between networks and Azure
A regional Layer 4 traffic distribution service that balances inbound connections across healthy virtual machines and backend instances
explanation: ExpressRoute offers 50 Mbps to 100 Gbps bandwidth with SLA-backed connectivity via partner network providers.

text: What is Azure Service Bus?
options: A compute platform for running scalable virtual machines and container workloads, with managed capacity, images, networking, and automated instance provisioning
A fully managed enterprise message broker with queues and publish-subscribe topics for decoupled async application integration
A managed observability service that collects metrics, logs, traces, and alerts from applications and infrastructure across an Azure subscription
A connectivity service for configuring virtual networks, private endpoints, routing rules, and secure links between Azure resources and on-premises sites
explanation: Service Bus is for enterprise messaging with ordering, dead-lettering, and sessions. Azure Storage Queues are simpler and cheaper for basic scenarios.

text: What is Azure DevOps?
options: A cloud-hosted operating system that manages application execution, hardware resources, user sessions, and updates across developer workstations
A suite of developer services including Boards, Repos, Pipelines, Test Plans, and Artifacts for planning, building, and delivering software
A monitoring and observability tool that collects application logs, infrastructure metrics, traces, dashboards, and alerts from production environments
A private container registry that stores, scans, tags, and replicates OCI images for deployment to Azure Kubernetes Service and other runtimes
explanation: Azure DevOps Pipelines support CI/CD for any language, deploying to Azure or any on-premises or cloud target.

text: What is Azure Policy used for?
options: Managing invoices, budgets, subscriptions, and spending alerts to control cloud costs and allocate charges across teams and projects
Defining and enforcing organisational standards, and assessing compliance across Azure resources at scale
Creating users, groups, service principals, and authentication rules, then granting them access through directory and sign-in configurations
A network configuration service that creates virtual networks, subnets, routes, firewall rules, and private links for Azure resources
explanation: Policies can Audit, Deny, or DeployIfNotExists. Assign at management group scope to enforce governance across all subscriptions.

text: What is Azure Front Door?
options: A specialized virtual machine size optimized for serving web applications, with built-in global routing, edge caching, and automatic failover capabilities
A global Layer 7 load balancer providing intelligent traffic routing, SSL offloading, WAF, and caching at the network edge
A managed DNS hosting service that resolves domain names and returns records for clients, without performing application-layer traffic inspection or caching
A regional API gateway focused exclusively on authenticating requests, transforming payloads, applying quotas, and routing calls to backend services
explanation: Front Door uses Microsofts global WAN with Anycast for low-latency routing to the nearest healthy origin.

text: What is the Azure Landing Zone concept?
options: A collection of recommended virtual machine deployment patterns defining image standards, sizing guidance, and autoscaling rules for application teams
A pre-configured governed Azure environment following the Cloud Adoption Framework — subscriptions, networking, identity, and policy ready for workloads
A physically isolated Azure datacenter zone within a region, designed to protect workloads from failures in other availability zones
A predefined Azure storage configuration specifying replication, performance, encryption, and retention settings for application data
explanation: Landing zones accelerate adoption by providing enterprise-grade scaffolding before workloads are deployed.

text: What is Azure Traffic Manager?
options: A Kubernetes container orchestration service scheduling workloads, managing clusters, scaling pods, and exposing applications through ingress controllers
A DNS-based global load balancer distributing traffic across endpoints using routing methods like priority, weighted, performance, and geographic
A globally distributed content delivery network caching static and dynamic content at edge locations and accelerating downloads for clients
An Azure application gateway operating only at the HTTP layer, terminating TLS and applying WAF rules within a single region
explanation: Traffic Manager works at DNS level and does not proxy traffic, so it cannot inspect or modify HTTP payloads.

text: What is the difference between Azure AD B2B and B2C?
options: B2B is a consumer identity platform for public applications, while B2C invites business partners into your workforce tenant through guest accounts and collaboration policies
B2B federates external partner or employee identities into your tenant; B2C is a customer identity solution supporting social and local accounts for consumer apps
B2B and B2C are equivalent directory features; both primarily support employee sign-in and differ only in licensing, branding, and the number of applications
B2B is designed for consumer registration with social providers, while B2C is intended for partner collaboration using guest users in an organization's tenant
explanation: B2B uses guest user accounts in your directory; B2C has its own separate directory designed for millions of external consumers.

text: How do you handle request validation errors in FastAPI?
options: Manually with try/except around every endpoint, converting each Pydantic failure into a response chosen by the developer
FastAPI automatically returns 422 Unprocessable Entity with a JSON body detailing which fields failed Pydantic validation
Using a custom exception handler registered for validation errors, rather than relying on FastAPI's default JSON response
Returning a 400 response manually from each route whenever an input field cannot be parsed or does not satisfy constraints
explanation: Pydantic validation errors are automatically caught and returned as structured 422 responses with field-level error details.

text: What does git init do?
options: Downloads a remote repository and checks out its default branch locally
Initialises a new Git repository in the current directory
Records all current file changes as the first commit in the repository
Creates a new remote-tracking branch from the current repository configuration
explanation: git init creates a hidden .git folder that stores all version history and configuration for the repository.

text: What does git status show?
options: Displays the complete sequence of commits and their messages for the current branch
The current state of the working directory and staging area compared to the last commit
Lists every local and remote branch with its latest commit reference
Reports the configured remote repositories and their fetch and push URLs
explanation: git status shows untracked files, modified files, and files staged for the next commit.

text: What is the staging area in Git?
options: A server-side location where shared repository changes are stored
A preparation zone where you place changes before committing them
A permanent record containing the files from the most recent commit
A named pointer that selects one line of development in the repository
explanation: The staging area (index) lets you precisely control which changes go into the next commit.

text: What does git add . do?
options: Creates a commit containing every modified and untracked file in the repository
Stages all changes in the current directory and subdirectories for the next commit
Sends all staged and committed changes to the configured remote repository
Creates a new branch containing the current files and staged changes
explanation: Use git add -p to stage changes interactively, choosing specific hunks rather than everything.

text: What is a Git branch?
options: A complete independent copy of the repository with its own commit history
A lightweight movable pointer to a commit, enabling parallel lines of development
A server-hosted repository used to exchange commits with local clones
A permanent name attached to one specific commit for later reference
explanation: Branches are cheap to create and delete in Git because they are just 41-byte files pointing to a commit hash.

text: What does git pull do?
options: Uploads local commits and working-tree changes to the configured remote repository
Fetches changes from the remote and merges them into the current branch
Creates and switches to a new branch based on the current commit
Displays the commit history retrieved from the current remote repository
explanation: git pull is shorthand for git fetch followed by git merge. Use git pull --rebase for a cleaner history.

text: What is a commit hash?
options: A human-readable name that points to a branch in the repository
A unique SHA-1 identifier for each commit in the repository history
A marker inserted into files when two branches cannot be merged
The network address used to locate the repository on a remote server
explanation: Hashes ensure integrity — any change to a commit produces a completely different hash, making tampering detectable.

text: What does git stash do?
options: Deletes all uncommitted changes from the working tree so they cannot be restored later
Temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch context, then restores them later
Creates a temporary commit on a hidden branch and removes the changes from the working tree
Resets the staging area while leaving all modified files in the working tree unchanged
explanation: git stash pop restores the most recent stash. Use git stash list to see all stashed states.

text: What is a fast-forward merge?
options: A type of merge conflict that occurs when two branches modify the same lines before integration
A merge where the target branch pointer simply advances to the source commit because no divergent history exists
A forced push that moves the remote branch pointer without checking whether commits would be lost
A rebase variant that combines multiple commits while preserving their original parent relationships
explanation: Fast-forward merges produce no merge commit. Use --no-ff to always create a merge commit for auditing purposes.

text: What is git revert vs git reset?
options: git revert and git reset are identical: each removes the selected commit from history while leaving the working tree unchanged
git revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous commit (safe for shared history); git reset moves the branch pointer back (rewrites history)
git reset is safer for shared history because it records an undo commit, while git revert only moves the local branch pointer and discards commits
git revert rewrites history by deleting the original commit and its descendants, while git reset preserves them through a new inverse commit
explanation: Never use git reset --hard on commits already pushed to a shared branch — use git revert instead.

text: What is a .gitignore file?
options: A file defining the standard structure and placeholder text for commit messages
A file listing patterns for files and directories Git should not track
A configuration specifying which branches may receive pushes and required review checks
A script Git runs automatically during selected repository operations and lifecycle events
explanation: Use global .gitignore for editor temp files and per-repo .gitignore for build artefacts and secrets.

text: What is a merge conflict?
options: A situation where Git rejects a push because the remote branch contains commits missing from the local branch
When two branches have made different changes to the same part of a file and Git cannot automatically reconcile them
An error indicating that a commit referenced by the current branch is missing from the repository history
A checkout state in which the working directory is linked to a commit that no longer exists on any branch
explanation: Resolve conflicts by editing the conflict markers, staging the resolved files, and completing the merge with git commit.

text: What does git tag do?
options: Creates a new branch pointer from the current commit and switches the working directory to that branch
Marks a specific commit with a human-readable name, typically used for release versions
Temporarily saves modified and staged files so the working directory can be restored later
Moves the current branch pointer backward to an earlier commit and discards subsequent history
explanation: Annotated tags (git tag -a v1.0 -m message) store extra metadata. Lightweight tags are just a named pointer.

text: What web server does FastAPI use in production?
options: Gunicorn alone, used as the application server without Uvicorn or another ASGI server
Uvicorn (ASGI server) or Hypercorn, often with Gunicorn as the process manager
Apache HTTP Server, using its traditional WSGI integration to run FastAPI applications in production
uWSGI, configured as FastAPI's standard ASGI server for production deployments
explanation: FastAPI is an ASGI framework. Uvicorn runs the async event loop; Gunicorn manages multiple Uvicorn worker processes for production.

text: What is a Git hook?
options: A rule that determines how Git combines conflicting changes when histories from different branches are merged
A script triggered automatically at specific Git lifecycle events such as pre-commit, pre-push, or post-merge
A local name that stores the URL and connection settings for a repository hosted on another server
A repository policy that restricts direct pushes and requires reviews or automated checks before merging
explanation: Pre-commit hooks can enforce linting or tests before a commit is recorded locally.

text: What is interactive rebase used for?
options: Publishing the current branch history to a remote repository, including uploading new commits and updating its remote-tracking reference
Editing, squashing, reordering, or dropping commits in the current branch history before sharing
Combining the current branch with another branch by creating a merge commit and resolving any resulting file conflicts
Downloading new commits and branch references from a remote repository without changing the files or commits on the current branch
explanation: git rebase -i HEAD~5 opens an editor to manipulate the last 5 commits. Used to clean up feature branches before a PR.

text: What is a shallow clone?
options: A clone configured without local branches, retaining only a detached checkout of the selected commit and no branch references
A clone with truncated history (--depth N) downloading only the most recent N commits, saving time and disk space
A clone configured to omit all tag references and annotated release metadata while retaining the complete history of every commit
A clone created in a temporary directory for testing, with the repository automatically deleted after the checkout operation finishes
explanation: Shallow clones are common in CI systems where full history is unnecessary and clone speed matters.

text: What is the Gitflow branching strategy?
options: A workflow that keeps one permanent production branch and creates temporary branches for every change, integrating each directly after review
A workflow with long-lived main and develop branches plus short-lived feature, release, and hotfix branches
A workflow that uses only short-lived feature branches, merging them immediately into the production branch without separate release or hotfix lines
A workflow that develops directly on a single trunk, using automated testing and frequent integration instead of long-lived release branches
explanation: Gitflow suits release-based software. Trunk-based development with feature flags is often preferred for continuous delivery.

text: What is Terraform?
options: A containerisation tool that builds images, creates isolated runtime environments, and deploys application containers across multiple hosts
An open-source Infrastructure as Code tool that provisions and manages infrastructure using declarative configuration files
A server configuration management tool that connects to machines and imperatively installs packages, edits files, and starts services
A cloud monitoring service that collects infrastructure metrics, evaluates alert rules, and displays operational dashboards for deployed resources
explanation: Terraform uses HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) and supports 1000+ providers across all major clouds and services.

text: What does terraform plan do?
options: Applies the configuration changes to infrastructure immediately, without first displaying a proposed execution plan
Shows what changes Terraform will make to infrastructure without actually making them
Deletes every resource tracked in the current state file and removes its associated infrastructure
Initialises required providers and downloads their plugins before validating the configuration
explanation: Always review the plan output carefully before running apply. Use -out to save the plan for later.

text: What does terraform apply do?
options: Generates a proposed execution plan showing potential infrastructure changes without applying any of them
Executes the planned changes to create, update, or delete infrastructure resources
Terminates and removes every resource managed by the current configuration without prompting for changes
Reformats Terraform configuration files to match the canonical style used by the Terraform language
explanation: terraform apply prompts for confirmation unless you pass -auto-approve or apply a saved plan file.

text: What is Terraform state?
options: The generated execution plan showing the actions Terraform intends to take during the next apply operation
A file (terraform.tfstate) recording the current known state of all managed resources so Terraform can detect drift
The provider configuration containing credentials, regions, endpoints, and feature settings used for API access
An isolated workspace preference that selects which environment Terraform should target during execution
explanation: State maps your configuration to real-world resources. Never edit it manually — use terraform state commands.

text: What is a Terraform variable?
options: A declaration describing the kind and arguments of an infrastructure object Terraform should create
A parameterised input allowing configurations to be reused with different values
A provider extension that translates Terraform configuration into requests against an external service API
An entry in Terraform state that records an existing managed object and its attributes
explanation: Variables are declared with variable blocks and can be set via .tfvars files, environment variables, or command-line flags.

text: What is the purpose of terraform fmt?
options: Executes the configuration and creates, updates, or deletes the declared infrastructure resources
Automatically formats Terraform configuration files to follow the canonical style
Checks configuration for syntactic and structural errors and reports invalid arguments
Calculates and displays the actions Terraform would take without changing infrastructure
explanation: Run terraform fmt in CI to enforce consistent formatting across your team.

text: What is remote state in Terraform?
options: Storing the state file only on the operator’s local machine, where Terraform reads and updates it during each run
Storing the state file in a shared backend (e.g. S3, Azure Blob, GCS, Terraform Cloud) enabling team collaboration and state locking
A read-only representation of infrastructure returned by a backend, which Terraform can inspect but never modify
A workspace capability that creates isolated state files without requiring shared storage, locking, or backend configuration
explanation: Remote state with locking prevents concurrent applies that would corrupt the state file.

text: Which option is a valid Scala function definition with typed parameters and return type?
options: def add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b
def add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int = a + b
def add(a Int, b Int): Int = a + b
function add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b
explanation: Scala functions can be defined with def, parameter types after parameter names, and a return type after a colon. The body follows an equals sign.

text: What is a Terraform workspace?
options: A reusable collection of resources, variables, and outputs that packages a common infrastructure design for callers
A named state file allowing multiple environments (dev, staging, prod) to be managed from the same configuration
A shared storage service that persists state remotely and coordinates locking between concurrent Terraform operations
A provider constraint that selects which release of a cloud integration Terraform should download and use
explanation: Workspaces are useful for simple multi-environment setups, but many teams prefer separate root modules per environment for stronger isolation.

text: What is the for_each meta-argument?
options: A numeric repetition argument that creates a fixed number of resource instances addressed by consecutive index values
Creates multiple resource instances from a map or set, with each instance independently addressable
A dependency mechanism that forces every resource in a module to wait for all resources in another module
A replacement operation that removes existing instances before recreating them from the revised configuration
explanation: for_each is preferred over count when instances have unique identities, as removing one does not shift the indices of others.

text: What is terraform validate?
options: Applies the configuration changes to infrastructure and creates or updates resources through the configured providers
Checks that the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent without accessing providers
Generates an execution plan showing proposed resource changes and provider operations without applying them
Reformats Terraform configuration files into canonical syntax and standard indentation without validating their meaning
explanation: terraform validate is fast and can be run offline. Use it in CI before running plan.

text: What is a data source in Terraform?
options: A managed resource declaration that creates and updates infrastructure through a configured provider during an apply
A way to read information from an existing resource or API without managing it, e.g. looking up an AMI ID
A typed input value supplied to a module, with a declared type, description, and optional default value
A provider configuration block that specifies credentials, regions, endpoints, and settings for API access
explanation: Data sources are declared with data blocks and are refreshed during terraform plan and apply.

text: What is the moved block in Terraform?
options: A resource alias that gives one declaration an alternate name while preserving its original address in the state
A configuration block that tells Terraform a resource was renamed or moved to a module, avoiding destroy-recreate during refactoring
A workspace command that transfers resources between separate workspaces without changing their configuration addresses
A provider migration tool that upgrades managed resources and converts their state to a newer provider schema
explanation: The moved block was introduced in Terraform 1.1 and is the safe way to refactor resource addresses without destroying infrastructure.

text: What is Terragrunt?
options: A Terraform provider that exposes Terragrunt-specific resources for configuring modules, state backends, and deployment dependencies
A thin wrapper around Terraform that adds DRY configuration, remote state management, and dependency ordering across multiple Terraform modules
A Terraform alternative that uses its own declarative language and state engine to provision infrastructure independently
A testing framework that executes Terraform modules against temporary environments and verifies their resulting infrastructure
explanation: Terragrunt is popular in large organisations to manage many Terraform root modules without duplicating backend configuration.

text: What is the purpose of lifecycle blocks in Terraform?
options: Provider configuration settings that control credentials, regions, endpoints, and plugin initialization for each resource
Controlling resource lifecycle behaviours: prevent_destroy, create_before_destroy, and ignore_changes
State management controls that determine how snapshots are stored, locked, refreshed, and recovered during operations
Module versioning metadata that selects released module sources and controls compatibility between nested configurations
explanation: create_before_destroy is essential for resources like load balancers where downtime during replacement is unacceptable.

text: What is a Terraform provider alias?
options: A named module identifier that selects which reusable module implementation Terraform should load
A way to use the same provider with different configurations in the same root module, e.g. two AWS regions
A workspace-specific configuration that creates an isolated state history for each deployment environment
A resource reference syntax that lets one Terraform object read attributes from another object
explanation: Provider aliases are declared with alias in the provider block and referenced with provider = aws.us-west in resource blocks.

text: What is the Terraform Registry?
options: A remote state storage service that locks Terraform state files and preserves historical state versions
A public repository of providers and modules that can be referenced directly in Terraform configurations
A hosted automation platform that runs Terraform plans and applies as part of a repository-based workflow
A rules service that evaluates Terraform plans and blocks resources violating organizational compliance requirements
explanation: The Registry at registry.terraform.io hosts official, verified, and community providers and modules.

text: What does CI stand for in CI/CD?
options: Container Integration — connecting application containers to shared registries and service discovery systems automatically
Continuous Integration — automatically building and testing code on every commit
Cloud Infrastructure — provisioning and configuring cloud resources whenever a repository change is submitted
Code Inspection — reviewing source changes for defects and security problems before they reach a release branch
explanation: CI catches integration bugs early by running builds and tests on every push rather than waiting for a manual release cycle.

text: What is Cloud Run?
options: A batch compute service that queues container jobs and runs them on provisioned worker machines until completion
A fully managed serverless platform running containerised applications that automatically scales to zero when not in use
A Kubernetes control plane that schedules pods, manages cluster nodes, and exposes services through ingress resources
A virtual machine orchestrator that creates instance groups and adjusts their capacity according to application demand
explanation: Cloud Run builds on Knative and charges only for the CPU and memory used during request processing.

text: In Scala, what does the type Unit most closely represent?
options: A method that completes without a meaningful result
A value that can contain any possible Scala object
A collection that contains exactly one element
A numeric type used for fractional calculations
explanation: Unit is Scala's equivalent of a void-like result type. It indicates that an expression or method completes primarily for its side effects.

text: What does echo do in Bash?
options: Repeats the last command
Prints text or variable values to standard output
Reads user input
Copies files
explanation: Use echo -n to suppress the trailing newline, or printf for more control over formatting.

text: What is a build artifact?
options: The original application source files and version-controlled configuration that a build consumes before producing outputs
The output of a build step — a compiled binary, Docker image, or packaged archive — stored for use in later pipeline stages
A machine-readable summary of test cases, assertions, coverage measurements, and pass-or-fail results generated by the pipeline
A chronological record of commands, warnings, errors, and diagnostic messages emitted while a build or deployment runs
explanation: Artifacts should be immutable: the same artifact built from a commit should be deployed to every environment.

text: What is a webhook in CI/CD context?
options: A network integration point that exposes an internal listener for accepting arbitrary connections from external services
An HTTP callback that a source control system sends to a CI server when events like pushes or pull requests occur
An executable deployment script that packages an application and copies its files directly onto the production hosts
An automated test execution service that discovers test files, runs assertions, and reports failures back to developers
explanation: Webhooks allow GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket to trigger pipeline runs automatically on code events.

text: What are pipeline stages?
options: Named Git branches that isolate parallel lines of development and preserve separate histories for features, releases, and fixes
Logical divisions of a pipeline (e.g. build, test, deploy) where each stage must pass before the next begins
Build targets that identify individual compilation outputs, dependency graphs, and packaging commands within a project configuration
Read-only filesystem layers created by a container build, each recording one image instruction and its resulting file changes
explanation: Stages provide clear separation of concerns and enable parallel execution and fast-fail behaviour.

text: What is a deployment environment in CI/CD?
options: A source code location such as a repository, branch, or commit reference from which the pipeline retrieves application files
A target infrastructure tier such as development, staging, or production that a pipeline deploys to
A remote image repository that authenticates clients and stores versioned container images for later pulls and deployments
A temporary storage area that preserves downloaded dependencies and intermediate files to accelerate subsequent pipeline builds
explanation: Environment-specific secrets and approval gates control which pipelines can deploy to sensitive tiers like production.

text: What is a matrix build in CI?
options: A process that scans each build for known vulnerabilities and reports security findings before release
Running the same pipeline steps across multiple combinations of variables (e.g. OS and language version) simultaneously
A workflow that divides compilation, testing, packaging, and deployment into sequential stages with approval gates
A deployment technique that publishes the same release to several production targets at the same time
explanation: Matrix builds ensure compatibility across environments without maintaining separate pipeline files.

text: What are pipeline secrets and how should they be managed?
options: Sensitive values written directly into source files or scripts so every pipeline step can read them without external lookup
Sensitive values like API keys injected at runtime from a secrets manager or CI platform vault, never stored in code
Values defined in version-controlled environment configuration and referenced by jobs during each pipeline execution
Credentials kept in committed configuration files with access controlled only through repository permissions
explanation: Use GitHub Encrypted Secrets, HashiCorp Vault, or AWS Secrets Manager — never commit credentials to version control.

text: What is a blue-green deployment?
options: A branching model that keeps separate stable and experimental Git lines, then merges validated changes into the release branch after review and integration testing
Running two identical production environments; traffic switches from the live (blue) to the new (green) release instantly, enabling zero-downtime deploys and fast rollback
A release technique that sends a small, controlled percentage of production traffic to the new version while monitoring errors before expanding its audience
A release technique that replaces old application instances with new ones gradually in controlled batches while keeping the service available throughout the update
explanation: Blue-green keeps the old environment alive for fast rollback by simply switching traffic back.

text: What is a rolling deployment?
options: Stopping the service and replacing every running instance with the new version during one coordinated maintenance operation
Incrementally replacing instances of the old version with the new version one at a time or in small batches
A deployment model that maintains separate complete environments and switches all user traffic to the newly released environment
A release method that exposes the new version to a small selected group of users before enabling it for everyone
explanation: Rolling deployments are simpler than blue-green but require the new and old versions to be compatible during the transition.

text: What is a Jenkins pipeline?
options: A set of Git branching conventions that specifies how feature, release, and hotfix branches are created and merged
A definition of a Jenkins CI/CD workflow written in Jenkinsfile using declarative or scripted pipeline DSL syntax
A virtual network configuration that lets Docker containers discover one another and communicate over isolated channels
A server or cloud resource selected to receive application artifacts after a build has completed successfully
explanation: Jenkinsfile stored in source control (pipeline as code) makes Jenkins pipelines auditable and reproducible.

text: What is artifact promotion in a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Building a separate environment-specific artifact at each promotion stage, with configuration and compilation repeated for dev, staging, and production
Taking the same immutable artifact built once and promoting it through environments (dev -> staging -> prod) with approval gates
Rebuilding the application independently in every environment so dependencies and settings are resolved differently before each deployment
A release versioning strategy that assigns progressively higher numbers to deployments as they move from development through production
explanation: Build once, deploy many is a core CI/CD principle. Rebuilding per environment risks environment-specific differences.

text: What does declaring an object named Logger create in Scala?
options: A singleton instance that can be accessed by its name
A class requiring new before each method can be called
A mutable collection storing values under string keys
A package containing several automatically generated classes
explanation: An object declaration creates a singleton, meaning Scala provides one instance associated with that name. Its members can be accessed without creating an object with new.

text: What is DORA metrics and why do they matter?
options: A monitoring tool that collects dashboards and alerts about build duration, deployment status, application health, and infrastructure utilization
Four key metrics (Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Change Failure Rate, Time to Restore) that measure software delivery performance
A testing framework that runs unit, integration, and acceptance tests to determine whether a software release meets its functional requirements
A security scan type that checks source code, dependencies, container images, and infrastructure definitions for known vulnerabilities before release
explanation: High-performing teams deploy frequently with short lead times, low failure rates, and fast recovery when things go wrong.

text: What is supply chain security in CI/CD?
options: Protecting physical servers, storage devices, and data-center access controls that host build agents and deployment infrastructure from unauthorized entry
Ensuring the integrity of the entire software delivery pipeline — signed commits, dependency scanning, container image signing, and SBOM generation
