A network security practice that segments pipeline systems with firewalls, private subnets, and access-control rules to restrict communication between services
A deployment gate that requires a designated approver to authorize production releases after automated tests and compliance checks have completed
explanation: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) is a framework for incrementally improving pipeline security posture.

text: What is environment promotion pipelining?
options: A release pattern that sends a newly built application directly to production after a successful build, without intermediate environments or staged validation
A pattern where the same artifact progresses through increasingly production-like environments with automated tests and manual gates at each stage
A source-control strategy that organizes application changes into development, release, and production branches and merges them according to team policies
An observability pattern that compares logs, metrics, and traces from separate deployments while tracking service health across multiple runtime environments
explanation: Promotion pipelines prevent environment-specific surprises and give stakeholders confidence before production release.

text: What is an on-call rotation?
options: A recurring timetable where engineers plan and perform software releases across environments during scheduled windows
A schedule where team members take turns being responsible for responding to incidents and alerts outside business hours
A structured program assigning engineers to attend training sessions and complete operational exercises each quarter
A recurring assignment in which developers take turns reviewing and approving changes before they are merged
explanation: Healthy on-call practices include clear escalation paths, runbooks, and post-incident learning.

text: What is the four golden signals framework?
options: Four logging categories—debug, info, warning, and error—used to classify messages emitted by an application
Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation — the four key metrics for monitoring the health of any service
Four sequential deployment stages—development, testing, staging, and production—used to promote software safely
Four service-level objective categories—availability, latency, throughput, and cost—used to define reliability targets
explanation: Defined in the Google SRE book, the four golden signals are the minimum set to understand service behaviour.

text: What is trunk-based development?
options: A workflow where developers work on long-lived feature branches and merge them only during scheduled release windows
All developers integrate small, frequent commits directly to the main (trunk) branch using feature flags for incomplete features
A branching model that uses dedicated develop, release, and hotfix branches to isolate changes until production release
A release practice that deploys every committed change automatically to production without requiring branch integration
explanation: Trunk-based development enables continuous integration at scale and is correlated with high DORA performance.

text: What is a service mesh and how does it relate to CI/CD?
options: A container networking plugin that assigns pod addresses, configures routes, and enforces network policies between workloads across cluster nodes
Infrastructure layer handling service-to-service communication (mTLS, retries, circuit breaking); enables traffic-based canary deployments in CD pipelines
A centralized observability platform that collects application metrics, visualizes dashboards, and evaluates alerts across distributed services
A centralized secrets manager that encrypts credentials, controls access, and distributes configuration values to applications at runtime
explanation: Istio and Linkerd provide traffic splitting used in progressive delivery tools like Flagger and Argo Rollouts.

text: What is an SLO?
options: A support ticket recording a customer’s reported service problem, priority, assigned owner, and resolution status
Service Level Objective — a target reliability goal expressed as a percentage, e.g. 99.9% of requests return in under 200ms
A service agreement with a customer that specifies compensation, response obligations, and minimum availability commitments
A monitoring alert generated when observed latency or availability crosses a configured threshold for a service
explanation: SLOs are internal targets. SLAs are contractual commitments usually set below the SLO to provide a buffer.

text: What is an SLA?
options: A log aggregation tool that collects, indexes, and searches application events from hosts and containers
Service Level Agreement — a contractual commitment between a service provider and customer defining minimum acceptable reliability
An internal reliability target used by engineering teams without contractual language or customer compensation provisions
A monitoring metric that records actual availability and latency measurements for a service over time
explanation: SLA breaches typically carry financial or other penalties, which is why they are set below internal SLO targets.

text: What is Prometheus?
options: A cloud provider that provisions virtual machines, managed databases, and networking resources across multiple regions
An open-source monitoring and alerting system that scrapes metrics from configured targets and stores them as time-series data
A logging platform that ingests structured events, indexes message fields, and supports searching application logs
A distributed tracing tool that records request spans and visualizes call paths across interconnected services
explanation: Prometheus uses a pull model, scraping metrics from /metrics endpoints, and stores data in its own time-series database.

text: How do you define a route in FastAPI?
options: @app.route('/path') applied to a handler, using a single decorator for every HTTP method
@app.get('/path'), @app.post('/path'), etc. on async or sync functions
app.add_route('/path', handler) called directly, with the handler registered outside decorator syntax
Using a Django-style urls.py file to map URL patterns to FastAPI view functions and class-based controllers
explanation: FastAPI decorators (@app.get, @app.post, @app.put, @app.delete) map HTTP methods to handler functions with automatic parameter parsing.

text: What is a RED metric approach?
options: Availability, Capacity, Failures, and Throughput — four infrastructure metrics for assessing the health of servers and networks
Rate, Errors, Duration — a focused set of request-oriented metrics suitable for monitoring microservices and APIs
Structured, verbose, and searchable event records — a logging strategy for investigating application behaviour over time
Spans, Context, Sampling, and Baggage — a tracing approach for following requests across distributed application components
explanation: RED is complementary to the USE method (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors) which focuses on resource health.

text: What is alerting fatigue?
options: A monitoring condition in which alerts are deliberately reduced so on-call engineers receive only a small number of notifications during each shift
When too many low-quality or non-actionable alerts cause on-call engineers to start ignoring them, increasing the risk of missing critical incidents
A temporary failure in alerting software that prevents notifications from being generated, delivered, or displayed correctly to the on-call team
A documented on-call policy defining who receives operational notifications, how shifts are scheduled, and when incidents must be escalated
explanation: Fix alerting fatigue by making every alert actionable, raising alert thresholds, and eliminating flapping alerts.

text: What is the USE method?
options: A deployment framework for releasing services by measuring rollout utilisation, saturation, and error rates before promoting a new version
Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — a framework for analysing system resource health by examining each resource on these three dimensions
A logging framework that classifies records by their storage utilisation, ingestion saturation, and formatting or delivery errors
A testing method for evaluating application behaviour through representative workloads, injected faults, and assertions about expected results
explanation: USE is most applicable to hardware resources (CPU, memory, disks, network interfaces). RED suits request-driven services.

text: What is a circuit breaker pattern?
options: A physical safety mechanism that interrupts electrical current when excessive load or dangerous conditions are detected in a powered circuit
A resilience pattern that detects failures and short-circuits requests to a failing service, returning errors immediately and allowing the downstream to recover
A load-balancing capability that distributes requests across healthy and unhealthy service instances according to connection counts and routing weights
A retry strategy that repeatedly resubmits failed requests with increasing delays until the downstream service responds successfully or attempts are exhausted
explanation: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures where one slow service exhausts connection pools across many callers.

text: What is Alertmanager in the Prometheus ecosystem?
options: A metrics scraper that periodically discovers Prometheus endpoints, collects time-series samples, and stores them for querying against configured retention limits
A component handling alert routing, deduplication, grouping, and silencing, sending notifications to receivers like PagerDuty or Slack
A dashboard tool that renders Prometheus queries as graphs, tables, and status panels for operators monitoring service health and performance
A service discovery tool that locates application instances through labels, DNS records, or orchestration APIs so monitoring targets can be configured automatically
explanation: Alertmanager separates alert evaluation (Prometheus rules) from notification routing (Alertmanager config).

text: What is chaos engineering?
options: A deliberately unstructured practice of disrupting systems without defined hypotheses, safeguards, or measurements in order to observe whatever failures happen to occur
A disciplined practice of injecting controlled failures into production systems to discover weaknesses before they cause real incidents
A deployment strategy that releases software gradually across environments or user groups, using staged promotion and rollback controls to reduce release risk
A testing framework limited to simulated environments, where predefined test cases verify expected application behaviour without intentionally affecting production systems
explanation: The Simian Army (Netflix) popularised chaos engineering. GameDays are structured chaos experiments run by the team.

text: What is error budget policy?
options: A documented agreement on how engineering teams may spend the infrastructure budget, including approval thresholds, forecasting rules, and cost-reporting responsibilities
A documented agreement on how to respond when the error budget is consumed — typically freezing feature releases and prioritising reliability work
A documented agreement on how customer support handles billing disputes, including refund limits, escalation paths, and invoice correction procedures
A formal definition of the service's availability commitment, including target percentages, measurement exclusions, and contractual remedies
explanation: Error budget policies create alignment between product and engineering teams on when to slow feature delivery.

text: What is a Service Level Indicator (SLI)?
options: A quantitative business-performance measure such as revenue per user or conversion rate, used to evaluate organizational outcomes rather than service behaviour
A carefully defined quantitative measure of a service behaviour relevant to users, used as the numerator in SLO calculations
A software component that collects, stores, and visualises telemetry from applications and infrastructure for operational analysis
A predefined condition on a service metric that triggers an incident notification when observed values cross a configured boundary
explanation: Good SLIs measure things users care about — availability (successful requests / total requests) is the most common.

text: What is observability and how does it differ from monitoring?
options: Two interchangeable names for collecting telemetry and displaying alerts, with no meaningful distinction in whether engineers detect failures or investigate their causes
Monitoring tells you when something is wrong; observability lets you ask arbitrary questions about system state to diagnose unknown-unknowns using metrics, logs, and traces
Observability is a lightweight form of monitoring focused on a few predefined dashboards, while monitoring provides complete diagnostic access to internal system state
Monitoring is the broader discipline that exposes arbitrary internal state, whereas observability only reports known failures through predefined alerts
explanation: The three pillars of observability are metrics, logs, and distributed traces — together they enable understanding of complex systems.

text: What is a good first step when a prompt produces an unclear answer?
options: Revise the prompt by adding clearer goals and useful constraints
Assume the model understood and submit the answer without review
Remove all context so the model can make a completely free choice
Repeat the identical prompt until the response becomes more accurate
explanation: Prompting is often iterative, so adding specific goals, context, format, or constraints can improve results. Reviewing and refining the output is more reliable than simply repeating the same request.

text: What is a reliability hierarchy of needs?
options: A framework for ranking engineering investments, placing developer productivity and feature delivery ahead of operational monitoring and incident response
The principle that monitoring and incident response must be solid before focusing on testing, then capacity, then change management, then developer productivity
A staffing model that assigns reliability responsibilities by team seniority, beginning with developers and ending with a central operations group
A deployment priority scheme that requires capacity planning before monitoring, alerting, and incident response are established
explanation: Neglecting foundational reliability (monitoring, on-call) while investing in advanced features creates a fragile system.

text: What is Ansible?
options: A container orchestration platform that schedules workloads across clusters and manages service discovery, scaling, and rolling updates
An open-source agentless automation tool for configuration management, application deployment, and orchestration using SSH
A CI/CD platform that builds source code, runs automated tests, and promotes artifacts through staging and production environments
A cloud monitoring service that collects metrics and logs, evaluates alerts, and displays dashboards for distributed applications
explanation: Ansible is agentless — it connects to targets over SSH or WinRM and requires only Python on the managed node.

text: What is an Ansible inventory?
options: A file containing ordered tasks and handlers that Ansible executes against selected hosts to enforce configuration changes
A file or dynamic source listing the hosts and groups Ansible will manage, along with variables and connection details
A catalog of built-in and community modules, including their parameters, return values, and supported operating systems
A reusable directory of tasks, templates, handlers, and defaults that packages automation content for inclusion in playbooks
explanation: Inventories can be static YAML/INI files or dynamic scripts querying cloud APIs for current host lists.

text: What is idempotency in Ansible?
options: The ability to execute independent tasks concurrently across several managed hosts, reducing the total time required for a playbook run
The property that running a playbook multiple times produces the same result as running it once — tasks only make changes when needed
A category of Ansible module that compares desired values with current state but always reports a change when invoked
A network connection method that lets Ansible authenticate to managed hosts through encrypted channels without installing an agent
explanation: Idempotency is fundamental to safe automation — reruns do not cause unintended side effects.

text: What is Ansible Galaxy?
options: A web-based dashboard for browsing playbook runs, viewing host status, and approving changes across multiple Ansible projects
A public repository of Ansible roles and collections shared by the community, installable with ansible-galaxy install
A hosted infrastructure provider that provisions virtual machines and networks through Ansible modules and managed APIs
A continuous integration service that tests roles, builds collections, and deploys playbooks automatically after repository changes
explanation: Use ansible-galaxy collection install to install collections, which bundle modules, plugins, and roles together.

text: What is a handler in Ansible?
options: A task that runs automatically whenever a preceding task changes, commonly used to validate configuration syntax after edits
A task triggered only when notified by another task, typically used to restart services after configuration file changes
A special error-recovery task invoked when a play fails, usually used to roll back changes or restore unavailable services
A reusable module wrapper that defines how Ansible connects to a service and applies configuration settings across hosts
explanation: Handlers run at the end of the play and only once regardless of how many tasks notify them.

text: What are Ansible variables?
options: Connection settings that define SSH users, ports, authentication methods, and privilege escalation behavior for each managed host
Named values that parameterise playbooks and templates, enabling the same playbook to behave differently across environments or hosts
Module parameters supplied directly to tasks, controlling one operation but not available to templates, conditionals, or other tasks
Inventory hostnames that identify managed machines and automatically provide each host's operating-system facts and connection details
explanation: Variables can be defined in inventory, playbooks, roles, group_vars, host_vars, or passed at runtime with -e.

text: What are Ansible Vault encrypted variables?
options: Publicly accessible variables encoded with Base64 so they can be committed to version control and substituted into playbooks at runtime
Sensitive variables encrypted with AES-256 that can be stored safely in version control and decrypted at runtime by Ansible
Module parameters protected by Ansible's vault password, allowing task arguments to be hidden while inventory data remains unencrypted
Inventory plugins that encrypt host and group definitions with AES-256, then decrypt connection details automatically during gathering
explanation: Use ansible-vault encrypt_string to inline encrypt individual values, keeping most of the variable file readable.

text: What is a Jinja2 template in Ansible?
options: A YAML file containing task definitions that Ansible parses and applies directly to hosts, with variables substituted only in module arguments
A text file with Jinja2 expressions that Ansible renders with variable values before copying to managed hosts, used for dynamic config files
A module type that generates configuration content on the controller and transfers it without evaluating expressions or host variables
A role component that stores handlers and defaults, rendered automatically as a complete configuration file whenever the role is invoked
explanation: Templates use the .j2 extension and the template module, which also validates the rendered file before deployment.

text: What is an Ansible collection?
options: A named set of hosts and child groups defined in inventory, optionally assigned variables and connection settings
A packaging format that bundles modules, plugins, roles, and playbooks into a distributable, versioned unit
A transport component that selects SSH, WinRM, or local communication and controls how Ansible reaches each managed host
A naming convention used by modules and roles to identify variables, files, and commands within a playbook
explanation: Collections replaced the older roles-only sharing model and are the standard distribution format for Ansible content.

text: What is the purpose of APIRouter in FastAPI?
options: A URL rewriting component that transforms incoming paths before the request reaches the application, without grouping routes or applying shared configuration
A way to organise routes into separate modules/files, with optional prefix, tags, and dependencies applied to all routes
A rate-limiting component that counts requests per client and rejects excessive traffic before any endpoint function is called
A reverse-proxy component that forwards requests to backend services, balances connections, and manages upstream server failures
explanation: APIRouter enables modular route organisation — similar to Express Router or Django urls.py include() — keeping large apps manageable.

text: What is a custom Ansible module?
options: A modified copy of an existing built-in module whose defaults or argument handling have been changed for one environment
A Python script placed in a library directory that implements new functionality Ansible can execute on managed hosts
A role extension written in YAML that adds reusable tasks and variables without introducing executable module code
A collection plugin that registers an alternate inventory, connection, or callback implementation for Ansible to load
explanation: Custom modules return JSON and follow the AnsibleModule pattern. Document with DOCUMENTATION, EXAMPLES, and RETURN blocks.

text: What is the difference between ansible-pull and ansible-push?
options: Both commands use the same execution model, with a control node either checking out or transmitting playbooks according to configuration
ansible-pull inverts the model — each node checks out its own playbook from git and runs it locally; push is the default where a control node connects to targets
ansible-pull is the older interface for centralized execution and has been deprecated, while push execution remains the supported approach
ansible-push is the newer distributed command that runs playbooks on targets, whereas ansible-pull uses the original centralized workflow
explanation: ansible-pull scales to thousands of nodes since there is no central control node managing all connections.

text: What is the Ansible content collection development workflow?
options: Using Galaxy's web interface to create and version content, with testing handled by the platform and publication performed automatically
Developing with ansible-galaxy collection init, following the collection structure, testing with molecule, and publishing to Galaxy or a private repository
Writing a single playbook with local task files and variables, then distributing that file directly without creating a collection package
Using only built-in modules and roles from the Ansible installation, avoiding collection scaffolding, Molecule tests, and repository publication
explanation: Molecule is the standard testing framework for Ansible roles and collections, supporting Docker, Podman, and cloud drivers.

text: What is a block in Ansible?
options: A set of hosts selected by inventory patterns, allowing variables and connection settings to be shared across matching machines
A way to group tasks together, apply shared directives (when, become, tags), and handle errors with rescue and always sections
A named option passed to a module that changes its behavior, validates input, or supplies values for a single task
A repetition mechanism that selects items from a sequence and invokes a task once for each item during execution
explanation: block/rescue/always mirrors try/catch/finally from programming, enabling structured error handling in playbooks.

text: What does become: yes do in Ansible?
options: Adds an account to the target system with a chosen username, shell, home directory, and authentication settings
Escalates privileges (typically via sudo) to run tasks as a different user, usually root
Configures the SSH daemon and distributes authorized keys so Ansible can establish remote connections to hosts
Stores the output of a task under a chosen name so later tasks can inspect its status, data, and changes
explanation: Use become_user to specify which user to escalate to. Limit become to tasks that actually require elevated privileges.

text: What is an Ansible fact?
options: A result produced after a module runs, containing its return code, changed status, messages, and any returned data
Information automatically gathered about managed hosts (OS, IP addresses, CPU, memory) and available as variables during playbook execution
A reusable operation implemented in Python or another supported language that performs one kind of change on a managed host
A value declared in host or group configuration that supplies settings such as ports, usernames, paths, or feature flags
explanation: Use gather_facts: false to skip fact gathering when speed matters and facts are not needed.

text: What is a dynamic inventory in Ansible?
options: A YAML or INI configuration maintained by an administrator that lists hosts, groups, aliases, and connection variables
A script or plugin that generates inventory at runtime by querying external sources like AWS EC2, GCP, or Azure
An already-resolved collection of hostnames and group memberships loaded before playbook execution begins
A reusable directory structure containing tasks, handlers, templates, files, defaults, and variables for one automation component
explanation: Dynamic inventories ensure playbooks always target the current set of running instances without manual updates.

text: What is Google Compute Engine (GCE)?
options: A serverless compute platform that runs event-driven code without requiring users to manage virtual machines
An IaaS service providing scalable virtual machines running on Googles infrastructure
A managed relational database service that provisions highly available SQL instances on Google's infrastructure
A managed container orchestration service that schedules and scales application workloads across clusters
explanation: GCE VMs support custom machine types, preemptible (spot) instances, and live migration for high availability.

text: What is Google Cloud Storage (GCS)?
options: A network file system that mounts shared directories for applications across multiple compute instances
An object storage service for storing and serving any amount of unstructured data with high availability and global access
A managed relational database service for storing structured records and executing SQL queries at scale
A content delivery network that only caches static objects at edge locations and does not provide storage
explanation: GCS has four storage classes: Standard, Nearline, Coldline, and Archive — chosen based on access frequency.

text: What is Cloud IAM on GCP?
options: A virtual private network service that connects GCP subnets, routes traffic, and controls network access
Identity and Access Management — controlling who can do what on which GCP resources using roles and policies
A managed database service that stores application records and provides replication, backups, and query access
A monitoring and observability tool that collects metrics, logs, traces, and alerts from cloud resources
explanation: GCP IAM uses the principle of least privilege with predefined, basic, and custom roles assignable to members.

text: What is CORS and how do you handle it in FastAPI?
options: A database security policy for restricting which applications may read tables, configured through connection roles, privileges, and encrypted credentials
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — FastAPI handles it via CORSMiddleware, specifying allowed origins, methods, and headers
An authentication standard for exchanging user identity and access claims between independent applications, commonly implemented with signed bearer tokens
A browser and server caching mechanism that controls how responses are stored, revalidated, and reused across requests from different clients
explanation: CORSMiddleware from Starlette is added to a FastAPI app, allowing browsers to make cross-origin API requests.

text: What are GCP availability zones and regions?
options: A single geographic boundary that combines regional and zonal resources without isolation between deployment locations
Regions are geographic locations; zones are isolated data centers within a region. Deploying across zones provides high availability
Zones are larger geographic areas containing multiple regions and provide the primary level of global isolation
Regions are smaller subdivisions inside zones, usually representing individual data centers used for redundancy
explanation: GCP has 40+ regions globally. Deploy across multiple zones within a region for resilience against zone-level failures.

text: What is the difference between Cloud Functions and Cloud Run?
options: Cloud Functions and Cloud Run are identical serverless products with the same deployment model, triggering options, container support, and scaling behaviour
Cloud Functions is event-triggered, source-code based, and limited to one function; Cloud Run deploys any containerised workload with more flexibility
Cloud Run is a managed virtual machine service requiring customers to configure operating systems, patch servers, and maintain instance capacity manually
Cloud Functions is a container orchestration platform that deploys multi-container applications, exposes arbitrary services, and requires users to manage Kubernetes nodes
explanation: Cloud Run is preferred for existing containerised apps; Cloud Functions suits simple event handlers with minimal code.

text: What is BigQuery Omni?
options: A BigQuery storage variant that replicates tables between GCP regions, improving durability and query performance without supporting data outside Google Cloud
BigQuery multi-cloud analytics capability allowing SQL queries to run directly against data in AWS S3 or Azure Blob without moving it to GCP
A managed data transfer service that copies objects from AWS S3 or Azure Blob into BigQuery storage before SQL queries can access the imported data
A content delivery feature that caches BigQuery query results at worldwide edge locations, reducing latency for users running repeated analytical reports
explanation: Omni uses Anthos to deploy BigQuery compute workers in other clouds while centralising governance in GCP.

text: What is GKE Autopilot vs Standard mode?
options: The two GKE operating modes provide identical node management and billing; the different names only describe whether clusters use regional or zonal control planes
Standard mode gives full control over node configuration; Autopilot mode fully manages nodes, enforces pod security, and charges per Pod resource request
Autopilot is always cheaper than Standard because Google manages every resource, regardless of workload size, requested capacity, idle time, or scheduling requirements
Standard mode is a legacy configuration that Google no longer supports for new clusters, while Autopilot is the mandatory replacement for all existing Kubernetes workloads
explanation: Autopilot simplifies operations by eliminating node management overhead and applying security hardening by default.

text: How do you read user input in Bash?
options: The input variable reads a line from standard input and automatically assigns the captured text to the variable named after the command
The read command reads a line from stdin and stores it in the named variable
The get variable command accepts keyboard input from the terminal and stores the resulting line in a shell variable for later use
The scan variable command reads whitespace-separated input from standard input and places each entered value into the specified Bash variable
explanation: Use read -p to display a prompt inline: read -p "Enter name: " username

text: What is Pub/Sub on GCP?
options: A fully managed synchronous request-routing service for tightly coupling applications with exactly-once delivery and regional scale
A fully managed asynchronous messaging service for decoupling services with at-least-once delivery and global scale
A managed object storage service for retaining messages as durable files, with bucket-based access controls and cross-region replication
A private network connectivity service for linking GCP projects and on-premises systems through encrypted global tunnels
explanation: Pub/Sub is the backbone for event-driven architectures on GCP and integrates with Dataflow for stream processing.

text: What is VPC on GCP and how does it differ from AWS VPC?
options: GCP VPCs are regional and their subnets are global, while AWS VPCs are global and use account-wide subnet ranges shared across regions
GCP VPCs are global (single VPC spanning all regions) while AWS VPCs are regional; GCP subnets are regional
GCP VPCs exist only inside a single region, and each subnet must be duplicated manually in every zone; AWS VPCs instead span all regions with global subnets
GCP VPCs are regional networks tied to one location, while AWS VPCs are global; GCP subnets span all regions and ignore regional boundaries
explanation: The global nature of GCP VPCs simplifies multi-region networking — resources in different regions can communicate within the same VPC.

text: What is Workload Identity Federation on GCP?
options: A GCP user account type for employees and automation that issues permanent service account keys and grants external workloads direct access to projects
Allowing external identities (GitHub Actions, AWS, on-prem) to authenticate to GCP without service account keys, using short-lived tokens
A network connectivity feature that establishes private tunnels between external identity providers and GCP VPCs, without involving authentication tokens or IAM policies
An IAM role type that bundles permissions for GitHub Actions, AWS workloads, and on-premises applications, replacing service accounts with long-lived credentials
explanation: Workload Identity Federation eliminates the need for long-lived service account JSON keys, significantly reducing credential exposure.

text: What is Cloud CDN on GCP?
options: A network transport protocol integrated with Cloud Load Balancing to route HTTP requests between regional backends without caching content at edge locations
A content delivery network integrated with Cloud Load Balancing to cache content at Googles edge PoPs globally
A managed object storage service integrated with Cloud Load Balancing to retain static files in buckets and replicate them globally for applications
A global DNS resolution service integrated with Cloud Load Balancing to answer hostname queries and select the nearest backend without caching web content
explanation: Cloud CDN uses Googles global network of 100+ edge locations and integrates with GCS and backend services.

text: Why might a user ask a generative AI model to cite its sources?
options: To make supporting information easier to check and verify
To ensure every generated sentence is automatically factually correct
To allow the model to browse any website without user permission
To make the model provide longer answers with additional detail
explanation: Citations help users inspect the evidence behind a response and identify possible errors. They improve transparency, but citations alone do not guarantee that every claim is correct.

text: What is Dataproc on GCP?
options: A data pipeline service for designing scheduled ETL workflows that move and transform data between Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and operational databases
A managed Spark and Hadoop service for running big data processing frameworks without managing cluster infrastructure
A serverless analytical database that stores structured and semi-structured datasets, automatically scales queries, and eliminates the need to provision compute clusters
A managed streaming service for ingesting continuous event data from applications and delivering it to subscribers with low latency and automatic scaling
explanation: Dataproc clusters start in under 90 seconds. Use ephemeral clusters (create, process, delete) to minimise cost.

text: What is Vertex AI on GCP?
options: A compute service for provisioning virtual machines and container clusters, handling autoscaling and capacity management but offering no model training or deployment workflows
A unified ML platform for building, training, deploying, and managing ML models and pipelines, integrating Google AI services and AutoML
A managed data warehouse for storing large analytical tables, running SQL queries, and building dashboards without providing model development or experiment tracking
A monitoring service that collects infrastructure metrics and logs, creates operational alerts, and visualises service health without training or deploying machine-learning models
explanation: Vertex AI consolidates AI Platform, AutoML, and other Google ML services into a single managed platform.

text: What is TypeScript?
options: A standalone programming language with its own runtime and syntax, designed to replace JavaScript in browsers rather than compile into JavaScript for execution
A typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript, adding static types and modern features
A runtime environment for executing JavaScript applications on servers, providing type checking and package management but not introducing a separate compile step
A JavaScript UI framework for building component-based web applications, providing rendering, routing, and state management instead of static typing
explanation: TypeScript was created by Microsoft. Any valid JavaScript is also valid TypeScript, making adoption incremental.

text: What is the key difference between interface and type in TypeScript?
options: interface and type are interchangeable in every context; neither supports capabilities that the other lacks, including object composition and reusable declarations
interface defines object shapes and supports declaration merging; type supports unions, intersections, and primitives
type cannot describe object structures and is limited to aliases for primitive values, while interface is required for every object-shaped contract
interface supports unions and conditional combinations directly, whereas type can define only named object shapes and cannot represent primitive aliases
explanation: Use interface for extensible object shapes; use type for unions, mapped types, and conditional types.

text: What are TypeScript utility types?
options: Runtime helper functions such as Partial and Pick that clone objects and remove or add properties while the program runs
Built-in generic types like Partial<T>, Required<T>, Pick<T,K>, Omit<T,K>, and Record<K,V> that transform existing types
Custom modules exported by an application to reuse interfaces, classes, and aliases across independently compiled packages
Interface extension declarations that automatically merge properties from several object types into a single generated runtime schema
explanation: Readonly<T> makes all properties readonly; NonNullable<T> removes null and undefined from a type.

text: What does enabling strict mode in tsconfig.json do?
options: Enables stricter runtime checks including bounds checking, automatic null guards, and validation of thrown exceptions
Enables stricter checks including noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, and strictFunctionTypes
Enables JavaScript compilation with implicit any, nullable values, and permissive assignments between unrelated function types
Enables the compiler to infer every value as any, suppressing type errors and removing the need for explicit annotations
explanation: Enable strict: true from the start of a project. Retrofitting it onto existing code is painful.

text: What is type inference in TypeScript?
options: The compiler requiring explicit annotations for every variable and parameter before it can determine any types automatically
The compiler automatically determining the type of a value from its assignment or usage context
The compiler examining assigned values at runtime and dynamically updating their types while the program executes
The compiler using a linting feature to report stylistic inconsistencies in annotations without affecting type checking
explanation: TypeScript infers const x = 5 as number. Rely on inference for obvious cases and annotate function signatures explicitly.

text: What is the void return type used for?
options: Indicating a function must return an Error object whenever execution finishes without producing a normal result
Indicating a function does not return a meaningful value — used for functions called only for side effects
Indicating a function always produces an empty string, rather than undefined or another meaningful value
Indicating a function returns null specifically, while allowing no other value when execution completes
explanation: void differs from undefined. A void function can technically return undefined but callers should not rely on the return value.

text: What does the readonly modifier do?
options: Makes every property in an imported module immutable, including nested objects and exported functions
Prevents a property from being reassigned after initialisation
Marks fields as optional so callers may omit them when constructing an object with that declared shape
Enables deep immutability at runtime by freezing objects and preventing mutations in generated JavaScript
explanation: readonly is compile-time only. It does not prevent runtime mutation — use Object.freeze for that.

text: What are generics in TypeScript?
options: Type parameters that create runtime classes for each supplied type, allowing JavaScript to inspect generic arguments after compilation
Type parameters that make functions and types reusable across different types while preserving type safety, e.g. function identity<T>(x: T): T
Type parameters that are limited to module declarations and cannot be used in functions, interfaces, or type aliases
Type parameters that automatically convert every input to any while allowing reusable declarations without compile-time constraints
explanation: Generics are the key to writing reusable, type-safe utilities like Array<T>, Promise<T>, and Record<K, V>.

text: What is a pointer in Go and when do you use one?
options: A reference to a slice's backing array, used when indexing collections or changing their capacity
A variable holding a memory address; used to mutate values inside functions or to avoid copying large structs
A reference to a channel endpoint, used to control whether sends or receives block
A map key containing an address, used to identify entries without copying the associated value
explanation: Go passes values by copy. Pointers (`*T`, `&x`) let functions modify the original value or share large data without copying.

text: How do you declare a variable in Bash?
options: var name=value
name=value with no spaces around the equals sign
Prefixing with dollar equals value
let name=value for all cases
explanation: Spaces around = are a syntax error in Bash. Access the value with a dollar-sign prefix or the brace expansion form.

text: What is the unknown type and how does it differ from any?
options: unknown and any are interchangeable top types, so both permit property access, calls, and assignments without prior narrowing
unknown is type-safe — values cannot be used until narrowed via a type guard, unlike any which skips all checks
unknown disables the compiler's type analysis for a value, whereas any preserves strict checking through explicit annotations
unknown is a subtype of any, meaning unknown values can be assigned freely to any specific type without assertions
explanation: Use unknown instead of any for values whose type you genuinely do not know — it forces you to verify before use.

text: What is the satisfies operator (TypeScript 4.9+)?
options: An equality check comparing two runtime values and returning a boolean, with no effect on their inferred static types
An operator validating a value matches a type at assignment without widening the inferred type
A type assertion that forces the compiler to accept a value as a specified type while suppressing compatibility errors
An optional chaining operator that stops property access when a value is nullish and produces undefined at runtime
explanation: satisfies catches type errors while keeping the most specific inferred type, unlike explicit annotation which widens to the declared type.

text: What are conditional types in TypeScript?
options: JavaScript-style expressions that choose a value during program execution according to a Boolean condition, rather than selecting types during compilation
Types choosing between two types based on a condition: T extends U ? X : Y, evaluated at the type level
A rule that restricts which concrete types may be supplied for a generic parameter, without selecting a resulting type from two alternatives
A syntax for iterating over the keys of an object type and producing a new property type for each key found in the original definition
explanation: Conditional types power built-in utilities like ReturnType<T>, Parameters<T>, and Awaited<T>.

text: What is the infer keyword in conditional types?
options: A module-related keyword used to bring declarations from another file into the current scope, typically alongside import and export statements
A keyword used inside conditional types to capture a type that TypeScript infers from the pattern, enabling type extraction
An explicitly declared generic type parameter that callers must provide when invoking a generic function or instantiating a generic class
A built-in utility type that transforms an existing type by making its properties optional, readonly, or otherwise structurally modified
explanation: Pattern: type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never — infer R captures the return type.

text: What is the never type in TypeScript?
options: A type used for functions that return no meaningful value, including procedures that finish normally without producing a result for their callers
A type representing values that can never occur — the return type of always-throwing functions and the bottom type in the type system
A permissive type representing an unknown value that may be assigned to any other type without checking, while allowing operations on the value
A compiler-generated error type assigned to expressions that fail type checking, allowing invalid programs to continue through later analysis stages
explanation: never enables exhaustiveness checking: a default branch asserting never catches unhandled union members at compile time.

text: What are TypeScript decorators?
options: Ordinary comments placed before declarations to document the intended behavior of classes, methods, properties, and parameters without changing generated code
Special syntax for annotating and modifying classes, methods, properties, and parameters — a stage 3 JavaScript proposal
Compile-time type annotations attached to classes and members to describe their parameter types, return types, and property types for the checker
Syntax for exporting classes and members from a module so that other files can import them, without altering their behavior or receiving metadata
explanation: Decorators are widely used in Angular, NestJS, and TypeORM. Enable with experimentalDecorators in tsconfig.

text: What is variance in TypeScript generic types?
options: Whether a generic type is evaluated at runtime or compile time, determining when its type arguments affect emitted JavaScript behavior
Whether a generic type is covariant (preserves subtype relationship) or contravariant (reverses it), affecting type assignability
A mapped-type mechanism that transforms each property of a generic object according to modifiers such as readonly and optional
A conditional-type mechanism that selects one generic branch or another by testing whether a type satisfies a constraint
explanation: Function parameters are contravariant; return types are covariant. strictFunctionTypes enforces correct variance for function types.

text: What is type-level programming in TypeScript?
options: Using runtime JavaScript operations to inspect and transform values, with annotations that document the results but do not affect compilation
Using the type system to perform computations at compile time — recursive types, type-level algorithms, and complex invariants with no runtime overhead
Using decorators and metadata at runtime to generate classes, validate members, and enforce object invariants after the program starts executing
Using JSX syntax and component types to construct interfaces, infer properties, and describe rendered output during application execution
explanation: Advanced patterns include type-safe SQL parsers, recursive template literal processing, and compile-time state machines.

text: What is a shebang line in a shell script?
options: A comment line placed at the beginning of a script for human readers, with no effect on how the operating system launches the file
The first line specifying the interpreter, e.g. #!/bin/bash, which tells the OS which shell to use
The first line printed after a script fails, describing the shell error and identifying the command that could not be executed
A variable declaration at the beginning of a script that stores the selected shell name for later command expansion
explanation: Using #!/usr/bin/env bash is more portable as it finds bash from PATH rather than a hardcoded location.

text: You want to run containers without managing servers. Which service is best?
options: ECS with Fargate
EC2
EBS
CloudFront
explanation: Dynamically adjusts EC2 instances based on demand.

text: Which command changes file permissions?
options: chmod
chperm
perm
setmode
explanation: `chmod` changes Unix permission bits.

text: How do you write a comment in Bash?
options: A line beginning with two forward slashes is a comment and is ignored by Bash when the shell reads the script
A line beginning with a hash symbol is a comment and is ignored by the shell
Text enclosed between slash and asterisk delimiters forms a multiline comment that Bash skips before executing surrounding commands
A line beginning with two hyphens is a comment in Bash and is ignored unless it appears inside a quoted argument
explanation: There is no multi-line comment syntax in Bash. Each comment line must begin with its own hash symbol.

text: What does the pipe operator | do in Bash?
options: Connects stderr of one command to stdout of the next, forwarding diagnostic output between commands
Connects stdout of one command to stdin of the next, chaining commands together
Executes the command on the left only after the command on the right completes, controlling command order
Combines the output of multiple commands into one file, preserving each command's separate stream
explanation: Pipes are the foundation of the Unix philosophy: small single-purpose tools composed together.

text: What does set -euo pipefail do at the top of a script?
options: set -euo pipefail enables verbose tracing, exports variables automatically, and makes every command run with administrator privileges
set -e exits on error; -u treats unset variables as errors; -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails
set -euo pipefail disables error exits, initializes unset variables to empty strings, and ignores failures inside pipelines
set -euo pipefail selects POSIX compatibility, enables command tracing, and converts all shell warnings into fatal errors
explanation: These three options together create a much safer script that fails fast rather than silently continuing after errors.

text: What is a Bash indexed array?
options: A dynamically sized string collection declared with arr='(a b c)' and accessed through ordinary scalar expansion syntax
A zero-indexed collection declared with arr=(a b c) and accessed or iterated with Bash expansion syntax
A keyed collection declared with arr=(a b c) whose elements are addressed by arbitrary string names rather than numeric indexes
A read-only sequence produced by filename expansion, with values assigned automatically from matching filesystem paths
explanation: Access one element with the index expansion form, all elements by expanding the full array, and iterate with a for loop.

text: What is a here-document (heredoc) in Bash?
options: A single-line filename reference expanded by the shell, using << to open an existing document as a command
A multi-line string redirected as stdin to a command using the << DELIMITER syntax
A loop construct that repeats commands until a delimiter is encountered, with << marking the loop body
A function-definition syntax that stores commands between delimiters and invokes them later as a named shell routine
explanation: Use a single-quoted delimiter to prevent variable expansion inside the heredoc body.

text: What is a Bash function?
options: A standalone file of commands invoked by pathname, with its variables isolated from the calling shell
A named block of reusable code that accepts positional arguments and can be called by name
A separately installed package that exports commands through an import mechanism before a script can use them
A file loaded automatically at shell startup whose definitions persist without requiring an explicit function call
explanation: Functions share the calling scripts variables unless declared local. Use the local keyword inside functions to limit variable scope.

text: What is process substitution in Bash?
options: A pipeline syntax that connects several commands through an anonymous stream, without creating any pathname for the data
Using the <(command) form to treat command output as a file path, letting commands that expect filenames receive piped data
A redirection form that writes command output into a temporary regular file, then substitutes that filename
A parameter-expansion form that evaluates a command and inserts its output directly into the surrounding word
explanation: Comparing sorted versions of two files without creating temp files is a classic process substitution use case.

text: What is parameter expansion in Bash?
options: Starting an external command after replacing a variable reference with its current text and passing resulting arguments
Transforming a variable value using operators for defaults, substring removal, and substitution without spawning a subshell
A subshell mechanism that copies the environment, runs grouped commands, and returns their status to the parent
An array operation that appends, slices, and reindexes elements while preserving the original scalar variable
explanation: Parameter expansion is fast because it runs in the current shell. Learn defaults, suffix/prefix stripping, and substitution forms.

text: What are Bash nameref variables (declare -n)?
options: A variable alias created with ordinary assignment, copying another variable's current value rather than tracking later changes
A reference variable acting as an alias for another variable, enabling functions to modify a callers variable by name without eval
A global variable declared at top level, allowing every function to access shared state without passing an argument
An indexed array type whose elements are named references, allowing one array to store pointers to other variables
explanation: Declare a nameref inside a function with the variable name passed as an argument to safely modify the callers variable.

text: What is Bash extended globbing (extglob)?
options: A regular-expression dialect used by Bash commands to match arbitrary text, including capture groups and backreferences
Enhanced pattern matching enabled with shopt -s extglob, adding zero-or-more and one-or-more match patterns
A feature of find that adds recursive filename predicates and evaluates matching expressions before returning paths
A POSIX-standard globbing mode available in every conforming shell, requiring no shell option to activate
explanation: Extended globbing matches complex file sets without invoking find or sed, keeping scripts fast and dependency-free.

text: What is the difference between AND-list and OR-list operators in Bash?
options: The AND operator runs the next command when the previous failed; the OR operator runs it when the previous succeeded
The AND operator runs the next command only if the previous succeeded; the OR operator runs the next only if the previous failed
The AND-list and OR-list operators pass command output between processes, with AND merging streams and OR selecting a pipe
The AND-list and OR-list operators launch commands asynchronously, with AND suppressing output and OR detaching them from the shell
explanation: Chaining AND then OR is a common idiom, but the OR branch also catches a failure in the AND branch command.

text: What is an interface in C#?
options: A concrete type whose methods are inherited by implementing classes without requiring inheritance or member definitions
A contract defining method/property signatures that implementing types must provide
An abstract class that can be inherited by one type and supplies default implementations for its declared members
A namespace-like container that groups related classes and automatically exposes their public methods
explanation: Interfaces (e.g. `IDisposable`, `IEnumerable`) define contracts; any class that implements all members satisfies the interface.

text: Which hook is used to manage local component state in React?
options: useEffect
useContext
useState
useRef
explanation: useState returns a stateful value and a setter function for managing local state in functional components.

text: What does the useEffect hook do?
options: Creates a context provider
Performs side effects after render
Memoizes a computed value
Manages form state
explanation: useEffect lets you synchronise a component with an external system or run side effects after rendering.

text: What is a React component?
options: A CSS class
A reusable, independent piece of UI
A database model
A build tool
explanation: A React component is a function or class that returns JSX and can accept props.

text: What are props in React?
options: Internal state variables
Inputs passed from parent to child components
CSS class names
API response objects
explanation: Props (properties) are read-only data passed from a parent component to a child component.

text: How do you conditionally render content in React?
options: Using if/else inside JSX with {}
Using a <switch> JSX element
Using the render() method only
Using CSS display:none
explanation: You can use JavaScript's && operator, ternary operator, or if/else inside braces to conditionally render JSX.

text: Which Next.js function fetches data at build time for static generation?
options: getServerSideProps
getStaticProps
useQuery
fetchData
explanation: getStaticProps runs at build time and provides data to a page component for SSG.

text: What command creates a new Next.js application?
options: npx create-react-app
npx create-next-app
npm init next
next new app
explanation: npx create-next-app scaffolds a new Next.js project with the recommended configuration.

text: How do you navigate between pages in Next.js?
options: Using <a> tags only
Using React Router's <Link>
Using Next.js's <Link> from next/link
Using window.location.href only
explanation: Next.js provides a <Link> component from 'next/link' that enables client-side navigation with prefetching.

text: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?
options: useMemo memoizes a value; useCallback memoizes a function reference
Both memoize functions
useMemo is for async, useCallback for sync
They are identical
explanation: useMemo caches the result of a computation. useCallback caches the function itself to prevent unnecessary re-renders of children.

text: What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) in Next.js?
options: Pre-rendering pages at build time
Rendering pages on the server on every request
Rendering pages purely in the browser
Fetching data client-side on mount
explanation: SSR (getServerSideProps) renders the HTML on the server for every incoming request, useful for dynamic data.

text: What does useReducer do in React?
options: Combines multiple context providers
Manages complex state logic with a reducer function
Reduces bundle size
Memoizes API responses
explanation: useReducer is an alternative to useState for complex state with a (state, action) => newState reducer pattern.

text: What is React.memo?
options: A hook that memoizes state values between renders without comparing component props
A higher-order component that prevents re-render if props haven't changed
A library for coordinating enter and exit animations across React components
A server component decorator that forces rendering to happen only on the server
explanation: React.memo wraps a component and skips re-rendering if props are shallowly equal to the previous render.

text: In Next.js App Router, what is a Server Component?
options: A component that executes exclusively in the browser and always requires a client-side JavaScript bundle
A component rendered on the server with no client-side JS bundle by default
A REST API endpoint that handles requests and returns serialized data from the application server
A getServerSideProps replacement that fetches page data during every request in the App Router
explanation: React Server Components render on the server and don't ship their JS to the client, reducing bundle size.

text: What is the purpose of mktemp in shell scripts?
options: Creates ordinary files with user-chosen names for later reuse, so scripts can reliably access a permanent path without collisions
Safely creates uniquely named temporary files or directories, avoiding race conditions and predictable-name security attacks
A string utility that generates temporary-looking names without creating filesystem objects or protecting them from concurrent processes
A pipe command that stores command output in a temporary stream, deleting the data automatically when the pipeline finishes
explanation: Register cleanup with trap to ensure temp files are removed on exit regardless of how the script terminates.

text: What is IFS in Bash and why does changing it matter?
options: An ignored variable: Bash does not consult it during expansion, so changing its value has no effect on word boundaries or command arguments
Internal Field Separator: the characters Bash uses to split words during expansion, controlling how strings are tokenised
A signal name used by Bash to interrupt commands and notify jobs, with its value selected from the shell's trap configuration
A file permission bit that controls whether scripts may split input fields, with its setting inherited from the containing directory
explanation: Save and restore IFS around any changes to avoid hard-to-debug splitting behaviour in the rest of the script.

text: What is JSX in React?
options: A JavaScript XML syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like code in JS
A JSON format for styling components that React parses into CSS rules during rendering
A state management library that stores component data and coordinates React updates
A React testing framework that renders components and simulates browser events
explanation: JSX is a syntax extension that looks like HTML and gets compiled to React.createElement() calls.

text: What is the Virtual DOM in React?
options: A server-side DOM implementation that renders components without a browser
A lightweight in-memory copy of the real DOM used for diffing
The browser's native DOM API for directly updating live page elements
A database for component state that persists props across page reloads
explanation: React maintains a Virtual DOM and diffs it with the real DOM, minimising expensive DOM operations.

text: What is the purpose of Next.js API routes?
options: Client-side data fetching helpers
Serverless backend endpoints co-located with the frontend
CSS-in-JS utilities
Image optimisation handlers
explanation: API routes in pages/api (or app/api in App Router) create serverless functions that serve as backend endpoints.

text: What is Entity Framework Core?
options: A web framework for defining HTTP endpoints, middleware pipelines, and JSON serialization in .NET applications
An ORM for .NET that maps C# classes to database tables, providing LINQ-based querying and migrations
A unit testing framework for organizing test fixtures, parameterized cases, assertions, and isolated test execution
A distributed caching library for storing serialized application objects in memory or Redis and expiring them automatically
explanation: EF Core generates SQL from LINQ queries, handles migrations, and supports multiple databases (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite).

text: How do you read a file asynchronously in Node.js?
options: fs.readFileSync()
fs.readFile() with a callback
http.get()
process.read()
explanation: fs.readFile() reads a file non-blocking and calls the callback with (err, data) when done.

text: What is Express.js?
options: A database ORM for Node.js
A minimal, unopinionated web framework for Node.js
A templating engine
A test runner
explanation: Express is the most popular Node.js HTTP framework, providing routing, middleware, and request/response handling.

text: What problem does the useTransition hook solve?
options: Batching all state updates automatically so multiple setState calls produce one render
Marking state updates as non-urgent to keep the UI responsive during heavy renders
Cancelling in-flight fetch requests when a transition is interrupted before the response arrives
Managing concurrent effects by delaying side effects until rendering has fully completed
explanation: useTransition defers non-urgent updates so urgent ones (like typing) remain responsive while expensive renders run concurrently.

text: How does Next.js middleware work?
options: It's a class-based Express middleware that runs inside Node.js after a route handler has been selected
It runs Edge Functions before a request is matched to a route, enabling auth, redirects, and rewrites
It's a React hook for performing side effects after a page component has rendered in the browser
It runs only during build time to precompute redirects and rewrite rules before deployment
explanation: Next.js middleware runs at the Edge before cache lookup, allowing you to intercept requests for auth, locale, and A/B testing.

text: What is a custom React hook and when should you create one?
options: A hook provided by third-party libraries that cannot be composed from application-defined functions
A function starting with 'use' that composes built-in hooks to extract and share stateful logic
A global state manager beginning with 'use' that stores shared values outside the component tree
A class component method beginning with 'use' that encapsulates lifecycle logic for reuse
explanation: Custom hooks let you extract component logic into reusable functions. They must start with 'use' and can call other hooks.

text: How does Next.js handle image optimisation?
options: It doesn't; you need a CDN to resize, convert, cache, and lazy-load images before serving them to users
The next/image component automatically resizes, converts to WebP, serves from a built-in CDN, and lazy-loads images
It minifies SVGs only, while raster images are served unchanged without resizing, conversion, or lazy loading
Images are processed at build time only, producing one fixed format and size for every device and request
explanation: next/image handles responsive sizing, format conversion (WebP/AVIF), lazy loading, and CLS prevention automatically.

text: What is a React Error Boundary?
options: A try/catch for async functions that catches rejected promises anywhere in a component subtree
A class component that catches JS errors in its subtree and renders a fallback UI
A Next.js middleware feature that intercepts failed requests and returns a fallback response
A linting rule that detects unsafe component code and prevents runtime exceptions from reaching the browser
explanation: Error Boundaries are class components implementing componentDidCatch and getDerivedStateFromError to catch rendering errors in child components.

text: What is code splitting in React?
options: Splitting a stylesheet into independently loaded CSS modules for each component
Loading JavaScript bundles on demand using React.lazy and Suspense
Separating component inputs from locally managed state during rendering
Organizing one component's implementation across several source files
explanation: Code splitting defers loading of route or component code until it's needed, reducing the initial bundle size.

text: What is React's reconciliation algorithm?
options: A method for updating component props by copying new values into child elements during rendering
The diffing algorithm that compares Virtual DOM trees to determine minimal real DOM updates
A server rendering technique that converts components into HTML before sending the response
A state synchronisation protocol that keeps separate browser and server stores consistent
explanation: React's reconciliation uses a heuristic O(n) tree diffing algorithm, assuming elements of different types produce different trees and keys identify elements in lists.

text: What is Node.js?
options: A browser-based JavaScript runtime embedded in Chrome's V8 engine
A server-side JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine
A client-side JavaScript framework built around reusable UI components
A relational database engine designed to store application records
explanation: Node.js is a runtime that executes JavaScript outside the browser, commonly used to build servers and CLIs.

text: What is npm?
options: Node Package Manager — the default package manager for Node.js
A Node.js process monitor used to inspect running application instances
A network protocol module that routes requests between Node.js services
A JavaScript testing framework for executing unit and integration tests
explanation: npm is the default package manager for Node.js, hosting over 2 million packages.

text: What is the purpose of package.json?
options: Stores environment variables used to configure an application across deployments
Describes a Node.js project's metadata, scripts, and dependencies
Configures the Node.js runtime by defining its engine and execution settings
Defines database schemas and migration rules for an application's data models
explanation: package.json holds project metadata, lists dependencies, and defines npm scripts.

text: What does require() do in Node.js?
options: Imports an npm package or local module using the CommonJS system
Installs an npm package or local module into the project's dependencies directory
Creates a new operating-system process through Node.js's child-process facilities
Declares an environment variable for use by the current Node.js application
explanation: require() is the CommonJS module loader that loads built-in, npm, or local modules.

text: What is lifespan event handling in FastAPI?
options: Using request and response lifecycle hooks to wrap every individual HTTP exchange, running setup before each request and cleanup immediately after its response
Using @asynccontextmanager on a lifespan function to run startup (DB connections, caches) and shutdown (cleanup) logic
Using a scheduled task mechanism that repeatedly launches background jobs at fixed intervals during application operation and cancels them when requests stop
Using middleware dedicated to creating and releasing database connections around requests, rather than a single application-wide startup and shutdown context
explanation: The lifespan context manager (FastAPI 0.93+) replaces deprecated on_event handlers, providing structured startup/shutdown for resources.

text: What is the purpose of the node_modules folder?
options: Stores application source code
Contains installed npm dependencies for the project
Holds build artefacts
Stores environment config
explanation: node_modules contains all locally installed packages listed in package.json and their transitive dependencies.

text: What is middleware in Express?
options: A database connection layer that opens, pools, and closes connections for each request
A function with (req, res, next) signature that processes requests in a pipeline
A template renderer that converts request data into HTML before sending the response
A test utility that creates mock requests and responses for Express route tests
explanation: Middleware functions can read/modify request and response objects and call next() to pass control to the next middleware.

text: What is the difference between setTimeout and setImmediate?
options: They are identical in timing and scheduling; both callbacks execute at the same phase after pending I/O and use the same delay semantics
setTimeout fires after a minimum delay; setImmediate fires after I/O events in the current iteration of the event loop
setImmediate is deprecated in favor of setTimeout, which provides the supported way to schedule callbacks after I/O events
setTimeout is for async code only, whereas setImmediate is reserved for synchronous callbacks and cannot be used with I/O
explanation: setImmediate executes in the check phase of the event loop (after I/O callbacks), while setTimeout(fn, 0) executes in the timers phase.

text: What are Node.js Streams?
options: Objects that buffer an entire file or network payload before allowing reads or writes to begin
Objects that let you read or write data in chunks rather than all at once
Objects that generate asynchronous values only through iterators and cannot be written to or piped
Objects that maintain persistent WebSocket connections and expose messages only as complete packets
explanation: Streams handle data piece by piece (e.g. file reading, HTTP responses), reducing memory usage for large datasets.

text: How do you handle uncaught exceptions in Node.js?
options: Use try/catch everywhere, wrapping each request and callback so the process can continue after any exception or rejected promise
Listen to process 'uncaughtException' and 'unhandledRejection' events, but prefer structured error handling
Node.js handles them automatically by logging the error and restarting the failed request without requiring application-level cleanup
Use a global catch variable that receives every thrown error and rejected promise before Node.js terminates the affected operation
explanation: process.on('uncaughtException') and process.on('unhandledRejection') catch unhandled errors, but should trigger graceful shutdown — not resume.

text: What is clustering in Node.js?
options: Grouping related npm packages into a single dependency bundle for installation
Spawning multiple worker processes to utilise multi-core CPUs
Distributing requests across servers through a central load balancer
A caching strategy that stores frequently used results in shared memory
explanation: The cluster module forks worker processes sharing the same port, allowing CPU-bound tasks to run on multiple cores.

text: How do you implement JWT authentication in a Node.js app?
options: Store credentials in cookies only, then trust the cookie contents on each request without signing, encrypting, or verifying them
Sign a JWT token on login with a secret, send it to the client, and verify it on protected routes using middleware
Use sessions only, keeping the authenticated user's identity in server memory and never issuing or validating a signed token
Use OAuth exclusively, delegating every login and API authorization decision to an external identity provider without creating JWTs
explanation: jsonwebtoken's sign() creates tokens and verify() validates them in middleware, enabling stateless authentication.

text: What is the purpose of dotenv in Node.js?
options: A linting tool that checks JavaScript style and reports formatting violations
Loads environment variables from a .env file into process.env
A database migration tool for applying versioned schema changes
A bundler for combining JavaScript modules into optimized browser assets
explanation: dotenv reads .env files and populates process.env, keeping secrets out of source code.

text: What is backpressure in Node.js streams?
options: A type of network error reported when packets are delayed, dropped, or delivered out of order during transmission
When a writable stream cannot consume data as fast as a readable stream produces it; handled via pause/resume or pipe
Memory pressure caused when large objects remain referenced and progressively exhaust the process heap during normal request processing
A rate-limiting technique that deliberately caps request throughput to protect a service under sustained load
explanation: pipe() handles backpressure automatically by pausing the readable when the writable buffer is full.

text: What is the difference between process.nextTick and Promise microtasks in the event loop?
options: They are identical because both callbacks use the same microtask queue and always have the same scheduling priority
process.nextTick callbacks run before any I/O or Promise microtasks; Promise .then() runs in the microtask queue after nextTick
Promises run first, because the Promise microtask queue is drained before Node processes its nextTick callbacks
Both run after I/O, since Node postpones nextTick and Promise callbacks until the current event-loop phase completes
explanation: nextTick callbacks are processed after the current operation but before the event loop continues. Microtasks (Promises) come next, before I/O callbacks.

text: How would you implement graceful shutdown in a Node.js HTTP server?
options: Call process.exit(0) immediately after SIGTERM, terminating requests without waiting for connections to finish
Listen to SIGTERM, stop accepting new connections with server.close(), wait for in-flight requests, then exit
Use a cluster restart to replace the process, without explicitly closing the listening server or draining requests
Use process.abort() on SIGTERM so the operating system can terminate the server and release its resources
explanation: Graceful shutdown: catch SIGTERM, server.close() stops new connections, wait for active requests to finish, clean up DB connections, then exit.

text: How does FastAPI handle async vs. sync route functions differently?
options: There is no execution difference: both async and sync route functions run directly on the event loop, so blocking synchronous work can pause other requests
Async route functions run on the event loop; sync functions run in a thread pool to avoid blocking the event loop
Sync route functions run in a separate operating-system process for isolation, while async route functions execute in the main event-loop process
Both async and sync route functions are submitted to thread pools, with async functions losing their event-loop scheduling and running like ordinary blocking callables
explanation: def (sync) handlers are automatically run in a thread pool executor, preventing blocking of the async event loop. async def runs directly on the loop.
