text: What is Flask?
options: A Django plugin
A lightweight WSGI Python web microframework
A database migration tool
A JavaScript library
explanation: Flask provides routing and request handling but leaves choices like ORM and auth to the developer.

text: What does the MTV pattern in Django stand for?
options: Model-Template-View
Module-Type-Variable
Module-Template-Variable
Model-Type-View
explanation: Django uses Model-Template-View (equivalent to MVC): Models define data, Templates render HTML, Views handle logic.

text: How do you start a new Django project?
options: django new myproject
django-admin startproject myproject
python -m django create myproject
pip create django myproject
explanation: django-admin startproject creates the project directory with settings.py, urls.py, wsgi.py, and manage.py.

text: What is Flask's @app.route decorator used for?
options: Defining database models
Mapping a URL pattern to a view function
Setting response headers
Configuring the Flask app
explanation: @app.route('/path') registers a URL rule so Flask calls the decorated function when that URL is requested.

text: What file contains URL routing configuration in Django?
options: settings.py
urls.py
models.py
views.py
explanation: urls.py maps URL patterns (using path() or re_path()) to view functions or class-based views.

text: How do you return JSON from a Flask view?
options: return json(data)
return jsonify(data)
return JSON.stringify(data)
return render_json(data)
explanation: Flask's jsonify() serialises a Python dict to a JSON response with the correct Content-Type header.

text: How do you profile a memory leak in a Node.js application?
options: Increase the process memory limit and restart the service repeatedly, using its improved capacity to prevent leaked objects from exhausting the heap
Use --inspect with Chrome DevTools heap snapshots, or heapdump/clinic.js to compare allocations over time
Add detailed console.log statements throughout the application and inspect the printed values to identify which variables remain allocated unexpectedly
Use the cluster module to distribute requests across worker processes, assuming that process isolation will reveal and eliminate the underlying leak
explanation: Heap snapshots taken at intervals let you compare retained objects. clinic.js and node --inspect provide CPU and memory profiling.

text: What is Django?
options: A Python data-science library for performing numerical analysis, statistical modelling, and dataframe transformations on large datasets
A high-level Python web framework with built-in ORM, admin, and auth
A JavaScript framework for building interactive browser interfaces with reusable components, client-side routing, and state management
A database system that stores relational records, manages indexes, and provides SQL queries for applications written in multiple languages
explanation: Django follows the 'batteries included' philosophy, providing an ORM, admin interface, auth system, and URL routing out of the box.

text: What is Django's ORM?
options: A UI component library that provides reusable Python widgets, form controls, layouts, and templates for constructing Django application pages
An Object-Relational Mapper that lets you interact with databases using Python classes
A URL routing engine that matches incoming paths to view functions and extracts named parameters from the request before dispatching
A caching system that stores rendered responses and database query results in memory to reduce repeated work on later requests
explanation: Django's ORM maps Python model classes to database tables and provides a Pythonic query API.

text: What are the trade-offs of using Node.js for CPU-intensive applications?
options: None, Node.js is ideal for all workloads because asynchronous APIs prevent CPU operations from blocking requests
The event loop can be blocked by synchronous CPU-intensive code, causing latency for all concurrent requests
Node.js is faster than Go for CPU tasks because V8 optimizes intensive loops automatically
CPU tasks automatically run in parallel through the event loop, allowing every request to use a separate core
explanation: Node's single-threaded event loop means CPU-bound work blocks all I/O. Worker Threads or microservices are needed to mitigate this.

text: What is a Django serialiser?
options: A class that stores serialized objects in a cache and returns previously generated representations
A class that converts complex data types (querysets, model instances) to Python primitives and validates input
A class that maps URL patterns to view functions and resolves incoming route parameters
A template component that renders model instances directly into complete HTML responses
explanation: Serialisers handle both serialisation (to JSON) and deserialisation (from JSON with validation) in DRF.

text: What is Flask-SQLAlchemy?
options: Flask's built-in ORM for defining models and database queries
An extension that integrates SQLAlchemy ORM with Flask
A Flask extension for generating and applying database migrations
A Flask extension for caching responses and database query results
explanation: Flask-SQLAlchemy simplifies using SQLAlchemy with Flask by managing sessions, connections, and model declaration.

text: How does Django handle CSRF protection?
options: It provides no built-in CSRF defense, so every application must implement token validation itself
Via a middleware that validates a CSRF token included in POST forms and AJAX requests
It authenticates POST requests exclusively with JWTs rather than form-specific CSRF tokens
It relies on HTTPS enforcement to prevent cross-site request forgery without validating a token
explanation: CsrfViewMiddleware checks the csrfmiddlewaretoken field in non-GET requests against the session token.

text: What is a Flask Blueprint?
options: A reusable starter project containing default settings, routes, templates, and deployment files
A way to organise a Flask app into modular components that can be registered on an application
A deployment configuration describing workers, environment variables, and production server settings
A database schema definition that declares tables, columns, relationships, and indexes for an application
explanation: Blueprints group routes, templates, and static files into reusable modules, making large Flask apps more organised.

text: How do you run background tasks in Django?
options: Using Django's built-in task scheduler
Using Celery with a message broker like Redis or RabbitMQ
Using threading only
Using asyncio directly
explanation: Celery is the standard Django solution for async/background task processing with Redis or RabbitMQ as the broker.

text: What is CSRF protection in Laravel?
options: SQL injection prevention through parameterized queries and escaped bindings applied to database statements by Laravel
Cross-Site Request Forgery protection via a hidden `@csrf` token in forms, verified by middleware
XSS protection through automatic HTML escaping of Blade output and sanitization of untrusted content in responses
Password hashing with Laravel's Hash facade and configurable algorithms such as bcrypt or Argon2 for stored credentials
explanation: Laravel's `VerifyCsrfToken` middleware rejects POST/PUT/DELETE requests without a valid token, preventing CSRF attacks.

text: What annotation marks the main entry point of a Spring Boot application?
options: @SpringApplication
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@SpringBootApplication
@MainClass
explanation: @SpringBootApplication combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan.

text: What annotation creates a REST controller in Spring Boot?
options: @Controller
@Service
@RestController
@Component
explanation: @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, making all handler methods return JSON/XML by default.

text: What is Django's middleware stack and how does it work?
options: A layered set of database-specific hooks that rewrite SQL before queries run and transform rows after the database responds
A layered set of hooks that process requests and responses globally before/after views
A URL-routing pipeline that matches paths, selects views, and converts route parameters before dispatching the request
An ORM extension layer that defines model behavior, manages migrations, and supplies reusable database query implementations
explanation: Each middleware's process_request runs before the view and process_response runs after, wrapping the view in a stack-like fashion.

text: How do you implement custom Django model managers?
options: Override the model's __init__ method to add database operations, then expose those operations through a custom constructor on each instance
Subclass models.Manager and define custom queryset methods; assign to the model's objects attribute
Monkey-patch the model class after import so new query methods are attached directly to its generated database fields
Define configuration inside the model's Meta class to replace the default manager and register custom filtering behavior automatically
explanation: Custom managers encapsulate common query patterns (e.g. PublishedManager returning .filter(status='published')) at the model level.

text: How do you handle database transactions in Django?
options: Transactions are committed automatically after each individual model save, so related operations cannot be rolled back together as one unit
Use atomic() context manager or decorator to wrap operations in a transaction that rolls back on exception
Use raw SQL BEGIN and COMMIT statements for every operation, because Django's ORM cannot control transaction boundaries safely
Django does not provide transaction management; rollback behavior must be implemented entirely by the database driver or application code
explanation: transaction.atomic() ensures that all database operations inside succeed or all are rolled back, maintaining data integrity.

text: What is Django Channels and when would you use it?
options: A Django admin plugin that adds channel-based dashboards and lets staff broadcast model updates through the administration site
An extension that adds WebSocket and async protocol support to Django using ASGI
A REST API layer that serializes Django models into JSON and routes HTTP requests through DRF-style resources
A background task library that schedules long-running jobs in worker processes and retries them after failures
explanation: Django Channels extends Django to handle WebSockets, long polling, and other async protocols via ASGI consumers.

text: What is the difference between Flask's request and g objects?
options: They are interchangeable context objects that expose the same request-scoped data and attributes
request holds incoming request data; g is an application context namespace for storing data during a request
g stores application-wide configuration shared across all requests, rather than temporary request data
request represents the outgoing response object, including status, headers, and rendered body content
explanation: g is reset for each request and used to store per-request data (e.g. current user) accessible throughout the request lifecycle.

text: What is ASGI and how does it differ from WSGI in Django?
options: ASGI is synchronous; WSGI supports async handlers, WebSockets, and long-lived connections while ASGI handles only regular HTTP
WSGI is synchronous; ASGI supports async handlers, WebSockets, and long-lived connections alongside regular HTTP
WSGI and ASGI use the same synchronous interface, and neither provides native WebSocket or long-lived connection support in Django
ASGI is Django's template interface; WSGI is the protocol for asynchronous handlers, WebSockets, and long-lived connections
explanation: Django 3.1+ supports ASGI, enabling async views and Django Channels. WSGI remains for synchronous HTTP workloads.

text: What is Spring Boot?
options: An opinionated Java UI framework that generates desktop interfaces with auto-configuration and embedded browser servers
An opinionated framework that simplifies Spring application setup with auto-configuration and embedded servers
A build tool that compiles Spring applications and packages dependencies, while embedded servers are provided separately by the JDK
A testing library that discovers integration tests and configures assertions for Spring applications without requiring application setup
explanation: Spring Boot eliminates boilerplate XML configuration, embedding Tomcat/Jetty and auto-configuring beans based on classpath.

text: What is dependency injection in Spring?
options: A mechanism for importing external libraries into a project, allowing the IoC container to resolve package dependencies automatically
The IoC container providing objects their dependencies instead of objects creating them
Injecting parameterized SQL queries into repository methods so the database can construct and execute application dependencies
A testing pattern in which mock objects create the classes under test, replacing the Spring IoC container during production startup
explanation: Spring's IoC container manages bean creation and injects dependencies via constructor, setter, or field injection.

text: What is a Spring Bean?
options: A Java annotation that marks a class for component scanning and bean registration
An object instantiated, assembled, and managed by the Spring IoC container
A database entity mapped to a table by JPA, independent of Spring's IoC lifecycle management
A REST endpoint definition that maps HTTP requests directly to controller methods
explanation: Beans are the fundamental unit of a Spring application — objects managed by the ApplicationContext.

text: What is Vue Server-Side Rendering (SSR) with Nuxt.js?
options: Executing Vue components only in the browser after JavaScript bundles have loaded, with Nuxt.js serving as a client-side routing layer
Rendering Vue components on the server per request, improving SEO and initial load time — Nuxt.js provides the full SSR framework
Generating static HTML during the Nuxt build and serving the same output for every request, without rendering components on the server
Selecting hosting, caching, and process settings for a Nuxt deployment, rather than describing how Vue components are rendered
explanation: Nuxt.js provides universal rendering: SSR by default, SSG for static pages, ISR for stale-while-revalidate, and client-only rendering.

text: What embedded server does Spring Boot use by default?
options: Tomcat
Jetty
Undertow
Nginx
explanation: Spring Boot embeds Apache Tomcat by default, though Jetty or Undertow can be substituted via dependency exclusions.

text: What HTTP annotations map specific methods in Spring MVC?
options: @RequestGet, @RequestPost, @RequestPut, @RequestDelete
@GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping
@HttpGet, @HttpPost, @HttpPut, and @HttpDelete
@Route('GET'), @Route('POST'), @Route('PUT'), @Route('DELETE')
explanation: @GetMapping, @PostMapping, etc. are composed annotations combining @RequestMapping with the HTTP method.

text: What is Spring Security and what does it provide?
options: A network firewall that filters inbound and outbound traffic for a Spring application
A comprehensive authentication and authorisation framework for Spring applications
A certificate manager that issues, renews, and installs SSL credentials for Spring applications
A web application firewall that blocks malicious HTTP requests using signatures and network rules
explanation: Spring Security provides authentication (who you are), authorisation (what you can do), CSRF protection, and more.

text: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, and @Repository?
options: They are unrelated annotations for separate runtime frameworks, with no shared component semantics or application-layer conventions
All are @Component specialisations; @Service marks service layer, @Repository marks DAO layer and adds exception translation
@Repository is intended for REST controllers, where it maps HTTP requests and serializes responses instead of accessing persistence
@Service directly creates REST endpoints and replaces controller mappings, while @Component is reserved for database access objects
explanation: These stereotypes are semantically equivalent for component scanning, but @Repository adds persistence exception translation.

text: How does Spring Boot handle transactions?
options: Requires developers to open, commit, and roll back every JDBC transaction manually inside each annotated service method
@Transactional annotation wraps methods in a transaction, rolling back on runtime exceptions by default
Can only be enabled through XML transaction definitions, because annotations do not participate in Spring transaction management
Uses application-configured AOP proxies that developers must create and wire manually before any method can begin a transaction
explanation: @Transactional uses Spring AOP to begin/commit/rollback transactions around annotated methods.

text: What is Spring Cloud and what problems does it solve?
options: A managed cloud hosting service that provisions virtual machines, storage, and databases for deploying Spring applications
A suite of tools for distributed system patterns: service discovery, config server, circuit breakers, gateways
A Kubernetes operator that schedules Spring workloads and reconciles deployments, services, and pods inside a cluster
A Docker-based packaging wrapper that builds container images and runs Spring applications without distributed-system features
explanation: Spring Cloud provides tools like Eureka (discovery), Config Server, Gateway, and Resilience4j for microservices.

text: How do you define custom Spring Data JPA queries?
options: Only relying on derived repository method names, without declaring @Query or writing JPQL/native SQL
Using @Query annotation with JPQL or native SQL, or by method name convention (findByFieldAndOtherField)
Writing JDBC templates and manually mapping ResultSet rows instead of using Spring Data repository queries
Defining every query in persistence.xml or repository XML descriptors, then loading them at startup
explanation: Spring Data derives queries from method names or you can use @Query for complex JPQL/SQL.

text: What is the difference between eager and lazy loading in Spring Data JPA?
options: EAGER and LAZY both load associations immediately, but differ in whether the SQL is issued in one query or several
EAGER fetches related entities immediately; LAZY defers fetching until the field is accessed (within an open session)
LAZY relationships are unsupported by JPA repositories, so every association must be loaded eagerly before use
They are equivalent fetch modes; the choice only changes entity annotations and never affects database access timing
explanation: LAZY fetch (default for collections) avoids unnecessary JOINs but requires an open persistence context when accessed.

text: How does Spring AOP work and what are its limitations?
options: It generates and modifies compiled class bytecode during application startup, so calls inside the same bean are intercepted
Spring AOP uses JDK dynamic proxies (interface) or CGLIB (class) proxies; it can't intercept internal method calls within the same bean
It intercepts every invocation made on a proxied object, including private, final, and self-invoked methods within the bean
It always relies on AspectJ load-time or compile-time weaving and does not use JDK or CGLIB proxies
explanation: Spring AOP proxies wrap beans — self-invocation bypasses the proxy. For full AOP use compile/load-time AspectJ weaving.

text: How do you implement distributed tracing in Spring Boot?
options: Using ordinary application logs to record request messages, without propagating correlation or trace context between services
Using Spring Cloud Sleuth (or Micrometer Tracing) to add trace/span IDs propagated across service calls, exported to Zipkin/Jaeger
Using Actuator metrics to measure request counts and latency, which automatically creates and exports distributed trace spans
Using Spring Security audit events to propagate authentication details as trace IDs through every downstream service
explanation: Sleuth/Micrometer Tracing adds trace context to HTTP headers and logs, enabling end-to-end request tracing across microservices.

text: What is N+1 query problem in JPA and how do you solve it?
options: A connection pool issue occurs when too few database connections are available, causing requests to wait or fail
Fetching N entities individually triggers N extra queries for related data; fixed with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or batch fetching
A transaction isolation issue occurs when concurrent transactions expose uncommitted data or produce inconsistent reads
A database index problem occurs when missing indexes make a single join query scan many rows instead of using lookup paths
explanation: @EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH in JPQL fetches associations in one query. spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size handles collections.

text: What is PHP-FPM?
options: A PHP version that adds a FastCGI interface and includes a built-in worker pool for serving web requests
FastCGI Process Manager — a PHP process manager that handles concurrent requests for Nginx/Apache
A Composer package that provides reusable PHP classes for connecting an application directly to Nginx or Apache
A web framework that routes HTTP requests to PHP controllers and manages templates, sessions, and application configuration
explanation: PHP-FPM spawns worker processes, enabling Nginx to serve PHP applications with high concurrency.

text: What type of database is MongoDB?
options: Relational (SQL)
Document-oriented NoSQL
Graph database
Key-value store
explanation: MongoDB stores data as BSON documents (binary JSON) in collections, making it a document-oriented NoSQL database.

text: What is the MongoDB equivalent of a SQL table?
options: Database
Collection
Document
Index
explanation: Collections hold documents — analogous to SQL tables holding rows.

text: How do you query documents in MongoDB?
options: SELECT * FROM collection
db.collection.find({filter})
FIND WHERE
db.query({filter})
explanation: find() returns a cursor of documents matching the filter; findOne() returns the first match.

text: What command starts the MongoDB shell?
options: mongo or mongosh
mongodb-cli
db connect
mysql -u admin
explanation: mongosh (MongoDB Shell) is the modern CLI for interacting with MongoDB; the legacy mongo shell is older.

text: What does $lookup do in an aggregation pipeline?
options: Looks up an index
Performs a left outer join with another collection
Searches text fields
Finds duplicate documents
explanation: $lookup joins documents from a foreign collection into the pipeline, similar to SQL JOINs.

text: What is a NoSQL database?
options: A database without any query language, where applications must inspect stored data directly
A non-relational database that stores data in formats other than tables (documents, key-value, graph, column-family)
A database designed specifically to run on Node.js rather than on a database server
A database that never enforces schemas or validates document structure in any situation
explanation: NoSQL encompasses document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), column-family (Cassandra), and graph (Neo4j) databases.

text: What is the MongoDB aggregation pipeline?
options: A data import tool that loads external files into collections and converts them into documents
A framework for data transformation using staged operators ($match, $group, $project, $sort, $lookup) applied sequentially
A replication mechanism that synchronizes collection changes between primary and secondary servers
An indexing strategy that creates specialized lookup structures for frequently queried fields
explanation: The aggregation pipeline processes documents through sequential stages, enabling complex analytics like grouping, joining, and reshaping.

text: What is sharding in MongoDB?
options: A maintenance process that permanently deletes old documents from collections to reduce storage usage
Horizontal scaling that distributes data across multiple shards based on a shard key
An encryption mechanism that protects database files and network traffic from unauthorized access
A backup strategy that creates additional copies of collections on separate storage systems
explanation: Sharding partitions data by a shard key across shards, enabling MongoDB to scale beyond a single server's capacity.

text: What are Spring Boot's main approaches to asynchronous processing?
options: Blocking Spring MVC controllers, synchronous JDBC calls, and request-thread execution without executors or reactive streams
@Async methods, Spring WebFlux reactive programming, @Scheduled tasks, and Kafka/RabbitMQ message consumers
Java virtual threads as the sole asynchronous mechanism, replacing @Async, WebFlux, schedulers, and message consumers
Celery worker processes handling every background job, with Spring limited to synchronous HTTP request handling
explanation: @Async runs methods in a thread pool. WebFlux uses Reactor for reactive streams. Messaging decouples async workloads.

text: How does Spring Security's OAuth2 resource server work?
options: It authenticates users by issuing signed access tokens from the application, rather than validating Bearer tokens on incoming requests
It validates incoming Bearer JWTs/opaque tokens against a JWK Set or introspection endpoint and populates the SecurityContext
It acts as a standalone OAuth2 authorization server, managing logins, consent, clients, and token issuance for other applications
It forwards every request to a Keycloak server for validation and does not use JWT decoders, JWK Sets, or introspection endpoints
explanation: A resource server validates tokens (via spring-security-oauth2-resource-server), not issue them. Authorization Servers (Keycloak, Auth0) issue tokens.

text: What are the trade-offs of microservices versus a monolith in Spring Boot?
options: Microservices require independent deployment but provide no meaningful scaling benefit, while avoiding most distributed-system latency and consistency concerns
Microservices offer independent deployment and scalability but add distributed system complexity (latency, consistency, operational overhead)
Monoliths cannot be deployed independently or scaled, so Spring Boot applications must be split into services for production use
Spring Boot is designed only for microservices, and its dependency injection and configuration model cannot support a modular monolithic application
explanation: Microservices decompose by business capability but require service discovery, distributed tracing, resilience patterns, and more infrastructure.

text: What is a BSON document in MongoDB?
options: A fixed-schema relational table row with predefined columns and SQL values
A binary JSON document with typed fields stored in a MongoDB collection
A MongoDB index structure containing sorted keys and query metadata
A MongoDB configuration file containing connection settings and collection definitions
explanation: BSON extends JSON with additional types like Date, ObjectId, and Binary, and is used for MongoDB's internal storage.

text: How do you insert a document in MongoDB?
options: An SQL INSERT statement targeting a relational table
db.collection.insertOne() or insertMany()
An ADD DOCUMENT command in the MongoDB shell
db.push() appends documents to a collection
explanation: insertOne() inserts a single document; insertMany() inserts an array of documents into a collection.

text: What is the _id field in MongoDB?
options: An automatically generated sequential integer assigned by MongoDB, equivalent to an SQL identity column
A unique identifier (ObjectId by default) that serves as the primary key for every document
A mandatory field that application code must explicitly define before MongoDB will accept any document
A text-only identifier stored as a string, because MongoDB does not support ObjectId or other identifier types
explanation: Every MongoDB document must have _id. If not provided, MongoDB generates a 12-byte ObjectId automatically.

text: What is the MongoDB $text operator?
options: Converts fields to strings
Performs a text search on fields with a text index
Encodes binary text
Validates text fields
explanation: $text operator requires a text index and enables full-text search with language-aware stemming and stop words.

text: What is a compound index in MongoDB?
options: An index on a nested field
An index on multiple fields in a defined order
An index created automatically
An index for text search
explanation: Compound indexes cover queries on multiple fields. The order matters — MongoDB uses prefix rules for compound index matching.

text: What is pattern matching in Rust?
options: A regular-expression feature that extracts matching substrings from text according to a specified pattern
The `match` expression that destructures values and matches against patterns, exhaustively handling all cases
A string-search operation that locates matching characters and returns their positions in the input
A loop construct that repeatedly executes a body until a matching condition becomes false
explanation: `match` is Rust's primary control flow for enums, structs, and ranges; the compiler enforces all variants are handled.

text: What command sets a key-value pair in Redis?
options: INSERT key value
SET key value
PUT key value
STORE key value
explanation: SET key value stores a string. SET key value EX 60 sets it with a 60-second TTL.

text: How does MongoDB handle schema validation?
options: It enforces a fixed relational schema and rejects any document that does not match every declared SQL column
Via JSON Schema validators on collections using $jsonSchema in db.createCollection() or collMod
Schema validation is unavailable in MongoDB, so collections accept every BSON document without server-side checks
Only at application level, where ODM models inspect documents before sending them and the database performs no validation
explanation: MongoDB's flexible schema can be constrained with JSON Schema validation rules on collections, enforcing structure at the DB layer.

text: What is the write concern in MongoDB and how does it affect durability?
options: Defines formatting rules for serialized writes, including field ordering, whitespace, and the representation of BSON values
Specifies acknowledgment level from how many replica set members must confirm a write before returning success (w:1, majority, 0)
Controls how query results are sorted and whether MongoDB returns them in index order or natural collection order
Sets the strictness of collection schema validation, determining which fields and BSON types may be written
explanation: w:majority ensures the write is committed to a majority of replica set members before acknowledging, preventing data loss on primary failure.

text: What is the aggregation pipeline $facet stage used for?
options: Performs schema transformation by rewriting every input document into a single standardized output structure before later stages
Running multiple aggregation sub-pipelines on the same input documents simultaneously (multi-faceted search)
Joins collections by matching local and foreign fields and embedding the related documents in each input result
Groups documents by calendar date and computes one aggregate result for each day without requiring a preceding $group stage
explanation: $facet allows computing multiple aggregation results (e.g. category counts, price ranges) in a single pipeline pass.

text: How do you optimise MongoDB query performance?
options: Increase RAM only; additional memory will resolve slow queries regardless of indexes, document size, projections, or data model
Use explain('executionStats'), add appropriate indexes, avoid large documents, use projection, and consider data model changes
Disable the query planner so MongoDB executes every operation using the collection scan path selected by the application
Always use $lookup to let MongoDB optimize related reads and replace indexes, projections, and appropriate denormalization
explanation: explain() shows the query plan (COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN). Proper indexes, projections, and schema design are the primary levers.

text: What is the MongoDB oplog?
options: An application collection in the local database that records authentication failures and server diagnostics
A capped collection in the local database that records all write operations for replication
A rotating file in the application database that stores query plans and index usage statistics
A temporary collection on each shard that records network requests and client connection events
explanation: The oplog (operations log) is used by secondaries to replicate writes from the primary. It powers change streams and point-in-time recovery.

text: How does read concern affect MongoDB query results?
options: Controls which indexes MongoDB may select, with local favoring primary indexes and majority requiring replicas to sort results
Determines the consistency of data read — local returns most recent data on node; majority returns data acknowledged by majority of replica set
Applies only to aggregation transactions, determining whether writes are committed before a query returns results
Provides SQL-style snapshot isolation for every query, ensuring all reads use one synchronized version across the replica set
explanation: readConcern 'majority' prevents reading data that could be rolled back if the primary fails, at the cost of slightly older data.

text: How would you implement full-text search in MongoDB vs. using Elasticsearch?
options: MongoDB text indexes and Elasticsearch provide the same phrase matching and relevance features, differing mainly in client libraries and deployment
MongoDB's text indexes provide basic full-text search; Elasticsearch offers advanced relevance scoring, faceting, and language analysis at scale
Elasticsearch is a MongoDB storage engine that automatically indexes collections and exposes its search API without data synchronization
MongoDB requires Elasticsearch for any text search because its indexes support only exact equality matches and prefix lookups
explanation: For advanced search requirements (relevance tuning, autocomplete, complex facets), Elasticsearch is preferred over MongoDB's built-in text indexes.

text: What is Redis?
options: A disk-based relational database that stores tables with schemas, joins, and foreign-key constraints
An in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, and message broker
A disk-based key-value database that persists every operation before responding and provides no in-memory data model
A distributed search engine designed for inverted indexes, relevance ranking, and full-text document retrieval
explanation: Redis stores data in memory for ultra-fast access, supporting rich data structures and persistence options.

text: What does the TTL (Time-To-Live) mean in Redis?
options: The maximum lifetime assigned to a client connection before Redis closes its socket
The remaining time in seconds before a key is automatically deleted
The number of seconds a transaction may wait in a queue before Redis discards its commands
A metadata field measuring how long a value has existed since it was first inserted
explanation: TTL specifies how long a key lives. EXPIRE key seconds sets it; TTL key queries it.

text: What is the purpose of AWS Auto Scaling?
options: To monitor logs
To adjust compute capacity based on demand
To replicate databases
To manage DNS
explanation: Elastic Kubernetes Service manages Kubernetes clusters.

text: How do you delete a key in Redis?
options: REMOVE key
DEL key
DELETE key
DROP key
explanation: DEL key (or UNLINK key for async deletion) removes one or more keys. It returns the number of keys deleted.

text: What does the MULTI/EXEC block do in Redis?
options: Replicates every command to connected replicas and waits for their acknowledgements before continuing execution
Queues commands in a transaction block — all commands execute atomically when EXEC is called
Marks commands as read-only so they can bypass transactional state changes and run safely on replicas
Creates a client-side pipeline that batches commands for transmission but executes each one independently
explanation: MULTI queues commands; EXEC executes them all atomically. DISCARD cancels the queued transaction.

text: What is a Redis eviction policy?
options: A rule that determines when a replica is promoted to primary after Redis detects a failed master
A rule that determines which keys are removed when Redis reaches its maxmemory limit
A mechanism that automatically assigns expiration times and deletes keys when their individual TTL reaches zero
A configuration that determines when in-memory data is written to an RDB snapshot or an append-only log
explanation: Policies like allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, allkeys-lfu determine which keys are evicted when memory is full.

text: What is the Redis SCAN command and why is it preferred over KEYS?
options: SCAN is a slower replacement for KEYS that still gathers every matching key before returning the complete result to the client
SCAN iterates keys incrementally with a cursor, avoiding blocking the server; KEYS returns all matches at once and blocks
They are identical commands with different names, and both return all matching keys in one blocking operation
KEYS is the newer nonblocking command designed for production databases, while SCAN is retained mainly for compatibility
explanation: KEYS blocks while scanning all keys — dangerous in production. SCAN returns a cursor for non-blocking incremental iteration.

text: How does Redis Cluster handle data partitioning?
options: Uses consistent hashing on a ring, assigning each key to the nearest node and moving only adjacent key ranges when membership changes
Uses 16,384 hash slots distributed across nodes; keys are assigned to slots via CRC16(key) % 16384
Distributes keys randomly among available nodes, relying on replication and retries to locate values during subsequent requests
Uses ordered key ranges divided between nodes, routing requests by comparing each key lexicographically with partition boundaries
explanation: Redis Cluster assigns hash slots to nodes. Keys with the same hash tag ({tag}) land on the same slot for multi-key operations.

text: What is caching and why is it used?
options: Storing infrequently accessed data in archival storage to reduce memory usage and improve durability
Storing frequently accessed data in fast memory to reduce latency and backend load
Organizing records with lookup metadata to accelerate database queries and avoid full-table scans
Encoding repeated data into smaller representations to reduce network bandwidth and disk storage requirements
explanation: Caching reduces expensive database or API calls by serving results from fast in-memory stores like Redis.

text: What does the INCR command do in Redis?
options: Atomically increments an integer value by 10
Atomically increments an integer value by 1
Returns an integer value without modifying the key or its stored value
Deletes the key after reading its current integer value
explanation: INCR is atomic, making it safe for distributed counters without race conditions.

text: What is a Redis List?
options: A collection of unique members maintained in ascending lexicographic order, without positional push or pop operations
A linked list of strings that supports push/pop from both ends (LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, RPOP)
A key-value structure that maps field names to string values and supports HSET and HGET operations
An array-like structure that stores strings at fixed indexes and supports random-access updates
explanation: Redis Lists are doubly-linked lists used for queues (RPUSH + BLPOP), stacks (LPUSH + LPOP), and timelines.

text: What is the difference between Redis EXPIRE and EXPIREAT?
options: They differ only in the command name; both interpret the argument as a Unix timestamp measured from the current time
EXPIRE sets TTL in seconds from now; EXPIREAT sets an absolute Unix timestamp when the key expires
EXPIREAT is deprecated and should be replaced with EXPIRE, which accepts an absolute expiration time in seconds
EXPIRE accepts milliseconds directly, while EXPIREAT accepts only relative durations in seconds from command execution
explanation: EXPIRE key 300 expires in 300 seconds. EXPIREAT key 1700000000 expires at a specific Unix timestamp.

text: What is Redis persistence (RDB vs AOF)?
options: Two replication strategies that determine whether commands are copied synchronously or asynchronously to secondary Redis nodes
RDB snapshots the dataset periodically; AOF logs every write operation for finer recovery granularity
Two clustering modes that divide keys across nodes or keep the entire dataset on one Redis server
Two eviction policies that decide whether Redis removes the oldest keys or the least recently used keys
explanation: RDB is compact and fast to restore; AOF has better durability (every write logged). Both can be used together.

text: How do Lua scripts improve Redis atomicity?
options: Lua scripts do not provide atomicity; EVAL queues each command separately, allowing other clients to interleave between script operations
Lua scripts execute atomically on the Redis server using EVAL, ensuring complex multi-step operations are never interleaved
Lua scripts execute concurrently in worker threads, so overlapping EVAL calls improve throughput without blocking Redis's event loop
Lua scripts bypass Redis's command processing and write directly to storage, avoiding the event loop and transaction coordination
explanation: EVAL script numkeys key [key ...] arg [arg ...] runs a Lua script atomically, avoiding race conditions between WATCH and EXEC.

text: What is Redis Streams and how does it differ from Pub/Sub?
options: Streams are transient fan-out notifications delivered once to currently connected clients, whereas Pub/Sub stores messages for later replay
Streams (XADD, XREAD, consumer groups) are persistent, replay-able message logs; Pub/Sub messages are ephemeral and fire-and-forget
Streams provide unordered low-latency broadcasts without retention, while Pub/Sub assigns entries to durable consumer groups
Pub/Sub messages are persistent log entries readable by ID, whereas Streams only deliver events to subscribers connected at publish time
explanation: Redis Streams persist messages, support consumer groups with acknowledgement, and allow replaying messages from any offset.

text: What does List(1, 2, 3).updated(1, 9) return in Scala?
options: A new list containing the elements 1, 9, and 3
The original list after changing its second element
A new list containing the elements 1, 2, and 9
An error because immutable lists cannot be updated
explanation: The updated method returns a new list with the element at zero-based index 1 replaced by 9. The original immutable list is not modified.

text: What does ACID stand for in databases?
options: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Availability, Consistency, Integrity, Distribution
Atomic, Complete, Independent, Durable
Asynchronous, Concurrent, Indexed, Distributed
explanation: ACID properties ensure reliable transaction processing: all-or-nothing atomicity, consistent state, isolated concurrent transactions, and durable committed data.

text: How do you list all databases in PostgreSQL?
options: SHOW DATABASES
\l or SELECT datname FROM pg_database
LIST DATABASES
SHOW TABLES
explanation: \l in psql lists databases. pg_database is the system catalog table for database metadata.

text: What does the EXPLAIN command do in PostgreSQL?
options: Lists table columns
Shows the query execution plan chosen by the planner
Explains a stored procedure
Displays table permissions
explanation: EXPLAIN shows the query plan (Seq Scan, Index Scan, Hash Join, etc.) without executing the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it.

text: What are the consistency trade-offs of Redis Cluster during network partitions?
options: Redis Cluster guarantees strong consistency during partitions by synchronously replicating every write to all replicas before acknowledging the client request
Redis Cluster prioritises availability — during a partition, the side with the master accepts writes that could be lost if it had not replicated yet
During partitions, Redis Cluster pauses writes on every master and replica until all nodes reconnect, preserving a single globally consistent history
Redis Cluster uses two-phase commit across masters and replicas, so a partitioned node cannot acknowledge a write until the distributed commit completes
explanation: Redis Cluster is AP (CAP theorem) — it continues operating during partitions but may lose writes that weren't replicated before failover.

text: What is the O(N) complexity risk in Redis and which commands should be avoided in production?
options: Redis operations are generally constant time because the server indexes every object, so scanning commands do not become slower as collections grow
Commands like KEYS *, SMEMBERS on large sets, LRANGE on full lists block the single-threaded server for N items
Only FLUSHALL is dangerous in production; commands such as KEYS, SMEMBERS, and full-range LRANGE remain bounded regardless of collection size
Redis write commands always scan every item in the affected database, making SET and HSET the primary O(N) operations that block the server
explanation: Redis is single-threaded for commands. O(N) commands on large datasets block all other clients. Use SCAN, SSCAN, HSCAN instead.

text: What are window functions in PostgreSQL?
options: Functions that render calculated values into a new result column while replacing the original rows
Functions that perform calculations across a set of table rows related to the current row without collapsing them
Functions that combine grouped rows into one summary record and remove individual row detail
Functions that execute analytical queries as reusable procedures independently of the current table rows
explanation: Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, SUM OVER PARTITION BY) perform analytics without losing row-level detail.

text: What is Vue's v-bind directive?
options: A directive that listens for DOM events and evaluates a JavaScript handler when the event occurs
Dynamically binds an HTML attribute or component prop to a JavaScript expression: :href='url' or v-bind:href='url'
A directive that conditionally includes or removes an element based on a Boolean JavaScript expression
A directive that repeats an element for every item in an array and provides the item as a local variable
explanation: v-bind (shorthand :) syncs attribute values with reactive data, e.g. :class, :style, :src.

text: What is PostgreSQL?
options: A document-oriented database that stores flexible JSON records without relational tables or SQL constraints
An open-source object-relational database system known for standards compliance and advanced features
A managed database service available exclusively through cloud providers, without local installation or self-hosting
A distributed key-value database that retrieves records by keys rather than supporting relational queries and joins
explanation: PostgreSQL (Postgres) is a powerful open-source RDBMS with advanced features like JSONB, full-text search, and custom types.

text: What is a FOREIGN KEY?
options: A key value maintained in a separate database or server, used to identify records outside the current database
A column that references the PRIMARY KEY of another table, enforcing referential integrity
An optional identifier whose values must be unique only when an application chooses to enforce that rule
An ordinary indexed column created to speed up searches, without requiring references or enforcing relationships
explanation: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity — the referenced row must exist in the parent table.

text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
options: Two interchangeable SQL clauses that filter rows and groups in exactly the same way
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY
HAVING filters rows before grouping, while WHERE filters aggregate groups afterward
WHERE is reserved for join predicates, while HAVING handles all other row conditions
explanation: WHERE filters individual rows. HAVING filters aggregated groups (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).

text: What is a serial / SERIAL data type in PostgreSQL?
options: A fixed-length character type that pads short values and enforces a predetermined number of stored characters
An auto-incrementing integer sequence — shorthand for creating a sequence and using nextval() as default
A universally unique identifier type that generates nonsequential values for identifying rows across systems
A floating-point numeric type used to store approximate decimal values with a configurable precision
explanation: SERIAL creates an implicit sequence. The modern equivalent is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY.

text: What is the difference between B-tree, Hash, GiST, and GIN indexes in PostgreSQL?
options: They are interchangeable index implementations with identical operators and performance; the choice only changes the index's internal storage format
B-tree (default): ordered, equality/range; Hash: equality only; GiST: geometric, full-text; GIN: multi-valued types like arrays/jsonb/tsvector
PostgreSQL supports only B-tree and Hash indexes for ordinary tables; GiST and GIN are query-planner strategies rather than index access methods
GIN is optimized primarily for scalar numeric comparisons and ordered ranges, while B-tree is intended for arrays, JSONB, and full-text values
explanation: Choosing the right index type is critical: GIN for full-text search and JSONB paths, B-tree for most scalar queries.

text: Which AWS service provides managed Kubernetes?
options: ECS
EKS
Lambda
CloudFormation
explanation: Query S3 data using SQL without infrastructure.

text: A company needs to analyze large-scale log data quickly. Which service should they use?
options: CloudWatch
Athena
RDS
DynamoDB
explanation: AWS’s managed data warehouse.

text: What are PostgreSQL roles and how do they differ from users?
options: They are the same; roles replaced users in PostgreSQL 8.1
Users are roles with LOGIN privilege; roles without LOGIN are used for privilege grouping
Roles are for schema access only
Users have passwords; roles don't
explanation: In modern PostgreSQL, CREATE USER is shorthand for CREATE ROLE ... LOGIN. Roles can be granted to other roles for privilege inheritance.

text: What is MVCC in PostgreSQL?
options: A constraint allowing one column to contain multiple values while coordinating updates across related transactions
Multi-Version Concurrency Control — PostgreSQL maintains multiple versions of rows to allow concurrent readers and writers without locking
A replication protocol that copies committed row changes from the primary server to standby databases
A query optimisation technique that rewrites SQL statements into faster execution plans before they run
explanation: MVCC allows reads to see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers. Old row versions are cleaned up by VACUUM.

text: What is VACUUM in PostgreSQL and why is it needed?
options: A defragmentation command that reorganises every table and index into contiguous disk blocks without changing row visibility
Reclaims storage from dead tuples created by UPDATE/DELETE (MVCC), updates statistics, and prevents transaction ID wraparound
A backup utility that copies committed table data to an archive and restores it after a server or disk failure
A compression tool that reduces the physical size of table pages and rewrites stored values into a smaller representation
explanation: MVCC leaves dead tuples after updates/deletes. VACUUM removes them. VACUUM ANALYZE also updates query planner statistics.

text: What is the difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE in PostgreSQL?
options: TRUNCATE and DELETE are equivalent commands; both scan qualifying rows, fire row-level triggers, and support identical filtering semantics
TRUNCATE removes all rows instantly without scanning (DDL), doesn't fire row-level triggers, and can't be conditionally filtered; DELETE is DML
DELETE is always faster because it removes rows directly without recording individual changes or checking row visibility
TRUNCATE supports WHERE clauses and joins for selective removal, whereas DELETE can only remove every row from a table
explanation: TRUNCATE is much faster for clearing tables but is less flexible. Both are transactional in PostgreSQL.

text: How does PostgreSQL's query planner choose between Seq Scan and Index Scan?
options: Based primarily on table size, choosing an index for small tables and a sequential scan for larger tables regardless of matching rows
Based on cost estimates using table statistics (pg_stats); index scans are preferred when a small fraction of rows match
Based on query complexity and the number of joins, without using column statistics or estimating how many rows will match
Always choosing an Index Scan whenever a usable index exists, because indexed access is assumed to be cheaper than reading the table
explanation: The planner estimates cost based on row counts, selectivity from pg_stats, and random_page_cost. Inaccurate statistics (stale ANALYZE) lead to bad plans.

text: What is logical replication in PostgreSQL and how does it differ from streaming replication?
options: Streaming replication publishes row-level DML changes through replication slots, while logical replication copies complete data files and WAL; both require identical server versions
Streaming replication copies WAL records (physical); logical replication publishes and subscribes to changes (DML) — allowing selective table replication and cross-version support
Logical replication sends every WAL record for an entire cluster, whereas streaming replication selects individual tables; logical is limited to same-version physical copies
Streaming replication is intended only for backup archives and cannot maintain a standby, while logical replication mirrors all databases automatically without subscriptions
explanation: Logical replication (PUBLICATION/SUBSCRIPTION) replicates specific tables and supports different schemas on subscriber, enabling zero-downtime upgrades.

text: What is the WAL (Write-Ahead Log) in PostgreSQL?
options: A sequential log of executed SQL statements written before query results are returned, primarily used for auditing and statement replay
A sequential log of all changes written before being applied to data files, ensuring durability and enabling replication and PITR
A durable log of application errors and transaction messages written by the server, used mainly for diagnostics rather than crash recovery
A rotating log of slow statements and checkpoint activity, collected by logging settings and unrelated to changes in database pages
explanation: WAL ensures crash recovery (REDO) and forms the basis of streaming/logical replication and point-in-time recovery (PITR).

text: How do deadlocks occur in PostgreSQL and how are they resolved?
options: They occur when a transaction waits too long for a lock; PostgreSQL resolves them by cancelling the lock wait after deadlock_timeout expires
When two transactions hold locks the other needs; PostgreSQL detects cycles and aborts one transaction with an error
They are prevented by lock_timeout, which terminates both conflicting transactions whenever they request incompatible row or table locks
They are avoided under READ UNCOMMITTED because that isolation level permits dirty reads and therefore never waits for conflicting locks
explanation: PostgreSQL's deadlock detector runs every deadlock_timeout (default 1s). The solution is consistent lock ordering in application code.

text: What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveal that EXPLAIN alone does not?
options: The optimizer's estimated costs, estimated row counts, index selectivity assumptions, and chosen plan before execution
Actual execution time, actual rows (vs. estimated), buffer hit/miss counts, and which plan nodes ran
The complete SQL parse tree, resolved data types, rewritten query text, and planner transformations before execution
Available indexes, table constraints, column statistics, and catalog metadata consulted by the planner
explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and compares actual rows/time with estimates, revealing planner miscalibrations and slow nodes.

text: How do you handle JSON deep querying efficiently in PostgreSQL?
options: Store JSON as TEXT, create a B-tree index, and search nested values with leading-wildcard LIKE predicates
Create a GIN index on a JSONB column and use @> (contains), ? (key exists), #>> (path extraction) operators
Cast JSONB to TEXT at query time and apply case-insensitive LIKE patterns for every desired key and value
Create a hash index on serialized JSON text and use POSIX regular expressions to locate nested keys
explanation: GIN indexes on JSONB support @> and ? operations efficiently. jsonb_path_query and @? support JSONPath expressions.

text: What is the relationship between FastAPI and Starlette?
options: FastAPI is a direct fork of Starlette that keeps its routing and middleware implementation unchanged, adding only a different name and command-line interface
FastAPI is built on top of Starlette, inheriting its ASGI core, middleware, WebSocket, and static files while adding Pydantic and OpenAPI
They are competing frameworks for the same ASGI use cases, with FastAPI providing validation and OpenAPI while Starlette focuses on unrelated synchronous web applications
Starlette uses FastAPI internally as its application layer, relying on FastAPI for ASGI dispatch while providing only lower-level request and response helper classes
explanation: FastAPI wraps Starlette with an added layer for type-based validation, dependency injection, and automatic API documentation.

text: What is a training set in ML?
options: A set of test scenarios
The labelled data used to train (fit) a model
The data used to evaluate model performance
The final production dataset
explanation: The training set is used to fit model parameters. The test set is held out for final evaluation.

text: What is the role of a loss function in ML?
options: To track the elapsed time and computational resources used during each training iteration
To measure the difference between predicted and actual values, guiding optimisation
To identify the most important input variables before fitting the predictive model
To create separate training and evaluation partitions from the available labelled examples
explanation: The loss function (e.g. MSE for regression, cross-entropy for classification) quantifies model error to minimise during training.

text: What is cross-validation and why is it used?
options: A data augmentation procedure that creates additional examples by applying transformations to the original observations
A technique to evaluate model performance by training/testing on different subsets (folds) of data to reduce variance in estimates
A hyperparameter search procedure that evaluates many configurations using one fixed validation partition
A regularisation approach that adds penalties to the objective to constrain model coefficients during training
explanation: k-fold cross-validation trains on k-1 folds and tests on 1 fold, repeating k times — giving a more reliable performance estimate.

text: What is regularisation in ML and what problem does it solve?
options: Rescaling every input variable to a common numerical range before optimisation to improve numerical stability
Penalising model complexity to prevent overfitting — L1 (Lasso) promotes sparsity, L2 (Ridge) shrinks weights
Changing the prediction objective so its numerical values are comparable across datasets and training runs
Increasing the number of labelled examples available to the learner so it can estimate patterns more reliably
explanation: L2 adds λ∑w² to the loss, shrinking weights toward zero. L1 adds λ∑|w|, zeroing some weights for feature selection.

text: What is feature engineering?
options: The process of selecting a neural network architecture and deciding how many layers and units it should contain
The process of creating, transforming, or selecting input features to improve model performance
The process of adjusting learning rates, batch sizes, and regularisation strengths using validation performance
The process of dividing observations into training, validation, and test partitions before model fitting
explanation: Feature engineering includes normalisation, encoding categoricals, creating polynomial features, and handling missing values.

text: What is machine learning?
options: Writing deterministic business rules that enumerate every possible input and specify the required output explicitly
A subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data without being explicitly programmed
A statistical software package that performs fixed calculations but does not adapt its behavior from observed examples
A database query language used to retrieve, filter, and aggregate records from structured application data
explanation: ML algorithms learn from training data to make predictions or decisions without hardcoded rules.

text: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
options: Supervised learning discovers structure in unlabelled examples, whereas unsupervised learning learns to predict labelled outcomes
Supervised learning uses labelled data; unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data
Supervised and unsupervised learning use the same training targets, differing only in the programming language used
Supervised learning always requires less data, while unsupervised learning needs labelled examples to identify reliable patterns
explanation: Supervised: classification/regression with labels. Unsupervised: clustering/dimensionality reduction without labels.

text: What is a feature in machine learning?
options: A learned coefficient or internal value adjusted during optimization rather than an input supplied for an individual prediction
An individual measurable property or input variable used to make predictions
The output value that the model is trained to predict, such as a class label, price, or probability
One complete pass through the training dataset used to update the model during the learning procedure
explanation: Features are the input columns (e.g. age, salary, pixels) the model uses to learn and make predictions.

text: What does scikit-learn provide?
options: A collection of neural-network frameworks designed primarily for GPU training, distributed tensors, and automatic differentiation
A Python ML library with consistent API for classical algorithms, preprocessing, and model evaluation
A Python package primarily for creating charts, statistical graphics, dashboards, and interactive visual reports
A low-level GPU computing library that provides CUDA kernels, device management, and hardware acceleration primitives
explanation: scikit-learn provides regression, classification, clustering, preprocessing pipelines, and cross-validation tools.

text: What is a Random Forest?
options: An ensemble of decision trees trained independently on the complete dataset, with their predictions combined by averaging
An ensemble of decision trees trained on random data subsets with random feature subsets, aggregated by voting/averaging
A multilayer neural architecture that learns hierarchical representations from randomly selected feature channels
A sequential tree ensemble in which each new tree focuses on correcting errors made by the preceding tree
explanation: Random Forest's bagging + random feature selection produces decorrelated trees, reducing variance while maintaining low bias.

text: What is transfer learning?
options: Moving a trained model between servers or software frameworks while preserving its parameters and deployment configuration
Reusing a pretrained model's learned representations as a starting point for a new but related task
Training a model from scratch on data transferred from another task, without reusing learned weights or representations
A distributed learning approach in which devices exchange model updates while keeping their local training data private
explanation: Transfer learning (fine-tuning) leverages general features learned on large datasets (e.g. ImageNet) for specific tasks with limited data.

text: What is dependency overriding in FastAPI testing?
options: An external mocking-library feature that replaces imported functions in tests, without using FastAPI's application dependency configuration
app.dependency_overrides allows replacing real dependencies (DB sessions, auth) with test doubles during testing
A Pydantic testing feature that changes request-model validation rules and substitutes schemas when test data is parsed
A pytest plugin that discovers FastAPI dependencies and replaces them through fixtures, without application configuration
explanation: app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = get_test_db replaces production database sessions with test sessions during FastAPI integration tests.

text: Which AWS service provides a fully managed data warehouse?
options: Redshift
RDS
DynamoDB
S3
explanation: Stores and rotates secrets securely.

text: What is a Kafka producer?
options: A Kafka server node
An application that publishes records to Kafka topics
A consumer group coordinator
A schema registry client
explanation: Producers write records to topics, choosing the partition via a key, round-robin, or custom partitioner.

text: What is a Kafka consumer?
options: A server that stores messages
An application that reads records from Kafka topics
A Kafka partition
A replication replica
explanation: Consumers read from topics, tracking their position via the offset. They can be organised into consumer groups for parallel processing.

text: What is the vanishing gradient problem in deep learning?
options: Gradients becoming increasingly large as they move backward through many layers, causing unstable updates and numerical divergence
Gradients shrinking toward zero as they propagate backward through many layers, making early layers train very slowly
A memory overflow issue caused by storing activations and gradients for too many layers during a single training step
A regularisation side-effect in which weight penalties suppress useful features and prevent the network from fitting training examples
explanation: Sigmoid/tanh activations squash gradients. ReLU activations, batch normalisation, residual connections, and careful weight init mitigate this.

text: What is batch normalisation and why is it used?
options: Normalising the number of examples in each mini-batch to a fixed size, improving throughput but not changing layer activations
Normalising layer inputs to zero mean and unit variance per mini-batch, accelerating training and reducing sensitivity to initialisation
Normalising the training loss to zero mean and unit variance after every batch, stabilising objectives without changing layer inputs
A weight regularisation technique that penalises large parameters during optimisation, reducing overfitting without rescaling activations
explanation: Batch norm reduces internal covariate shift, allows higher learning rates, and acts as mild regularisation, significantly speeding up convergence.

text: What is the difference between generative and discriminative models?
options: They use the same probability model and differ only in implementation, with neither class of model able to generate observations
Discriminative models learn P(y|x) (decision boundary); generative models learn P(x,y) and can generate new samples
Generative models always outperform discriminative models because modelling the full data distribution provides better classification
Discriminative models cannot classify unseen examples; they only estimate the input distribution and generate synthetic feature vectors
explanation: Examples: Logistic Regression (discriminative), Naive Bayes (generative), GANs/VAEs (generative), SVMs (discriminative).

text: What is data leakage in machine learning?
options: Data corruption caused by malformed, missing, or incorrectly encoded records, which reduces training quality without introducing outside information
When information from outside the training set (e.g. future data, test set labels) is used during training, giving falsely optimistic results
Data duplication caused by repeated records or copied samples, which can overweight examples but does not expose validation or test information
An imbalanced dataset issue where some classes are underrepresented, causing biased predictions without contaminating training with evaluation data
explanation: Common leakage: normalising using test set statistics, including target-correlated features, or time-series data leakage. Always fit preprocessing on train only.

text: What is MLflow and what problems does it solve?
options: A data pipeline tool for scheduling transformations and dependencies, rather than tracking runs, registering models, or packaging machine-learning projects
An open-source platform for ML experiment tracking, model versioning, packaging (MLproject), and model registry
A feature store for serving reusable training and online features, with no built-in experiment tracking, model registry, or MLproject packaging
A data labelling tool for annotating training examples and managing annotation workflows, rather than recording experiments or deploying registered models
explanation: MLflow tracks experiments (parameters, metrics, artefacts), enables model registry/versioning, and supports deployment across platforms.

text: What is federated learning?
options: Training on centralised data where all raw examples are uploaded to one server before optimisation, with no local updates or privacy-preserving aggregation
A distributed ML approach where models are trained locally on edge devices and only gradients/updates are aggregated centrally, preserving privacy
Multi-GPU training that splits batches across accelerators in one data centre, synchronising gradients without involving separate user devices
A cloud ML service that provides hosted notebooks and managed training jobs, rather than a distributed privacy-preserving approach across edge devices
explanation: Federated learning keeps data on device (privacy-preserving), aggregating model updates using federated averaging (FedAvg).

text: What is Apache Kafka?
options: A relational database that stores structured tables and supports transactional SQL queries across application workloads
A distributed event streaming platform for high-throughput, fault-tolerant real-time data pipelines
A point-to-point message queue that delivers transient messages to workers without maintaining a durable, replayable event log
A batch processing framework designed to schedule and execute periodic jobs over large collections of stored data
explanation: Kafka is a distributed log-based system where producers write events to topics and consumers read them, retaining events for a configurable time.

text: What is a Kafka partition?
options: A backup copy of topic records stored separately for disaster recovery and restored when the primary data is lost
An ordered, immutable sequence of records within a topic that enables parallelism and scalability
A Kafka server responsible for hosting multiple topic partitions and responding to client requests
A consumer group that coordinates several consumers while dividing topic records among their workers
explanation: Topics are split into partitions spread across brokers. Each partition is an ordered log — the unit of parallelism in Kafka.

text: How do you implement rate limiting in FastAPI?
options: FastAPI provides built-in distributed rate limiting for every route, automatically tracking clients and enforcing quotas without configuration or external services
Using slowapi (Limits library), Redis-based counters in middleware, or API gateway-level rate limiting (AWS API Gateway, Kong)
Implementing limits only in in-memory middleware is sufficient for a multi-worker deployment, because each process shares the same counters automatically
Rate limiting cannot be implemented in FastAPI routes, so quotas must be enforced exclusively by the database after request processing completes
explanation: slowapi wraps limits decorators around routes. For distributed rate limiting, Redis-backed counters ensure consistency across multiple FastAPI instances.

text: You want to secure secrets like API keys. Which service is best?
options: IAM
Secrets Manager
CloudWatch
Route 53
explanation: Simple Queue Service provides reliable message queuing.

text: What is Go?
options: A scripting language by Google
A compiled, statically typed language created by Google
A JavaScript runtime
A database query language
explanation: Go (Golang) is an open-source compiled language designed at Google for simplicity, efficiency, and strong concurrency support.

text: What is the role of ZooKeeper in older Kafka versions?
options: A storage service that persists topic records and serves them to producers and consumers on request
Managing cluster metadata, leader election, and configuration (replaced by KRaft in modern Kafka)
A consumer-group coordinator that assigns partitions and tracks the progress of active consumers
A message serialization service that converts application objects into bytes before publication
explanation: ZooKeeper managed broker metadata and controller election. Kafka 2.8+ introduced KRaft mode to eliminate the ZooKeeper dependency.

text: What is the replication factor in Kafka and why is it important?
options: The number of consumer instances assigned to each partition for balancing read workload
The number of copies of each partition maintained across brokers for fault tolerance
The number of distinct topics replicated across brokers to organise a Kafka deployment
The compression ratio applied to records before they are written to partition logs
explanation: A replication factor of 3 means each partition exists on 3 brokers. If a broker fails, another replica becomes the leader.

text: What are Kafka Streams?
options: A protocol for delivering live video streams from Kafka brokers to browser clients over HTTP with adaptive playback
A Java library for building stateful, fault-tolerant stream processing applications that consume and produce Kafka topics
An integration module that forwards Kafka records into Apache Spark jobs for batch analytics and reporting
A WebSocket-based interface that pushes Kafka records directly to connected browser sessions in real time
explanation: Kafka Streams runs as a library in the application (no separate cluster) and supports stateful operations, joins, windowing, and interactive queries.

text: What is the Confluent Schema Registry?
options: A browser-based Kafka dashboard for inspecting topics, consumer lag, partitions, and broker health across clusters
A centralised service for managing Avro/JSON Schema/Protobuf schemas, enforcing compatibility between producers and consumers
A command-line administration utility for creating topics, altering configurations, and reassigning partitions
A serialization component that converts application objects into binary records before producers send them to Kafka
explanation: Schema Registry stores schemas and enforces backward/forward/full compatibility, ensuring producers and consumers agree on data format.

text: How do you choose the number of partitions for a Kafka topic?
options: Always create a single partition because Kafka automatically scales its throughput and consumer parallelism as load increases
Based on desired throughput (target MB/s ÷ MB/s per partition), number of consumers, and key distribution to avoid hot partitions
Set the partition count equal to the number of brokers so each broker receives exactly one partition
Create the maximum practical number of partitions immediately to guarantee throughput, regardless of workload or key skew
explanation: Partitions = max(throughput, consumer parallelism). Too few limits parallelism; too many increases metadata overhead and rebalance time.

text: What is a Kafka Connect?
options: A client library that applications use to publish records and consume them directly from Kafka brokers
A framework for scalably and reliably moving data between Kafka and external systems using connectors
A cluster administration service that monitors broker health and automatically repairs failed Kafka nodes
A schema enforcement component that rejects incompatible records before they are written to Kafka topics
explanation: Kafka Connect (source connectors: import data; sink connectors: export data) simplifies integration with databases, S3, Elasticsearch, etc.

text: What is the difference between at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery?
options: At-most-once retries until acknowledgement; at-least-once suppresses duplicates; exactly-once permits occasional message loss
At-most-once may lose messages; at-least-once may duplicate; exactly-once guarantees no loss or duplication
At-most-once guarantees delivery without duplicates; at-least-once prevents retries; exactly-once provides ordering only
At-most-once and at-least-once differ only in latency; exactly-once is achieved whenever consumers commit offsets
explanation: The delivery guarantee depends on producer/consumer configuration. Exactly-once requires idempotent producers + transactions + idempotent consumers.

text: What is the ISR (In-Sync Replicas) set in Kafka?
options: Replicas that have responded recently to broker requests, including lagging followers and offline replicas; all replicas can lead
Replicas that are caught up with the leader within a configured lag threshold — only ISR members can become the new leader
All replicas assigned to a partition, regardless of replication lag or availability; the controller selects any replica as leader
Consumer group members that have fetched the latest records; Kafka uses their acknowledgements to choose the next partition leader
explanation: The leader tracks which replicas are in-sync. A write is committed only when all ISR replicas acknowledge it (configurable with min.insync.replicas).

text: What is the KRaft (KIP-500) architecture in Kafka and why was it introduced?
options: Kafka's internal compression and storage architecture, using Raft to encode message batches and replace replicated logs with local metadata
Kafka's internal metadata quorum (Raft consensus) replacing ZooKeeper, reducing operational complexity and enabling faster metadata operations
Kafka's client wire protocol for metadata requests, introduced to replace ZooKeeper with a faster format for producer and consumer traffic
Kafka's consumer coordination framework, using a Raft leader to assign partitions and manage offsets without changing broker metadata storage
explanation: KRaft embeds a metadata quorum in Kafka itself, eliminating ZooKeeper, reducing latency, and supporting millions of partitions.

text: What is the difference between `String` and `&str`?
options: Two interchangeable spellings for the same UTF-8 string representation, with no ownership distinction
String is a heap-allocated, owned, mutable string; &str is an immutable reference to UTF-8 data (a string slice)
