explanation: Commits are permanent snapshots. Write messages in the imperative mood, e.g. Add login form.

text: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
options: They perform the same operation, differing only in command syntax and output format while preserving the same history
Merge creates a merge commit preserving branch history; rebase replays commits on top of the target for a linear history
Rebase is always safer because it preserves shared history and automatically resolves conflicts without changing commits
Merge rewrites existing commits to produce a linear history, while rebase preserves the original branch structure and parents
explanation: Use merge for public branches to preserve context; use rebase to clean up local feature branches before sharing.

text: What does git cherry-pick do?
options: Reverts a selected commit by creating a new inverse commit and preserving the later history
Applies the changes from a specific commit onto the current branch without merging the whole branch
Merges the complete history of another branch into the current branch and creates any needed merge commit
Tags a selected commit with a lightweight reference and records it in the repository metadata
explanation: Cherry-pick is useful for applying a hotfix from one branch to another without a full merge.

text: What does git log --oneline show?
options: Only the uncommitted changes currently present in the working tree and not yet recorded in any commit
A compact one-line-per-commit view of the commit history
The names and tracking status of branches available on remote servers, including their latest commit references
The files currently added to the index and waiting for the next commit, without displaying previous repository history
explanation: Combine with --graph to visualise branch topology, e.g. git log --oneline --graph --all.

text: What is git fetch vs git pull?
options: git fetch and git pull perform the same operation, with both integrating remote commits into the current branch
git fetch downloads remote changes without merging; git pull fetches and then merges into the current branch
git pull is safer because it always creates a merge commit and prevents unreviewed remote changes from being applied
git fetch merges remote changes into the checked-out branch, while git pull only updates remote-tracking references
explanation: git fetch is safe to run at any time — it never modifies your working directory.

text: What is a detached HEAD state?
options: A repository condition in which the object database is damaged and Git cannot read required commit data
HEAD pointing directly to a commit rather than a branch, meaning new commits will not belong to any branch
A state in which incompatible edits prevent Git from completing a merge without manual resolution
A state in which Git rejects an attempt to send local commits because the remote branch has advanced
explanation: Commits made in detached HEAD state are at risk of garbage collection. Create a branch to preserve them.

text: What does git reflog track?
options: A record containing only commits and file updates that have been downloaded from configured remote repositories
A log of all HEAD movements including resets, checkouts, and rebases — useful for recovering lost commits
A history of files and modifications placed in the index after they have been selected with git add
A diagnostic record of connections, requests, authentication attempts, and transfer failures involving Git remotes
explanation: git reflog is your safety net — even after a git reset --hard you can find the lost commit hash and recover it.

text: How does git bisect work?
options: It divides one existing commit into multiple smaller commits while preserving the same overall file changes
It performs a binary search through commit history to find the first commit that introduced a bug
It combines the histories of two branches by creating a new commit with both lines of development as parents
It compares the final snapshots of two branches and reports differences without testing their individual commits
explanation: git bisect good/bad automates binary search, finding the culprit commit in log2(n) steps.

text: What is the difference between --soft, --mixed, and --hard reset?
options: --soft, --mixed, and --hard all reset HEAD, the index, and the working directory, differing only in how they report the resulting status
--soft resets only HEAD; --mixed resets HEAD and index (default); --hard resets HEAD, index, and working directory discarding all changes
--soft resets HEAD and the index; --mixed resets HEAD, index, and working directory; --hard resets only HEAD while preserving all files
--soft preserves HEAD and the index while resetting files; --mixed discards working-tree changes; --hard changes only the current branch reference
explanation: --mixed is the default and is useful for un-staging changes. --hard is destructive and cannot be undone without reflog.

text: What is the Git object model?
options: A graphical interface where files, branches, commits, and tags are displayed as separate records identified by repository names
A content-addressable store where every file (blob), directory (tree), commit, and tag is an object identified by its SHA-1 hash
A network protocol where files and commits are transferred between repositories through remote URLs and authenticated sessions
A branching strategy where commits, directories, and file versions are organised into feature, release, and maintenance lines
explanation: Understanding blobs, trees, commits, and tags explains why Git history is immutable and how every commit links to its parent.

text: What is Git LFS (Large File Storage)?
options: A Git merge strategy that stores conflicting revisions as compressed binary objects and chooses the largest version during synchronization
A Git extension that replaces large files in the repository with text pointers and stores the actual content on a remote server
A branch naming convention that marks repositories containing large assets with a special prefix and separate release-oriented branches
A hosted repository service that provides dedicated storage, authentication, and web access for projects containing large binary files
explanation: Use LFS for binaries, datasets, and media — keeping them out of the main .git object store keeps clone times fast.

text: What does terraform init do?
options: Destroys the resources described by the configuration, removes the state file, and clears downloaded providers from the working directory
Initialises a Terraform working directory, downloading required providers and modules
Applies the current configuration immediately, creating or updating every planned resource without first displaying a proposed execution plan
Calculates and displays the infrastructure changes Terraform would make, without preparing providers, modules, or the working directory
explanation: Always run terraform init first, or after adding new providers or modules to a configuration.

text: What is a Redis Hash?
options: A cryptographic digest used to verify integrity, without separately addressable fields or values
A Redis data type that maps field-value pairs, like a nested dictionary
A collection of unique members implemented with integer scores and automatic ordering for ranked retrieval
A sorted sequence of key-value entries that ranks fields numerically for ordered retrieval
explanation: Hashes (HSET, HGET, HGETALL) are ideal for representing objects (e.g. user profiles) with multiple fields.

text: What is a Terraform provider?
options: A cloud subscription or account that owns the credentials and resources Terraform is authorised to manage
A plugin that allows Terraform to interact with a specific cloud or service API (e.g. AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes)
A reusable collection of Terraform configuration files that groups resources and exposes inputs and outputs
An isolated Terraform working environment with its own state, variables, and resource instance tracking
explanation: Providers are distributed as plugins and versioned separately from Terraform itself.

text: What is a Terraform resource?
options: An input value declared in configuration and supplied by users to customise resource arguments
An infrastructure object Terraform manages, such as an AWS EC2 instance or an Azure virtual network
A read-only query definition that retrieves existing infrastructure information without creating or managing it
A plugin configuration that supplies Terraform with schemas and API operations for a service
explanation: Resources are declared with resource TYPE NAME blocks and are the core building block of Terraform configurations.

text: What does terraform destroy do?
options: Calculates and displays proposed infrastructure changes without modifying any managed resources
Terminates and removes all infrastructure managed by the current Terraform configuration
Reconciles remote objects with state and updates recorded attributes without deleting infrastructure
Reformats configuration files according to Terraform's canonical style without contacting providers
explanation: Use destroy with caution in production. It prompts for confirmation unless -auto-approve is passed.

text: What is a Terraform module?
options: A versioned plugin that connects Terraform to a cloud platform and implements resource and data source behavior
A reusable container of Terraform resources that encapsulates infrastructure patterns and accepts input variables
A serialized record of managed infrastructure, including resource attributes, dependencies, and provider metadata
A named execution context that selects a separate state snapshot while reusing the same Terraform configuration
explanation: Modules promote DRY infrastructure code. Source can be a local path, Git repository, or the Terraform Registry.

text: What is terraform import used for?
options: Provisioning new cloud resources from Terraform configuration and recording them in the state during the initial apply
Bringing existing infrastructure that was not created by Terraform under Terraform management
Removing managed infrastructure from the provider and deleting its corresponding resources from Terraform state
Comparing the current provider objects with the state file and updating tracked attributes without adopting unmanaged resources
explanation: After import, you still need to write the matching configuration — terraform import only updates the state file.

text: What is the terraform_remote_state data source?
options: A provider configuration that authenticates Terraform against a remote service and exposes its resources and data sources
A way to read outputs from another Terraform state file, enabling cross-stack references
A module input declaration that passes values from the calling configuration into a child module during planning
A workspace variable mechanism that selects environment-specific values from another state without reading exported outputs
explanation: This enables loose coupling between separate Terraform roots that need to share values like VPC IDs.

text: What does the depends_on meta-argument do?
options: Imports an existing object into the Terraform state by associating its provider identifier with a configured resource address
Creates an explicit dependency between resources, overriding Terraforms automatic dependency detection
Iterates over a collection of values to create repeated resource instances with distinct configuration and addresses
Changes a resource lifecycle setting so Terraform may omit creating it when a condition or input value is false
explanation: Use depends_on sparingly — prefer implicit dependencies via resource attribute references which Terraform detects automatically.

text: What are Terraform outputs?
options: Diagnostic messages generated during validation, planning, or apply operations to explain configuration and provider failures
Values exported from a module or root configuration, usable by other configurations or displayed after apply
Fallback values assigned to input variables when callers do not provide explicit arguments to a module
Internal records written by Terraform to track resource attributes, provider identifiers, and dependency information
explanation: Outputs declared with sensitive = true are hidden from CLI output but still stored in state.

text: What is Terraform state locking and why is it important?
options: A read-only execution mode that prevents Terraform from changing infrastructure while still inspecting the current state
Preventing concurrent terraform apply operations that would corrupt the shared state file by acquiring an exclusive lock during operations
A workspace-level setting that separates state snapshots and variables so multiple environments can be operated independently
An access-control mechanism that grants or denies users permission to run Terraform commands against shared infrastructure
explanation: DynamoDB is commonly used for state locking with S3 backends. Terraform Cloud provides built-in locking.

text: What is the difference between terraform taint and replace?
options: Identical mechanisms that both mark a resource for recreation immediately, with no difference in state or command behavior
taint (deprecated) marked a resource for recreation on next apply; -replace flag on plan/apply does the same without modifying state directly
taint is newer and safely replaces resources during planning, while -replace is the deprecated state-modifying approach
-replace destroys the existing object immediately before planning, while taint only changes the provider configuration
explanation: Use terraform apply -replace=resource.address instead of the deprecated taint command.

text: What are Terraform policy checks (Sentinel/OPA)?
options: Code formatting rules that rewrite Terraform files into a standard style before they are accepted by the configuration parser
Policy as Code frameworks that evaluate Terraform plans against organisational rules before apply, preventing non-compliant infrastructure
Variable validation rules that check input types and permitted values while Terraform loads module configuration
Provider constraints that restrict which plugin versions and resource schemas may be selected during initialization
explanation: Sentinel is a paid HashiCorp feature; Open Policy Agent (OPA) with Conftest is an open-source alternative.

text: What is the purpose of a test set in ML?
options: To fit model parameters by minimising prediction error on the labelled training examples
To evaluate the model's performance on unseen data after training
To choose hyperparameters by comparing validation scores across multiple model configurations
To remove missing values and inconsistent records before modelling begins
explanation: The test set gives an unbiased evaluation of model performance on data it has never seen during training.

text: What is infrastructure drift in the context of Terraform?
options: When Terraform cannot contact a provider endpoint and reports that the network connection has timed out
When the real-world state of resources diverges from what is recorded in the Terraform state file due to manual changes
When Terraform configuration files use inconsistent indentation, spacing, or formatting conventions across resources
When two module releases expose different input variables and require incompatible configuration arguments
explanation: terraform plan with -refresh=true detects drift. Prevent it by ensuring all changes go through Terraform.

text: What is a partial configuration in Terraform backends?
options: A Terraform configuration containing only some resource blocks, with the remaining infrastructure definitions added in another file
Omitting sensitive values from the backend block in code and supplying them at terraform init time via -backend-config flags or files
A backend mode that restricts state operations to one selected workspace and prevents switching between environments
A provider initialization defect that causes Terraform to accept some backend arguments while silently ignoring others
explanation: This pattern keeps secrets like bucket names and access keys out of version control.

text: What does CD stand for in CI/CD?
options: Code Deployment only — copying compiled application artifacts directly to production without a separate delivery stage
Continuous Delivery or Continuous Deployment — automatically delivering tested code to staging or production
Container Delivery — packaging container images and transferring them to a registry for later manual release
Cloud Distribution — replicating application binaries and configuration across multiple geographic cloud regions
explanation: Continuous Delivery requires manual approval before production; Continuous Deployment publishes automatically on every passing build.

text: What is a CI/CD pipeline?
options: A physical network cable that carries source files and build artifacts between developers, servers, and production systems
An automated sequence of steps — build, test, deploy — that code changes pass through from commit to production
A container networking layer that assigns virtual addresses and routes traffic between isolated application workloads
A Git branch that collects approved commits and represents the version of the application currently intended for release
explanation: Pipelines codify your release process, making it repeatable, auditable, and fast.

text: What is the purpose of a staging environment?
options: A development-only workspace where engineers experiment with unfinished code and local configuration before committing changes
A production-like environment used to validate changes before they reach real users
A standby infrastructure copy maintained primarily to restore services after a production outage or regional failure
A dedicated performance-testing server used exclusively to generate heavy traffic and measure system limits before release
explanation: Staging should mirror production as closely as possible to catch environment-specific bugs before they affect users.

text: What is GitHub Actions?
options: A project management service built into GitHub for assigning work, tracking milestones, and organizing team delivery schedules
A CI/CD platform built into GitHub using YAML workflow files to automate build, test, and deploy pipelines
A code review feature that compares pull-request changes and records reviewer comments without executing automation workflows
A hosted container registry in GitHub that stores, tags, scans, and distributes Docker images for deployment
explanation: GitHub Actions workflows are triggered by events and run in hosted or self-hosted runners.

text: What is a pipeline trigger?
options: A deployment command that selects a target environment and instructs the pipeline to publish an already-created application package
An event or condition that starts a pipeline run, such as a commit push, pull request, schedule, or manual dispatch
A pipeline build step that compiles source files, resolves dependencies, and produces binaries or other intermediate outputs
A test assertion that compares an observed value with an expected result and marks one case as passing or failing
explanation: Common triggers include push to specific branches, pull request creation, scheduled cron runs, and manual approvals.

text: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
options: Identical terms for the same practice: both produce a release package and automatically place every passing build into production
Continuous Delivery produces deployable artifacts requiring manual approval; Continuous Deployment automatically deploys every passing build to production
Continuous Delivery is the faster model because it skips approval checks, while Continuous Deployment waits for a scheduled release window
Continuous Deployment requires more testing because it targets production, whereas Continuous Delivery may publish artifacts without validating them
explanation: Most enterprises adopt Continuous Delivery with manual gates for regulatory or stability reasons.

text: What is caching in a CI pipeline?
options: Removing downloaded dependencies and intermediate files after each run to keep the runner workspace small
Storing dependencies (e.g. node_modules) between runs so they do not need to be reinstalled on every pipeline execution
An approach for releasing a new application version by shifting production traffic between service instances
A technique for speeding up tests by reducing assertions or skipping slow test cases during pipeline execution
explanation: Effective cache keys include a hash of the dependency lockfile so the cache is invalidated when dependencies change.

text: What is a canary deployment?
options: Publishing the new version to a single production instance while all other instances continue serving the previous release
Gradually routing a small percentage of traffic to the new version to validate it in production before a full rollout
Returning production traffic to the previous application version after monitoring detects errors or unacceptable performance
A separate pre-production environment where a release is tested with synthetic requests before any users can access it
explanation: Canary deployments limit blast radius — if the new version fails, only a small fraction of users are affected.

text: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC) in DevOps?
options: Provisioning servers by logging into each machine and applying operating-system, network, and access settings manually
Managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual processes
A practice of collecting infrastructure metrics, logs, and alerts to identify failures after services are deployed
A release approach that defines how application versions are promoted through development, staging, and production
explanation: IaC enables version control, peer review, and automated testing of infrastructure changes alongside application code.

text: What is GitOps?
options: A Git branching strategy that organizes development work into feature, release, and production branches with rules for merging changes
A deployment model where Git is the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications, with automated reconciliation to match the desired state
A continuous integration tool that runs builds and tests when developers push commits, then reports the results back to the repository
An observability practice that stores deployment configuration and operational dashboards in Git for reviewing changes to monitoring systems
explanation: Tools like ArgoCD and Flux implement GitOps for Kubernetes, continuously reconciling cluster state with Git.

text: What is a feature flag (feature toggle)?
options: A Git metadata marker that identifies the commit or release from which a particular feature implementation was introduced into the codebase
A software pattern allowing features to be enabled or disabled at runtime without deploying new code, enabling trunk-based development and controlled rollouts
A pipeline stage that pauses an automated build while reviewers validate requirements, test results, and deployment readiness before continuing
A separate deployment environment used to isolate experimental functionality from production traffic until the full application release is approved
explanation: Feature flags decouple deployment from release, allowing dark launches, A/B testing, and instant kill switches.

text: What is shift-left testing?
options: Moving tests later in the delivery pipeline so developers can finish implementation first and a dedicated QA phase can validate the completed release
Moving testing earlier in the development lifecycle — writing tests alongside code and running them in CI rather than deferring to a QA phase
A deployment strategy that gradually shifts production traffic between old and new application versions while observing error rates and user impact
A monitoring practice that places operational dashboards and alert review after deployment so production behavior can be evaluated by the support team
explanation: Shift-left catches defects when they are cheapest to fix and reduces cycle time by eliminating late-stage test bottlenecks.

text: What is the purpose of SAST and DAST in a pipeline?
options: Improving build performance by caching dependencies, parallelizing compilation steps, and reducing the time required for continuous integration jobs to finish
SAST (Static Analysis) scans source code for vulnerabilities; DAST (Dynamic Analysis) tests a running application for vulnerabilities
Managing external libraries by locking versions, downloading packages from approved registries, and updating dependency manifests through automated pull requests
Evaluating application throughput and response times under expected or peak load to identify bottlenecks before a release reaches production
explanation: Running both in CI provides defence in depth — SAST finds code-level issues, DAST finds runtime and configuration issues.

text: What is Grafana?
options: A time-series database that stores and queries metrics collected from applications and infrastructure
An open-source visualisation and analytics platform used to create dashboards from data sources like Prometheus
A log collection agent that forwards application and system records to a centralized observability platform
An incident alerting service that evaluates thresholds and notifies engineers when monitored systems degrade
explanation: Grafana supports dozens of data sources including Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch, and CloudWatch.

text: What is a postmortem (incident review)?
options: A formal assessment of an employee’s results, skills, and career progress conducted by a manager during a review cycle
A blameless document analysing a service incident — what happened, impact, root causes, and action items to prevent recurrence
A structured report describing a software release, its included changes, rollout sequence, and observed deployment results
A systematic examination of controls, configurations, and evidence to determine whether an organisation meets security requirements
explanation: Blameless postmortems focus on systemic failures and process improvements rather than individual blame.

text: What is a runbook?
options: A version-controlled script that automates building, packaging, and releasing an application to a specified environment
A documented set of procedures for responding to specific operational events or alerts, enabling consistent incident response
A standardised document for recording an incident’s timeline, contributing factors, and follow-up actions after resolution
A visual dashboard displaying current service metrics, alert states, and infrastructure health for an operations team
explanation: Good runbooks reduce cognitive load during incidents and enable on-call engineers to handle issues they have not seen before.

text: What is the difference between mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to recover (MTTR)?
options: MTTD and MTTR both measure the complete duration of an incident, from the first alert until normal service is restored
MTTD measures how long it takes to detect an incident; MTTR measures how long it takes to restore service after detection
MTTD measures restoration time after failure; MTTR measures how quickly monitoring detects the resulting incident
MTTD measures the time to repair a defect before impact; MTTR measures the time required to identify its root cause
explanation: Reducing MTTD requires good alerting and observability. Reducing MTTR requires runbooks, automation, and practice.

text: What is distributed tracing?
options: Capturing and analysing packets as they travel across network interfaces to diagnose routing, connectivity, and protocol problems
Tracking a request as it flows through multiple services, capturing timing and metadata at each hop to diagnose latency and failures
Collecting records from many applications and indexing them centrally so operators can search events across an entire system
A numerical observation such as a counter, gauge, or histogram that records system behaviour at a point or over time
explanation: Tools like Jaeger, Zipkin, and OpenTelemetry implement distributed tracing using trace IDs propagated across service boundaries.

text: What is chaos engineering in CI/CD context?
options: A practice of intentionally introducing random defects into build pipelines to test whether jobs recover automatically
Deliberately injecting failures into production systems to validate that resilience mechanisms work as expected
A release approach that progressively moves application versions between environments while minimizing deployment-related downtime
A software testing framework that generates synthetic cases and compares service outputs against predefined expectations
explanation: Tools like Chaos Monkey and LitmusChaos automate failure injection. Start in non-production and build a steady state hypothesis.

text: What is the access level of a private member in C#?
options: Accessible from any type in the same compiled assembly
Accessible only within the type where the member is declared
Accessible from derived types even when they are in another assembly
Accessible from all callers when an object reference is available
explanation: A private member can be accessed only from within the type that declares it, which helps hide implementation details.

text: What does SRE stand for?
options: Software Reliability Engineer — a role focused on application stability, performance testing, and operational support
Site Reliability Engineering — a discipline applying software engineering to operations and reliability problems
System Resource Evaluation — a process for measuring CPU, memory, and storage consumption across servers
Service Runtime Environment — a platform layer that manages application processes, configuration, and network connections
explanation: SRE was pioneered at Google to scale operations sustainably through automation and engineering rigour.

text: What is an error budget?
options: A financial reserve set aside to pay for outages, emergency repairs, and customer credits after reliability incidents
The allowed amount of unreliability implied by an SLO — if SLO is 99.9%, the error budget is 0.1% downtime per period
A projected financial estimate of the infrastructure and personnel costs required to operate a service
A capacity planning document that forecasts compute, storage, and network resources needed for future demand
explanation: Error budgets align dev and ops — when the budget is exhausted, reliability work takes priority over new features.

text: What is capacity planning in SRE?
options: A reactive procurement process that acquires additional servers only after existing infrastructure has reached its limits and users observe degraded performance
Forecasting future resource needs based on growth trends and ensuring sufficient capacity exists before it is needed
A financial optimisation strategy focused on reducing infrastructure expenditure by removing unused resources and negotiating lower provider rates
An incident response responsibility involving temporary resource increases, emergency provisioning, and coordination during a service outage
explanation: Capacity planning combines traffic forecasting, load testing, and headroom analysis to prevent saturation-related incidents.

text: What is log aggregation?
options: Writing application and system log records to local disk on each host, usually with rotation and retention rules to prevent files from consuming all available storage
Collecting logs from many services and hosts into a centralised system (e.g. the ELK stack or Loki) for unified search and analysis
A metrics collection approach that periodically gathers numerical measurements from services and stores them as timestamped time-series data for dashboards
A distributed tracing tool that records request spans across service boundaries, correlates trace identifiers, and displays end-to-end execution timing
explanation: Structured logging (JSON) makes log aggregation and querying far more effective than unstructured text.

text: What is a service dependency map?
options: A network diagram showing routers, switches, firewalls, subnets, and physical or logical connections between infrastructure components in an operating environment
A visualisation of how services depend on each other, used to understand blast radius and identify critical path dependencies during incidents
A deployment pipeline that describes build stages, approval gates, artifact promotion, and automated release steps used to move software between environments
A capacity plan estimating future compute, storage, and network requirements, together with procurement timelines and infrastructure expansion milestones
explanation: Service dependency maps are invaluable during incidents — knowing dependencies immediately narrows the root cause search.

text: What is the toil reduction principle in SRE?
options: Automating every operational task immediately, regardless of its frequency, risk, or impact on engineering capacity
Systematically identifying and eliminating repetitive manual operational work that scales with traffic, freeing engineers for project work
Reducing operational staffing by transferring repetitive support work to users, while retaining manual processes for critical production tasks
Limiting on-call participation to senior engineers so routine incidents are handled without disrupting feature development
explanation: Google SRE teams target spending no more than 50% of time on toil. Excess toil crowds out reliability improvements.

text: What is progressive delivery?
options: A release strategy that deploys the complete change to every production instance at once after a final validation in staging
A release strategy combining feature flags, canary releases, and automated metric analysis to gradually and safely roll out changes
A source-control workflow that merges small branches into main continuously, using pull requests and automated tests to manage integration
A monitoring practice that tracks deployment health after release and reports regressions through dashboards and alerts
explanation: Tools like Argo Rollouts and Flagger automate progressive delivery with automatic rollback based on SLO metrics.

text: What is multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting?
options: An alerting design that places related charts from several services on one dashboard, allowing operators to compare latency, traffic, and saturation during incidents
An alerting strategy that fires when the error budget is being consumed at dangerous speeds over both short (1h) and long (6h/3d) windows simultaneously, reducing false positives
A logging approach that records events from multiple components in a shared schema, retaining detailed request context for later search and troubleshooting
A metric-processing technique that combines measurements from several sources into one smoothed time series before displaying it to operators
explanation: This approach is described in the Google SRE Workbook and dramatically reduces alert noise compared to simple threshold alerts.

text: What is the strangler fig pattern?
options: A database migration technique that copies tables from a legacy schema into a new schema, then switches applications after the final synchronisation
Incrementally replacing a legacy system by routing traffic to new implementations feature by feature until the old system can be retired
A deployment strategy that replaces an entire application version in one controlled production event, usually behind a maintenance window
A load-balancing pattern that distributes requests across identical instances according to health, capacity, and connection count
explanation: The pattern allows zero-risk migration — the old system remains live and handles traffic that has not been migrated yet.

text: What is a synthetic monitor?
options: A generated measurement that resembles a real production signal but is not collected from an actual service request, user session, or infrastructure event
A scripted probe that simulates user actions against a production system at regular intervals to detect availability and performance issues proactively
A log-processing rule that removes repetitive records and sensitive fields before events are indexed, reducing storage costs and search noise
A controlled failure experiment that deliberately disrupts production dependencies to evaluate recovery procedures, resilience, and incident response
explanation: Synthetic monitors catch issues before real users are affected and validate that user-facing flows work end-to-end.

text: What is an Ansible playbook?
options: A shell script that executes administrative commands sequentially on one server, without defining hosts, variables, or desired system state
A YAML file defining an ordered set of plays that map hosts to tasks, describing the desired state of managed systems
A static configuration file that stores connection credentials and host addresses used by Ansible during remote execution
An inventory file that lists managed hosts, groups them by environment, and supplies variables for connecting to each machine
explanation: Playbooks are idempotent — running them multiple times produces the same result.

text: What is an Ansible module?
options: A section of a playbook that selects target hosts and defines variables, privilege settings, and the sequence of operations to run
A reusable unit of code that performs a specific task on managed hosts, such as installing packages, copying files, or managing services
A plugin that discovers hosts from external systems and supplies their addresses, groups, and variables to the inventory
A directory of reusable automation content containing tasks, handlers, templates, defaults, and files for a particular service
explanation: Ansible ships with thousands of modules. Use ansible-doc module_name to see documentation for any module.

text: What is an Ansible role?
options: A permission model that determines which users may execute particular playbooks, access variables, or modify managed hosts
A structured way to organise playbook content (tasks, handlers, variables, templates, files) into reusable, shareable units
A transport mechanism that selects SSH, WinRM, or a local connection for reaching hosts during playbook execution
A short alias assigned to a module so playbooks can invoke it under a customized name and hide its implementation
explanation: Roles follow a standard directory structure that Ansible automatically loads, making sharing via Ansible Galaxy easy.

text: What does the ansible command do vs ansible-playbook?
options: ansible runs ad-hoc tasks only on localhost; ansible-playbook runs one YAML task at a time without play structure
ansible runs ad-hoc single tasks against hosts; ansible-playbook runs full playbooks from YAML files
ansible-playbook is deprecated in favor of ansible, which now executes both ad-hoc commands and complete YAML playbooks
ansible runs complete playbooks from YAML files; ansible-playbook is limited to checking syntax and displaying planned changes
explanation: Ad-hoc commands are useful for quick one-off tasks like checking uptime or restarting a service.

text: What is the difference between include_tasks and import_tasks in Ansible?
options: They are identical at execution time; both load task files dynamically when the play reaches the statement, including under conditionals
import_tasks is static (processed at parse time); include_tasks is dynamic (processed at runtime), allowing conditional inclusion
include_tasks is deprecated and replaced by import_tasks, which should be used for every reusable task file and conditional block
import_tasks is dynamic and evaluated at runtime; include_tasks is static and expanded while Ansible parses the complete playbook
explanation: Use import_tasks for predictable static includes; use include_tasks when you need loop or when conditions at include time.

text: What is the when condition in Ansible?
options: A loop directive that repeats a task for each item in a list, optionally using a registered result to control later iterations
A conditional that controls whether a task runs on a given host based on variable values, facts, or registered results
A handler trigger that queues a service restart whenever a variable changes, regardless of whether the task reports a change
A module option that selects the transport or privilege settings used when Ansible connects to the managed host
explanation: when: ansible_os_family == Debian runs a task only on Debian-based systems, making playbooks cross-platform.

text: What is the register directive in Ansible?
options: A user registration step that adds a newly discovered account to the managed host and records its credentials for later tasks
A way to capture the output of a task into a variable for use in later tasks or conditionals
An inventory option that registers hosts returned by a discovery plugin and makes them available to subsequent plays
A handler declaration that registers a service restart and schedules it automatically after any task changes configuration
explanation: Registered variables contain the full return value of the module, including stdout, stderr, rc, and changed.

text: What is Ansibles check mode (dry run)?
options: Running a playbook only through parser validation, without contacting hosts or evaluating the changes tasks would request
Running a playbook with --check to simulate what changes would be made without actually making them
Executing each module in an isolated test harness to verify its arguments and return values without using real systems
Verifying SSH connectivity and authentication to every target while skipping all task execution and change prediction
explanation: Combine --check with --diff to see exactly what file changes would be applied without executing them.

text: What is the serial keyword in Ansible?
options: A host-level identifier that assigns each managed machine a stable position within the play's execution order
A play-level directive controlling how many hosts are updated at a time, enabling rolling updates across a fleet
A loop modifier that repeats a task over selected items while controlling the number processed in each iteration
A connection setting that limits how many simultaneous transport sessions Ansible opens to a remote host
explanation: serial: 1 updates one host at a time; serial: 20% updates 20% of the inventory at a time for safer rolling deploys.

text: What are Ansible callback plugins?
options: Plugins that establish transport sessions to managed hosts, select connection methods, and handle authentication during playbook execution
Plugins that intercept playbook events (task start, result, play complete) to customise output, send notifications, or record metrics
Plugins that provide alternate implementations of modules, allowing tasks to perform operations unavailable in the standard module set
Plugins that discover managed machines from cloud APIs, files, or external systems and construct dynamic inventory groups
explanation: The profile_tasks callback plugin measures task execution times, useful for identifying slow tasks to optimise.

text: What is tag-based execution in Ansible?
options: A release or version label attached to playbooks so operators can select tasks introduced in a particular deployment cycle
Tagging tasks and running only a subset using --tags or --skip-tags to speed up targeted playbook runs
An inventory group definition that assigns related hosts a shared label for targeting them in a play or command
A module parameter that changes how an individual module handles repeated operations, retries, or conditional execution
explanation: Tag always tasks that must run regardless of selected tags, such as variable loading and fact gathering.

text: Which Kubernetes object exposes an application through a stable network endpoint in a troubleshooting context?
options: Service
ConfigMap
Secret
Job
explanation: A Service provides stable discovery and load balancing for selected Pods.

text: What is Google Cloud Platform (GCP)?
options: An operating system distributed by Google that provides a desktop environment, system utilities, and virtualization features for enterprise computers
Googles public cloud providing compute, storage, networking, data analytics, AI, and managed services globally
An on-premises infrastructure solution that organizations install in their own data centers to manage servers, storage, and internal networks
A programming framework for building web and mobile applications, including language libraries, application tooling, and user-interface components
explanation: GCP runs on the same infrastructure that powers Google Search, Gmail, and YouTube.

text: What is the loop directive in Ansible?
options: A notification mechanism that queues a handler and runs it later when a task reports a change on the managed host
A way to run a task multiple times with different items from a list or dictionary, replacing the older with_items syntax
An expression that decides whether a task should execute, based on variables, facts, or registered results
A named value stored in play, host, group, or role scope and resolved when a task or template references it
explanation: Use loop with loop_control.label to improve output readability when looping over complex data structures.

text: What is Ansible Tower / AWX?
options: A command-line client for launching playbooks locally, with options for inventories, tags, verbosity, credentials, and limits
A web-based UI, REST API, and job scheduler for Ansible providing RBAC, audit trails, credential management, and centralised playbook execution
A repository of reusable Ansible modules and plugins that can be installed and referenced from playbooks by name
A hosted infrastructure platform that provisions virtual machines, networks, storage, and managed services through its own APIs
explanation: AWX is the open-source upstream of the commercial Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform.

text: What is the mitogen strategy plugin?
options: A reusable operation invoked by a task to install packages, manage files, create accounts, or configure services on a host
A third-party Ansible strategy plugin that dramatically speeds up playbook execution by replacing Ansibles default connection and execution method
A plugin that discovers hosts from a database, cloud API, or custom command and converts the response into inventory groups
A configuration provider that loads values from files, environment variables, or external secret stores before tasks execute
explanation: Mitogen can reduce playbook execution time by 1.5-10x by using Python remote execution rather than shell.

text: What is Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)?
options: A virtual machine provisioning service that creates and manages standalone compute instances without Kubernetes clusters
A managed Kubernetes service on GCP that automates cluster provisioning, scaling, and upgrades
A serverless function platform for deploying event-driven code without containers or cluster administration
A continuous integration and delivery service that builds, tests, and deploys software from source repositories
explanation: GKE Autopilot mode manages node provisioning and scaling automatically, charging per Pod rather than per node.

text: What is BigQuery?
options: A virtual machine service for launching configurable compute instances with attached disks and network interfaces
A serverless, highly scalable cloud data warehouse optimised for analytical queries over petabytes of data
A distributed key-value database designed for low-latency lookups of individual records at massive scale
A cloud file storage service that provides mounted directories for applications and shared enterprise data
explanation: BigQuery separates compute and storage, charges per query by bytes scanned, and can query data directly from GCS.

text: What is a GCP Project?
options: A billing account that records charges, applies payment methods, and controls spending across related cloud resources
The organisational unit in GCP that groups resources, APIs, billing, and IAM policies, serving as the isolation boundary for resources
A virtual network that defines subnets, routing rules, firewall policies, and connectivity for cloud workloads
A user account that represents an individual identity, stores credentials, and receives permissions to access services
explanation: Every GCP resource belongs to exactly one project. Projects have unique project IDs and numbers.

text: What is the gcloud CLI?
options: A web browser for opening Google Cloud consoles, viewing resources, and interacting with hosted applications
The primary command-line tool for managing GCP resources, configuring authentication, and scripting GCP operations
A monitoring agent installed on compute instances to collect system metrics, logs, and health information
A cost estimation tool that predicts monthly charges from selected services, regions, and usage assumptions
explanation: gcloud config configurations allow switching between multiple GCP projects and accounts quickly.

text: What is Preemptible (Spot) VM on GCP?
options: A premium VM tier offering guaranteed capacity, enhanced hardware, and priority scheduling at a higher price, with no automatic reclaim
A short-lived, deeply discounted VM (up to 91% off) that GCP can reclaim with 30 seconds notice, ideal for fault-tolerant batch workloads
A reserved VM commitment that provides a fixed instance at a reduced rate for a defined term, with guaranteed availability and no interruptions
A dedicated physical host assigned exclusively to one customer, providing isolated hardware, predictable performance, and protection from other tenants
explanation: Spot VMs are ideal for batch processing, simulations, and fault-tolerant workloads that can checkpoint and restart.

text: What is GCP Organization hierarchy?
options: A two-level hierarchy of Organizations and Projects, with resources attached directly to projects and no folders available for grouping or policy inheritance
A four-level hierarchy: Organization > Folders > Projects > Resources enabling centralised policy and IAM inheritance across all GCP resources
A three-level structure of Organization, Projects, and Billing Accounts, where IAM policies flow through billing relationships to every deployed resource
A billing-focused hierarchy containing accounts, invoices, and projects, without parent folders or inherited organization-wide governance across resources
explanation: IAM policies and Org Policies set at the Organization or Folder level are inherited by all Projects beneath them.

text: What is VPC Service Controls on GCP?
options: A stateful network firewall rule that filters packets between VPC subnets according to IP addresses, ports, protocols, and priority ordering
A security perimeter around GCP APIs and services to prevent data exfiltration even if IAM credentials are compromised
A private network gateway that routes traffic between VPC networks and service endpoints, providing connectivity while leaving API data-access permissions unchanged
An IAM policy mechanism that grants or denies principals access to individual APIs and resources, without restricting movement of data across network boundaries
explanation: VPC Service Controls protect sensitive data in services like BigQuery and GCS by restricting API access to trusted networks and identities.

text: What is Cloud Bigtable?
options: A fully managed relational SQL database with schemas, joins, and ACID transactions, primarily intended for business applications with strongly structured records
A fully managed, scalable NoSQL wide-column database designed for low-latency, high-throughput workloads like IoT, analytics, and time-series data
A durable object storage service that stores files and blobs in buckets, providing lifecycle rules and archival classes rather than row-based database queries
A managed message queue that buffers events between producers and consumers, supporting asynchronous delivery, acknowledgements, and retry processing for applications
explanation: Bigtable powers Google Maps, Search, and Analytics internally. It scales to petabytes with consistent single-digit millisecond latency.

text: What is the difference between Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner?
options: Cloud SQL is a globally distributed, strongly consistent database with horizontal scaling, while Cloud Spanner is a managed regional database compatible with MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server
Cloud SQL is a managed relational database (MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server); Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed, strongly consistent relational database with horizontal scaling
Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner are both managed relational databases with the same regional architecture and scaling model; the main difference is only their pricing and maintenance windows
Cloud Spanner is primarily a single-region relational database for traditional workloads, while Cloud SQL is designed for globally distributed transactions and automatic horizontal scaling
explanation: Cloud Spanner is used for global financial systems requiring ACID transactions at global scale. Cloud SQL suits regional workloads.

text: What is Cloud Dataflow?
options: A fully managed continuous integration and deployment service based on Apache Beam for building container images, testing code, and releasing applications
A fully managed stream and batch data processing service based on Apache Beam for ETL, real-time analytics, and pipeline execution
A managed virtual machine orchestration service for provisioning compute clusters, scheduling instances, and performing rolling infrastructure upgrades
A managed private connectivity and routing service for linking batch applications, streaming endpoints, and enterprise networks across regions
explanation: Dataflow automatically scales workers based on pipeline backlog and uses the Beam unified programming model.

text: What is Cloud Armor?
options: A centralized identity and access management service integrated with Cloud Load Balancing to authorize users and assign permissions to backend resources at the edge
A DDoS protection and Web Application Firewall (WAF) service integrated with Cloud Load Balancing to filter malicious traffic at the edge
A managed encryption and key-rotation service integrated with Cloud Storage to protect objects and automatically prevent unauthorized data access across projects
A network observability and traffic-analysis service integrated with Cloud Load Balancing to collect flow logs and visualize application performance at the edge
explanation: Cloud Armor supports OWASP Top 10 protection rules, rate limiting, and geo-based allow/deny policies.

text: What is the Anthos platform?
options: A Kubernetes cluster variant designed only for running workloads on GKE in Google Cloud, without support for on-premises data centers or other cloud providers
A managed application platform extending GKE and GCP services to on-premises data centers and other clouds for consistent hybrid and multi-cloud management
A centralized monitoring and policy-auditing tool for collecting logs from GKE clusters, but not for deploying or managing applications across environments
A serverless application platform that replaces GKE with automatically managed functions and containers, limited to workloads hosted within Google Cloud regions
explanation: Anthos uses Config Management (GitOps) and Service Mesh (Istio-based) for consistent policy and networking across environments.

text: What is the difference between Cloud Endpoints and Apigee?
options: Both products are lightweight GCP gateways with nearly identical features, differing mainly in branding and the regional endpoints used to expose APIs
Cloud Endpoints is a lightweight API gateway for GCP services; Apigee is a full enterprise API management platform with analytics, monetisation, and developer portal
Apigee is the simpler gateway for basic GCP APIs, while Cloud Endpoints provides enterprise analytics, monetisation, policy management, and developer portals
Cloud Endpoints is intended only for public external APIs, whereas Apigee is restricted to private internal services and cannot publish developer documentation
explanation: Apigee is preferred for large API programs with external developers; Cloud Endpoints suits simpler GCP-hosted API management.

text: What is GCP Shared VPC?
options: A public networking model that exposes a host project's VPC and firewall rules to internet users, allowing services to communicate without private connectivity
A networking model where a host project shares its VPC with service projects, enabling centralised network management with distributed resource ownership
A VPC peering configuration that links independent projects while keeping network administration separate and automatically synchronising their routes and firewall policies
A VPN configuration that connects a host project with service projects through encrypted tunnels, allowing centrally managed access to resources across separate networks
explanation: Shared VPC is the recommended pattern for multi-team GCP environments to enforce consistent network policies centrally.

text: What is the GCP Associate Cloud Engineer certification focused on?
options: Managing GCP billing accounts, budgets, invoices, and cost reports, with little emphasis on deploying applications or operating compute, storage, and network resources
Deploying applications, monitoring operations, and managing enterprise solutions using the GCP Console and CLI — covering compute, storage, networking, and IAM
Designing enterprise security architectures exclusively, including advanced threat detection, encryption policy, and compliance controls rather than routine platform operations
Using BigQuery to design data warehouses, optimise SQL queries, govern datasets, and build analytics pipelines, without covering general compute, networking, or IAM administration
explanation: The ACE certification validates ability to deploy and maintain GCP infrastructure. The Professional Cloud Architect is the next step.

text: What is a type annotation in TypeScript?
options: A documentation comment placed beside a declaration to describe its intended value, without affecting compiler checking or the generated JavaScript output
A syntax for explicitly specifying the type of a variable or parameter, e.g. const name: string
A runtime validation expression that checks values as the program executes and throws an error whenever an argument does not match the declared type
A linting rule configured in the project to enforce naming and formatting conventions, rather than syntax written directly on a declaration
explanation: Type annotations are erased at compile time — they exist only for the type checker and produce no runtime overhead.

text: Which command is used to build a Docker image?
options: docker run
docker build
docker create
docker exec
explanation: Defines base image.

text: What is a type guard in TypeScript?
options: A compile-time annotation that permanently converts a union into its first declared member without checking runtime values
A runtime check (typeof, instanceof, or a user-defined predicate) that narrows a union type within a code block
A generic type parameter rule that selects one union member based on its declared constraint during compilation
A compiler configuration option that enables strict null checks only inside functions containing conditional branches
explanation: A user-defined type guard returns a type predicate like param is SomeType, telling the compiler the narrowed type inside the if branch.

text: What is a discriminated union pattern?
options: A union whose members are unrelated primitive values and therefore cannot share a property used for narrowing in control flow
A union where each member has a shared literal property (discriminant) enabling exhaustive type narrowing in switch statements
A generic type parameter combining several possible instantiations under one reusable constraint without literal member tags
An intersection combining object members so that every value must satisfy all properties simultaneously before a switch can narrow it
explanation: Discriminated unions are ideal for modelling finite state machines and API responses with different shapes per status.

text: What is the keyof operator in TypeScript?
options: An object method that returns the names of an instance's own enumerable properties when called at runtime
A type operator producing a union of all property key types of an object type
A runtime function that reads a JavaScript object's keys and returns them as an array during program execution
A module operator that imports every exported property name as a value for use in a namespace declaration
explanation: keyof combined with generics enables type-safe property access: function getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K].

text: What is a mapped type in TypeScript?
options: A collection type that stores a variable number of values under numeric indexes while preserving their element type
A type created by iterating over the keys of another type and transforming each property
A utility function that loops over an object's properties at runtime and returns a transformed copy with new values
A conditional type that chooses between two complete object types after evaluating whether one type extends another
explanation: Mapped types power Partial, Required, and Readonly. The as clause enables key remapping during the transformation.

text: What are TypeScript declaration files (.d.ts)?
options: Compiled JavaScript output containing the executable implementations of modules after TypeScript removes their annotations and interfaces
Type information files describing the shape of JavaScript modules so TypeScript can type-check their usage
Source files containing the full JavaScript implementation of a library, including runtime statements and browser-facing behavior
Configuration files that define compiler options, module resolution rules, and the JavaScript target for a project
explanation: DefinitelyTyped packages provide .d.ts files for popular libraries that ship without built-in TypeScript types.

text: What is structural typing in TypeScript?
options: A type system where compatibility depends on the declared name or identity of a type, rather than on whether its properties have matching shapes
TypeScript checks type compatibility by structure (shape), not by name — an object with the right properties matches a type regardless of how it was declared
A runtime mechanism that inspects an object's declared type and rejects values whose properties do not match the original class definition
A compiler option that enables stricter checking of object assignments by requiring every value to use an explicitly declared interface name
explanation: Structural typing means interfaces are implicitly implemented. An object satisfies an interface if it has all required properties with compatible types.

text: What are template literal types in TypeScript?
options: A runtime operation that joins string values together while the program executes, producing an ordinary string rather than a compile-time literal type
A type-level feature constructing string literal types from combinations of other literals
A JavaScript interpolation syntax that evaluates embedded expressions immediately and stores the resulting characters in a mutable string value
A metadata annotation placed on string properties to describe formatting rules for serialization, validation, or other runtime processing
explanation: Template literal types power type-safe string APIs like CSS property names, event handler keys, and i18n key paths.

text: What is declaration merging in TypeScript?
options: Combining separately imported declarations from different files into one shared module scope so that their exports are exposed under a single import name
The ability to merge multiple declarations of the same identifier (interfaces, namespaces) into a single definition
A tsconfig compiler option that automatically joins source files with similar names into one output declaration file during the build process
A runtime process in which the JavaScript engine combines class definitions and namespace objects that happen to use the same identifier
explanation: Declaration merging enables module augmentation — adding properties to existing library types in ambient .d.ts files.

text: What is the TypeScript project references feature?
options: A module-aliasing feature that maps short import paths to source directories through tsconfig settings, without changing how projects are compiled
A feature splitting a large codebase into sub-projects with incremental compilation, improving build times and enforcing package boundaries
A monorepo orchestration tool that creates workspace packages, installs their dependencies, and coordinates scripts across independently configured projects
Bundler functionality that combines modules into optimized output files, performs code splitting, and determines dependency boundaries during packaging
explanation: Project references with composite: true enable incremental builds where only changed sub-projects are recompiled.

text: What is the any type in TypeScript?
options: A type that represents only values shared by every other type, rejecting operations that are not common to all possible values
A type that opts a value out of type checking entirely — an escape hatch that allows any operation
An error type produced whenever the compiler cannot infer a safe type, requiring the program to fail compilation before it runs
A union type automatically constructed from every possible member type, preserving strict checking for each alternative value
explanation: Overusing any defeats the purpose of TypeScript. Prefer unknown, proper types, or narrowed assertions instead.

text: What is a neural network?
options: A hardware communication architecture that connects computers and devices across a local network
A computational model inspired by the brain consisting of layers of interconnected nodes (neurons)
A supervised learning model that represents decisions as a sequence of binary splits
A database component that rewrites SQL statements to improve query execution plans
explanation: Neural networks learn hierarchical representations through layers of weighted connections, forming the basis of deep learning.

text: What is a union type in TypeScript?
options: A combined interface that merges separately declared properties into one object shape with all members required
A type that can be one of several types, written as string | number | null
An intersection of types that requires a value to satisfy every constituent, written using the vertical bar operator
A generic type that substitutes a placeholder parameter with one selected type when the declaration is instantiated
explanation: Union types model values that can legitimately be one of several types. Use type narrowing to handle each case safely.

text: What is an enum in TypeScript?
options: A list type that stores ordered values of one declared element type and provides indexed access at runtime
A set of named constants, either numeric or string-valued, improving code readability
A union type shorthand that creates aliases for string literals without emitting any JavaScript representation
A generic constraint that restricts a type parameter to a fixed collection of permitted named values
explanation: Prefer const enum for inlined values, or string literal union types for better narrowing and no runtime object.

text: What is the NoInfer utility type (TypeScript 5.4+)?
options: A utility that suppresses errors involving an inferred type, allowing incompatible arguments to compile without requiring an explicit annotation
A utility preventing TypeScript from using a type position as an inference site, forcing the caller to provide an explicit type argument
A conditional utility that prevents TypeScript from distributing a type over unions when the checked type appears inside a generic expression
A mapped utility that removes inferred properties from an object type, producing a version whose keys must be written explicitly
explanation: NoInfer<T> is useful in generic functions where you want the caller to explicitly annotate a type rather than having it silently inferred.

text: How do you make a shell script executable?
options: Run bash script.sh to grant the file execute permission permanently, allowing it to be started directly without specifying an interpreter
Use chmod +x script.sh to add execute permission to the file
Edit the file header to include an interpreter path, which changes the filesystem permission bits and makes the script executable
Use sudo only when launching the script, since elevated execution automatically supplies the missing execute permission for its owner
explanation: After chmod +x you can run the script with ./script.sh. Without it, run it explicitly with bash script.sh.

text: What does the special variable containing the last exit status hold?
options: The name of the script or command currently being executed, including the path used to invoke it from the shell
The exit status of the last command — 0 means success, non-zero means failure
The absolute path of the shell's current working directory, which changes whenever the script executes a cd command
The numeric identifier assigned to the current shell process, used to distinguish it from background jobs and child processes
explanation: Always check exit status after commands that might fail, or use set -e to exit automatically on any non-zero status.

text: What is the difference between single and double quotes in Bash?
options: Single and double quotes behave identically in Bash, preserving their contents literally and preventing all forms of expansion
Single quotes preserve everything literally; double quotes allow variable and command substitution
Double quotes provide stronger literal protection than single quotes, blocking variable expansion and command substitution inside the quoted text
Single quotes allow variables and command substitutions to expand, while double quotes preserve every character without interpreting shell syntax
explanation: Use single quotes when you want no interpretation. Use double quotes when you need variable expansion.

text: How do you redirect stdout to a file in Bash?
options: Use 2> to overwrite a file or 2>> to append standard output to a file
Use > to overwrite a file or >> to append output to a file
Use | to overwrite a file or || to append command output to a file
Use < to overwrite a file or << to append command output to a file
explanation: Use 2> to redirect stderr, and 2>&1 to merge stderr into the same destination as stdout.

text: What is the difference between single-bracket and double-bracket tests in Bash?
options: Single brackets are a Bash-only conditional syntax; double brackets invoke the external test command and require explicit quoting around every expansion
Single brackets are the POSIX test command; double brackets are a Bash built-in supporting regex, logical operators, and no word splitting
Double brackets are the POSIX test command; single brackets are Bash-specific and add regex matching, pattern operators, and arithmetic comparisons
Single brackets and double brackets differ only in whitespace rules; both invoke the same external utility and provide identical regex and logical-expression behavior
explanation: Prefer double brackets in Bash scripts for safety and power. Use single brackets only when writing portable POSIX sh.

text: What is command substitution in Bash?
options: Replacing the text of a command before execution, typically by assigning an alias or editing its source words
Capturing the output of a command into a variable using the dollar-parentheses syntax
A pipeline shorthand that sends a command's output directly into the next command without creating an intermediate value
A redirection form that writes a command's output into a file descriptor without storing the resulting text
explanation: Prefer the dollar-parentheses form over backticks — it is easier to read and supports nesting cleanly.

text: What does trap do in Bash?
options: Reports syntax errors immediately and prevents the shell from continuing, without registering handlers for signals or normal exits
Registers a command to execute when the script receives a signal or exits, used for cleanup operations
Suspends the current process until a specified signal arrives, then resumes execution automatically after the pause
Sets a global error-handling policy that automatically retries failed commands and logs every signal without running cleanup code
explanation: Use trap cleanup EXIT to ensure your cleanup function runs whether the script exits normally, on error, or on interrupt.

text: What is getopts used for in Bash?
options: A utility for locating files by pathname patterns and printing matching entries from selected directories
Parsing short command-line options in scripts in a POSIX-compatible, standardised way
A string-processing facility that replaces substrings and normalizes text values supplied as arguments
A looping construct that repeatedly executes a body while consuming positional parameters from the script
explanation: Use getopts in a while loop to handle flags and optional arguments with proper error reporting.

text: What is the difference between sourcing and executing a script?
options: Identical in effect: both run commands in the current shell context, sharing variables and leaving the same environment changes afterward
Source runs the script in the current shell sharing variables; executing creates a subshell so environment changes do not affect the parent
Executing is safer: it isolates all commands from the parent shell, whereas sourcing exposes variables and can overwrite settings
Source cannot run scripts: it only reads function definitions, while execution is required for commands, control flow, and external programs
explanation: Use source for scripts that set environment variables or define functions you need in the current shell session.

text: What is the purpose of ShellCheck?
options: A syntax-formatting utility that rewrites indentation, quoting, and spacing throughout shell scripts without analyzing behavior
A static analysis tool detecting bugs, anti-patterns, and portability issues in shell scripts with explanations and fix suggestions
A runtime debugger that pauses executing shell commands, inspects stack frames, and changes variables interactively
A performance profiler that measures command timings, process usage, and system-call overhead during script execution
explanation: Integrate ShellCheck into CI pipelines to catch shell scripting errors automatically before they reach production.

text: How do React Server Components differ from Client Components in the App Router?
options: Server Components use the 'use client' directive and browser APIs; Client Components render only on the server
Server Components have no interactivity or browser APIs; Client Components use the 'use client' directive and run in the browser
Server Components and Client Components both render in the browser, but only Server Components can use interactive hooks
Client Components have no browser APIs or interactivity; Server Components use 'use client' and manage event handlers
explanation: 'use client' marks a component as a Client Component boundary. Server Components can't use state, effects, or browser APIs but reduce JS bundle size.

text: What is the purpose of React's Concurrent Mode / concurrent features?
options: Running React rendering on multiple CPU threads so components can update in parallel
Allowing React to interrupt rendering to handle higher-priority updates
Improving server-side rendering by moving every component render to a background process
Integrating Web Workers so React can execute component logic outside the main browser thread
explanation: Concurrent React can pause, resume, or abandon renders, enabling features like Suspense, transitions, and startTransition.

text: What is the purpose of the 'key' prop in dynamic forms vs. lists?
options: It controls tab order by assigning keyboard-navigation positions to dynamically generated form fields and list items
Forcing a key change remounts the component, resetting its state — useful for clearing controlled form inputs
It's only used for ARIA accessibility, identifying each dynamic form field and list item to assistive technology
It prevents XSS attacks by assigning unique identities to dynamic form values before React renders them
explanation: Changing a component's key forces React to unmount and remount it, effectively resetting all internal state — a common pattern for form reset.

text: What is the React Context API used for?
options: Making HTTP requests to remote APIs and caching their responses
Sharing state across many components without prop drilling
Controlling mount, update, and unmount behavior within components
Fetching server-rendered data for pages before components are displayed
explanation: Context provides a way to pass data through the component tree without manually passing props at every level.

text: What is the key prop used for in React lists?
options: Applying CSS classes and visual styles to each list item
Helping React identify which items changed in a list
Assigning accessibility attributes and ARIA labels to list elements
Reordering list entries according to their values or indexes
explanation: Keys help React efficiently reconcile list changes by tracking which items were added, removed, or reordered.

text: What is the Suspense component used for in React?
options: Handling exceptions thrown during rendering by displaying an error boundary fallback
Showing a fallback UI while waiting for lazy-loaded components or data
Animating CSS properties during transitions between mounted and unmounted elements
Managing references to DOM nodes and preserving them across component renders
explanation: Suspense lets you specify a fallback (e.g. spinner) shown while children are loading asynchronously.

text: What is the difference between ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) and SSR in Next.js?
options: ISR re-generates pages in the background at a set interval without a full rebuild; SSR renders per-request
They are the same rendering strategy, with both generating pages on each request and never reusing previously rendered HTML
ISR is a client-side caching mechanism that updates rendered page data in the browser without server regeneration
SSR only works in the Pages Router, while the App Router supports exclusively static generation and client-side rendering
explanation: ISR uses revalidate in getStaticProps to regenerate static pages in the background without redeploying the whole site.

text: How does unquoted variable expansion cause bugs in Bash?
options: Unquoted variables are expanded literally as one argument, so only explicitly quoted wildcard patterns and spaces can alter filenames
Unquoted variables are split on IFS characters and glob-expanded, so filenames with spaces and wildcards break unexpectedly
