A browser-focused frontend language for building interactive pages without a managed runtime
explanation: C# is a general-purpose language created by Microsoft, running on .NET CLR. It supports OOP, functional, and async patterns.

text: What is the difference between `value types` and `reference types` in C#?
options: Value types are class-based objects allocated on the heap, while reference types embed their complete object data directly inside each variable
Value types (struct, int, bool) store data directly on the stack; reference types (class, string, array) store a reference on the stack pointing to heap memory
There is no semantic distinction: both categories always copy the complete object and are stored in the same location chosen by the garbage collector
Reference types cannot be null because every class, string, and array variable must always point to a valid heap object before it can be read
explanation: Value types are copied on assignment. Reference types share the same heap object when assigned.

text: What is LINQ?
options: A standalone relational database engine that stores tables and executes SQL queries independently of any application
Language Integrated Query — lets you query collections (and databases) using SQL-like syntax directly in C#
A diagnostic logging library that records query statements, exceptions, and performance timings from C# programs
A graphical user-interface framework for designing windows, controls, and event handlers in desktop applications
explanation: LINQ provides `Where`, `Select`, `GroupBy`, etc. as first-class C# expressions, working on IEnumerable and IQueryable.

text: What causes a goroutine leak and how do you detect it?
options: Unbounded memory allocation caused by retained slices or maps, detected primarily through heap profiles and garbage-collection statistics
Goroutines blocked forever on channels or locks, never exiting. Detected via runtime.NumGoroutine(), pprof goroutine dumps, or goleak in tests
Excessive CPU consumption from a busy loop, detected with CPU profiling and scheduler traces rather than goroutine counts
Heap fragmentation from many differently sized allocations, detected with allocator statistics and object-lifetime profiles
explanation: Leaked goroutines accumulate over time. goleak asserts no goroutines remain after tests; pprof goroutine profile shows stack traces.

text: How does Go handle interface satisfaction for pointer vs value receivers?
options: Both T and *T satisfy exactly the same interfaces, because Go automatically promotes pointer-receiver methods to every value type
A value type T only satisfies an interface if methods are value receivers; *T satisfies interfaces with either receiver type
A type with pointer receivers satisfies interfaces only when used through *T; value-receiver methods are excluded from pointer method sets
A value type T satisfies interfaces containing either receiver kind, while *T satisfies only interfaces whose methods use pointer receivers
explanation: If method M is on *T, only *T satisfies an interface containing M. If M is on T, both T and *T satisfy it.

text: How does Go achieve zero-downtime deploys?
options: Go's runtime automatically replaces the running binary after a deployment signal, preserving listeners and active requests without application code
Use SIGTERM handling + graceful shutdown (context cancel, server.Shutdown), not Go-specific but Go makes it easy
Restart the application with the --hot flag so the runtime swaps in new code while retaining existing connections
Use a goroutine reload mechanism that swaps package code in memory after SIGUSR1, without server handoff or graceful shutdown
explanation: Go's http.Server.Shutdown(ctx) stops accepting new connections and waits for in-flight requests, enabling rolling deployments.

text: What is the `using` statement in C#?
options: Imports namespaces for the duration of the block, making their types available without qualification
Ensures `Dispose()` is called on an IDisposable resource when the block exits, even on exception
Declares a compile-time alias for a namespace or type, allowing it to be referenced through a shorter name
Repeats a block while its IDisposable expression remains valid, automatically testing the resource on each iteration
explanation: `using (var conn = new SqlConnection(...)) { }` guarantees `conn.Dispose()` is called, releasing unmanaged resources.

text: What is a `delegate` in C#?
options: A base class that supplies default implementations for methods shared by related classes in an inheritance hierarchy
A type-safe function pointer that can reference methods with a matching signature
A property accessor that controls how a class reads and writes the value of a particular property
An async keyword that causes a method to execute on a background thread and return a Task automatically
explanation: Delegates are the foundation of events and lambdas in C#. `Func<>` and `Action<>` are built-in generic delegates.

text: What is the difference between `List<T>` and `IList<T>`?
options: There is no practical difference; both names refer to the same concrete collection type and expose identical implementation details
List<T> is a concrete ArrayList implementation; IList<T> is an interface. Program to the interface for flexibility
IList<T> is thread-safe and synchronizes concurrent mutations, whereas List<T> requires callers to provide their own locking
List<T> is immutable after construction, while IList<T> provides the mutable operations needed to change its contents
explanation: Coding to `IList<T>` or `IEnumerable<T>` decouples callers from the concrete implementation.

text: What is Dependency Injection in ASP.NET Core?
options: A testing pattern that creates mock services inside each class, allowing tests to replace production behavior without a container
A built-in IoC container that injects dependencies (services) into classes rather than creating them, improving testability
A data-access pattern that separates repositories from controllers and automatically manages database connections and transactions
A caching strategy that injects frequently used responses into memory and refreshes them automatically when dependencies change
explanation: ASP.NET Core's DI container registers services (`AddScoped`, `AddSingleton`, `AddTransient`) and injects them via constructors.

text: What is `ValueTask` vs `Task` in C#?
options: ValueTask is a reference type that always allocates on the heap, increasing GC pressure for synchronously completed operations
ValueTask is a struct that avoids heap allocation for operations that frequently complete synchronously, reducing GC pressure
Task is a value type optimized for synchronous completion, while ValueTask is the older heap-allocated abstraction for async work
ValueTask and Task have identical allocation behavior, and choosing between them only changes the method naming and return syntax
explanation: When an async method usually returns synchronously (cache hit), `ValueTask` avoids allocating a `Task` object, improving hot-path performance.

text: What is the `IHostedService` interface used for?
options: A service abstraction for hosting HTTP endpoints and accepting network connections, responsible for binding ports and managing web requests
Background services registered with ASP.NET Core's DI container, started when the host starts and stopped on shutdown
A middleware base class used to intercept every incoming request, configure the HTTP pipeline, and produce responses before endpoint execution
A health check interface used to report application readiness and liveness to load balancers, orchestrators, and monitoring systems
explanation: `IHostedService` / `BackgroundService` runs long-running tasks (queue consumers, timers) managed by the ASP.NET Core host lifecycle.

text: How does `async void` differ from `async Task` and why is it dangerous?
options: There is no meaningful difference because both signatures return the same kind of asynchronous result, and callers can await either one for exceptions
async void exceptions cannot be caught by the caller and fire-and-forget; async Task returns an awaitable the caller can observe
async void is faster because it avoids creating a Task, and its exceptions are automatically captured by the caller's await expression
async Task does not support exception propagation or cancellation, so failures from asynchronous methods can only be handled with async void
explanation: `async void` is for event handlers only. Unhandled exceptions crash the process. Always return `Task` from async methods.

text: What is `IMemoryCache` vs `IDistributedCache` in ASP.NET Core?
options: They are identical caching abstractions with the same storage scope, and either implementation automatically shares entries between every application instance
IMemoryCache is in-process (single instance); IDistributedCache (Redis, SQL) is shared across all server instances
IDistributedCache is always slower than IMemoryCache and should only be used for rare lookups, because network-backed caches cannot handle concurrent access
Only IMemoryCache is thread-safe; IDistributedCache requires application-level locking whenever multiple requests read or write the same cache entry
explanation: In load-balanced deployments, use IDistributedCache (Redis) so all nodes share the same cache. IMemoryCache is faster but node-local.

text: What is Minimal API in ASP.NET Core and how does it differ from controllers?
options: Minimal APIs are identical to MVC controllers because each endpoint requires a controller class, action method, and attribute-based route definition
Minimal APIs define endpoints as lambda functions directly on the app object without controllers or attributes, reducing boilerplate
Minimal APIs have no middleware support, so authentication, exception handling, logging, and other cross-cutting behavior must be implemented inside each handler
Minimal APIs are always less performant than controllers because endpoint lambdas require reflection and incur extra dispatch overhead for every request
explanation: Minimal APIs (introduced in .NET 6) are faster to write and benchmark higher than controller-based APIs due to less indirection.

text: What is the difference between `==` and `===` in PHP?
options: == compares values only when types match; === compares values after converting their types
== compares values with type coercion; === compares value AND type (strict)
== compares references for objects; === compares primitive values while ignoring their types
== performs strict comparison of values and types; === allows automatic type conversion
explanation: `0 == false` is true; `0 === false` is false. Always use `===` to avoid unexpected type juggling.

text: What is Blade in Laravel?
options: A PHP parser that converts source code into executable instructions before the application runs
Laravel's templating engine with `@` directives, template inheritance, and component support
A database query builder that constructs SQL statements through Laravel's fluent API
A Laravel test runner that discovers test files, executes assertions, and reports failures
explanation: Blade compiles to plain PHP and provides `@if`, `@foreach`, `@extends`, `@section` for clean view templates.

text: What is a Laravel Migration?
options: A Laravel command that exports selected database tables into versioned SQL files for deployment
A version-controlled PHP class that defines database schema changes, run with `php artisan migrate`
A PHP class that seeds predefined records and replaces existing application data during installation
A deployment configuration file that clears compiled views, routes, and cached application settings before release
explanation: Migrations provide `up()` and `down()` methods for applying and rolling back schema changes collaboratively.

text: How does Laravel's Queue system work?
options: Jobs are executed immediately during the request, while the queue records completed results in Redis or a database for later retrieval
Jobs are dispatched to a queue (Redis/database/SQS), processed by background workers (`php artisan queue:work`)
Jobs are submitted to the browser's JavaScript runtime, which periodically polls the server and performs each task for the user
Queues are scheduled PHP scripts launched by cron, with each script processing one fixed job and then terminating
explanation: Laravel queues defer time-consuming tasks (emails, API calls) to background workers, improving response times.

text: What are PHP traits?
options: Interfaces that provide method contracts and require implementing classes to define each declared operation
Code reuse mechanisms allowing methods to be included in multiple classes without inheritance
A special kind of concrete class that can be instantiated directly and inherited by several unrelated subclasses
Aliases that let PHP import a class under a shorter name without copying any of its methods or properties
explanation: Traits (`use Timestamps;`) resolve PHP's lack of multiple inheritance by letting unrelated classes share methods.

text: What is an Abstract class vs Interface in PHP?
options: Abstract classes may only declare abstract methods and cannot contain properties; interfaces provide concrete method bodies, and a class can extend several interfaces directly
Abstract classes can have concrete methods and state; interfaces only declare method signatures. A class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one abstract class
Abstract classes and interfaces are interchangeable contracts; both permit multiple inheritance of implementation, shared instance state, and concrete methods in every declaration
Interfaces define reusable base classes with protected state, while abstract classes contain only signatures; a class may extend multiple abstract classes but implement one interface
explanation: Use abstract classes for shared implementation; interfaces for contracts. PHP 8 allows interface constants.

text: What is Laravel Horizon?
options: A frontend administration toolkit for building Vue dashboards around Laravel applications, including reusable charts, navigation components, and browser-side state management
A queue monitoring dashboard for Redis queues with real-time metrics, failed job tracking, and supervisor configuration
A Redis-based caching layer that automatically stores rendered views, database results, and configuration values, with expiration policies and cache invalidation controls
A deployment automation tool that provisions servers, uploads Laravel releases, runs migrations, and switches traffic between versions during zero-downtime deployments
explanation: Horizon provides a beautiful UI for monitoring Laravel queues, throughput, and failed jobs, with configuration-driven worker pools.

text: What is the difference between Eager Loading and Lazy Loading in Eloquent?
options: Lazy loading uses with() to retrieve every relationship in the initial query, while eager loading waits until a property is accessed and can create additional N+1 queries
Eager loading (`with()`) fetches related models in upfront queries; lazy loading fetches them on access causing N+1 query problems
Lazy loading and eager loading issue the same relationship queries; the distinction only changes whether Eloquent serializes related models before or after the response
Eager loading always improves performance by retrieving every possible relationship immediately, whereas lazy loading is deprecated because deferred relationship queries are unsupported
explanation: The N+1 problem: looping 100 posts and accessing `post->author` lazily triggers 101 queries. `with('author')` does it in 2.

text: What are PHP Fibers (PHP 8.1)?
options: A threading API that creates independent operating-system threads for PHP functions, allowing parallel execution with shared memory and preemptive scheduling between thread contexts
Lightweight coroutines enabling cooperative multitasking — the foundation for async PHP libraries like ReactPHP/Swoole
A syntax alias for generators that automatically converts every yield expression into a background task, without introducing separate suspension and resumption control
A memory optimization facility that compresses inactive variables and moves them between heaps, reducing allocation overhead without affecting control flow or execution order
explanation: Fibers allow functions to pause and resume, enabling async patterns without callbacks. They underpin frameworks like Amp v3.

text: What is a PHP Generator?
options: A function that generates pseudorandom values on demand from a seed, primarily used for simulations rather than iterating through stored application data
A function using `yield` that produces values lazily, saving memory for large data streams vs loading everything into an array
A command-line code scaffolding tool that creates controllers, models, tests, and other standard PHP project files from predefined templates
An ORM feature that streams database records through a query builder while automatically mapping each result into a persistent model object
explanation: Generators return an iterator without storing all values in memory — ideal for large CSV files or database cursors.

text: What is event sourcing and how does it relate to Laravel Event/Listener?
options: Event sourcing is a replacement for Laravel's event dispatcher in which only the latest state is retained, while listeners synchronously update the database
Event sourcing stores all state changes as immutable events; Laravel's Event system dispatches domain events to Listeners asynchronously via queues
Laravel Events and Listeners are the same persistence mechanism as event sourcing, storing every model snapshot automatically and replaying it during requests
Event sourcing eliminates the need for migrations by deriving database schemas from queued Laravel listeners that process commands and modify current state
explanation: Laravel's queued Listeners enable event sourcing patterns where you replay events to rebuild state or build projections.

text: What is borrowing in Rust?
options: Importing a library by bringing its public names into the current module, allowing functions and types to be used without taking ownership of their definitions
Temporarily using a value via a reference (&T for shared, &mut T for exclusive) without taking ownership
Heap allocation that moves a value from the stack into dynamically managed storage, allowing multiple references to use the allocation without borrowing restrictions
Cloning data into a separate owned value so that modifications through one variable cannot affect the original value or require lifetime annotations
explanation: Rust enforces: either many shared references (&T) OR one mutable reference (&mut T) at a time — never both.

text: What is the `Option<T>` type?
options: A nullable pointer wrapper that stores either a memory address or a null pointer, with runtime checks used to determine whether the referenced object is available
An enum with `Some(T)` or `None` that forces explicit null handling at compile time
A trait defining a common interface for values that can be selected from several alternatives, with implementations determining which concrete variant is active
A reference type that always points to a valid value of type `T`, using lifetime metadata to prevent dangling references but never representing absence
explanation: Rust has no null; `Option<T>` must be handled with `match`, `if let`, or `unwrap()`, preventing null pointer errors.

text: What is a Rust trait?
options: A comment marker that documents intended behavior for functions and communicates guidance to the compiler
A collection of method signatures (and default implementations) that types can implement — similar to interfaces
A data structure that stores fields and values together under a named type for later access
A module declaration that groups related functions, types, and imports into one namespace for reuse
explanation: Traits like `Display`, `Iterator`, and `Clone` define shared behaviour. Generics are constrained with trait bounds.

text: What does `clone()` do in Rust?
options: Transfers ownership of the value to another binding without allocating a second copy
Creates a deep copy of a value, producing a new owned copy
Creates a temporary borrowed view of the value without taking ownership
Immediately deallocates the value and makes its storage available for reuse
explanation: `clone()` produces an independent copy. Prefer borrowing over cloning to avoid unnecessary allocation.

text: What is `async/await` in Rust?
options: Syntax for writing asynchronous code that automatically creates OS threads; no runtime is needed because the compiler schedules each future directly
Syntax for writing asynchronous code that compiles to state machines; requires a runtime (Tokio, async-std) to drive futures
Syntax for writing asynchronous code that compiles each future into a kernel task; the operating system drives execution without a Rust runtime
Syntax for writing asynchronous code that executes immediately when called; awaiting a future blocks its thread until the operation completes
explanation: `async fn` returns a `Future`. The runtime's executor polls futures to completion. Tokio is the dominant async runtime.

text: What is the `Deref` trait?
options: A trait that removes the value behind a pointer and releases its allocation, allowing custom containers to define their deletion behavior
Allows custom types to be dereferenced like pointers (`*x`), enabling smart pointers like `Box<T>` and `Arc<T>` to act like references
A trait that copies the complete contents of a referenced value into a new location, making smart pointers duplicate their data automatically
A trait that converts pointed-to values into displayable text, allowing pointer wrappers to choose their formatting implementation
explanation: `Box<T>` implements `Deref<Target=T>`, so `*box_val` yields `&T`. Deref coercion automatically converts `&Box<T>` to `&T`.

text: What are Rust macros?
options: Comments that are expanded by the compiler into executable statements before type checking, commonly used to generate repetitive Rust source code
Code that generates code at compile time using the `macro_rules!` system or procedural macros — like `println!`, `vec!`, `derive(Debug)`
Runtime functions that construct and execute new Rust statements while the program runs, providing dynamic code generation after compilation
C preprocessor directives supported directly by Rust, using textual substitution and conditional compilation before the Rust parser processes the source
explanation: Declarative macros (`macro_rules!`) pattern-match token trees. Procedural macros (`#[derive(...)]`) inspect and generate code from ASTs.

text: What is zero-cost abstraction in Rust?
options: Language features that allocate all data without charge, allowing programs to avoid paying for memory regardless of how much storage they use
Abstractions (iterators, generics, traits) that compile to the same code as hand-written equivalents — no runtime overhead
Abstractions that replace references with null pointers during optimization, eliminating runtime checks by representing absent values as address zero
Abstractions that force iterators, generics, and trait implementations onto the stack, preventing them from using heap allocation or dynamic dispatch
explanation: Rust's monomorphisation expands generics into specialised code at compile time. Iterator chains optimise to tight loops with no indirection.

text: What is NestJS?
options: A browser-focused TypeScript framework inspired by Angular, using components and templates for building interactive client-side applications
An opinionated TypeScript-first Node.js framework inspired by Angular, using decorators and DI for building scalable server-side apps
A database-focused Node.js framework providing entities, migrations, and query builders for managing persistent application data
A testing-focused TypeScript toolkit providing mocks, assertions, and fixtures for validating Node.js application behavior
explanation: NestJS wraps Express (or Fastify) under the hood and enforces a modular, Angular-like structure.

text: What is a NestJS Module?
options: A standard JavaScript module that exports reusable functions or values for any Node.js application, without NestJS metadata
A class decorated with @Module() that organises related controllers, providers, and imports into a cohesive feature
A request-processing component that runs before controllers and modifies HTTP requests or responses during the pipeline
A TypeScript annotation that marks a class or method with metadata but does not organise application dependencies or features
explanation: Every NestJS app has a root AppModule; feature modules group related functionality and can be imported by other modules.

text: What does the `@Module` decorator's `providers` array contain?
options: Controller classes and route handlers that define the HTTP endpoints exposed by the module to incoming application requests
Injectable services, repositories, and factories scoped to the module
Middleware functions and request-processing callbacks that execute before routing and can modify the raw HTTP request
Guard classes that evaluate authorization and decide whether a request may proceed to a protected route
explanation: Providers are instantiated by the DI container and can be injected into controllers or other providers within the module.

text: What is the difference between Guards, Interceptors, and Middleware in NestJS?
options: Guards transform request data; Interceptors select authorized users; Middleware catches application exceptions after the route handler finishes
Guards determine access (auth); Interceptors transform requests/responses or add logging; Middleware processes raw HTTP before routing
Guards format responses; Interceptors authenticate requests; Middleware validates DTOs after controller parameters have already been resolved
Guards run only after handlers; Interceptors define database access; Middleware is a NestJS-specific replacement for controllers and routing
explanation: Execution order: Middleware → Guards → Interceptors (before) → Route Handler → Interceptors (after) → Exception Filters.

text: What is monomorphisation in Rust?
options: A runtime specialization mechanism that selects generic implementations during execution, avoiding separate machine-code copies for each concrete type but adding dispatch overhead
The compiler generates a concrete copy of generic code for each concrete type used, producing fast specialised code at the cost of binary size
JIT compilation that postpones translating generic functions until they are first called, allowing runtime type information to guide optimization instead of compile-time monomorphisation
Type erasure that removes concrete generic type information before code generation, making one shared implementation serve all type arguments with uniform runtime representation
explanation: Unlike Java's type erasure, Rust creates a `max::<i32>` and `max::<f64>` from `fn max<T: Ord>(a: T, b: T)`, enabling inlining and optimisation.

text: What is the `Send` and `Sync` trait?
options: Serialisation traits: one converts values into bytes for transmission across threads, while the other reconstructs them safely when received by another worker
Marker traits: Send means ownership can be transferred across threads; Sync means shared references can be accessed from multiple threads
Memory alignment traits: one chooses layouts suitable for atomic access, while the other guarantees fields share cache-line boundaries on every thread
Async traits: one marks futures that may be moved between executors, while the other identifies futures that can be polled concurrently without coordination
explanation: The compiler auto-implements `Send`/`Sync` for types composed of Send/Sync parts. `Rc<T>` is neither; `Arc<T>` is both.

text: What is `impl Trait` vs `dyn Trait` in Rust?
options: Identical abstractions with different syntax: both compile generic code into the same dispatch mechanism, and the choice affects readability but not runtime performance
`impl Trait` is static dispatch (monomorphised at compile time, zero overhead); `dyn Trait` is dynamic dispatch (vtable lookup at runtime)
`dyn Trait` is deprecated in favor of `impl Trait`, because modern Rust always resolves trait calls statically and no longer supports vtables for object-safe traits
`impl Trait` only works in return position, where it hides a concrete type; it cannot be used in argument position, variable bindings, or trait implementations
explanation: Return `impl Trait` when you know the concrete type. Use `Box<dyn Trait>` for heterogeneous collections or when the type can vary at runtime.

text: What is the Tokio runtime in Rust?
options: A testing framework that supplies asynchronous test cases, deterministic task scheduling, assertion helpers, and fixtures for validating Rust futures without production networking
An async runtime providing a task scheduler, I/O driver (epoll/kqueue), timers, and sync primitives for async Rust applications
A web framework that maps HTTP routes to async handlers, manages request middleware, serves static files, and provides a default application server for Rust
A database driver that maintains connection pools, translates SQL queries into Rust values, and schedules database operations through a built-in asynchronous protocol
explanation: Tokio is the standard async runtime for Rust servers. It uses work-stealing across multiple threads. Axum, Actix-Web, and Tonic build on Tokio.

text: What is the orphan rule in Rust?
options: A garbage-collection rule that requires every heap allocation to have one owning tracing root, preventing unreachable Rust objects from being reclaimed too early
You can implement a trait for a type only if either the trait or the type is defined in your crate, preventing conflicting implementations
A lifetime rule that forbids references from outliving their owners, rejecting borrowed values whenever the compiler cannot infer a sufficiently long scope
A closure rule that limits which captured variables may be moved into a closure, preventing two closures in one crate from claiming the same environment
explanation: The orphan rule ensures coherence — only one implementation of a trait for a type can exist, preventing ambiguity across crates.

text: What is the Lifecycle of a NestJS provider?
options: Providers are instantiated only when first injected, and lifecycle hooks run exclusively for request-scoped instances during each incoming request
Providers are instantiated when their module is loaded, implementing OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy, OnApplicationBootstrap, OnApplicationShutdown hooks
Providers are recreated for every request by default, implementing initialization and shutdown hooks whenever the request processing pipeline begins or ends
Providers are instantiated by the garbage collector after module loading, with lifecycle hooks triggered automatically when references are released
explanation: Implement `OnModuleInit` to run setup code after DI resolution. `OnApplicationShutdown` handles graceful shutdown (close DB connections, stop queues).

text: What is lazy-loading modules in NestJS?
options: Loading modules during every request with LazyModuleLoader to avoid keeping providers in memory between serverless invocations
Loading modules on-demand using LazyModuleLoader to reduce startup time in serverless/CLI environments
Loading modules ahead of time with LazyModuleLoader to cache their providers and eliminate dependency-injection work during application startup
Loading modules only inside test suites with LazyModuleLoader so production applications can omit their providers from the compiled bundle
explanation: In Lambda/CLI, most routes are never hit. LazyModuleLoader defers module initialisation, cutting cold start times.

text: How does NestJS support gRPC?
options: Via `@nestjs/microservices` with `GrpcOptions`; controllers use `@MessagePattern()` to translate gRPC calls into REST endpoints without reading `.proto` definitions
Via @nestjs/microservices with `GrpcOptions`; controllers use `@GrpcMethod('ServiceName','methodName')` matching `.proto` definitions
Via `@nestjs/platform-express` with `GrpcOptions`; controllers use `@Get()` routes over HTTP/1.1 while a proxy converts JSON responses into gRPC messages
Via `@nestjs/microservices` with `GrpcOptions`; controllers use `@GrpcMethod()` only for WebSocket handlers, with service names inferred from HTTP route metadata
explanation: NestJS generates gRPC service implementations from `.proto` files. The client uses `@Inject(SERVICE_CLIENT) client: ClientGrpc`.

text: What is a NestJS custom transport strategy?
options: An implementation of `CustomTransportStrategy` + `ClientProxy` that replaces NestJS routing and selects HTTP controllers according to a custom URL-matching algorithm
An implementation of `CustomTransportStrategy` + `ClientProxy` that adds a new message broker (e.g. Pulsar) to the NestJS microservices system
An implementation of `CustomTransportStrategy` + `ClientProxy` that adds a database driver and maps repository methods to broker messages for persistence operations
An implementation of `CustomTransportStrategy` + `ClientProxy` that replaces NestJS authentication guards with a custom token-validation protocol shared by all controllers
explanation: Custom transports extend the microservices system to brokers not built into @nestjs/microservices.

text: What is the `ContextType` system in NestJS guards and filters?
options: The execution context abstraction that represents only HTTP requests — Guards and Filters use `host.getType()` to select controllers, routes, or middleware within the HTTP pipeline
The execution context abstraction that unifies HTTP, WebSocket, and microservice requests — Guards and Filters use `host.getType()` to branch behaviour
The TypeScript type abstraction that converts HTTP, WebSocket, and microservice requests into compile-time interfaces, with Guards and Filters branching through generic annotations
The dependency-injection context abstraction that creates separate providers for HTTP, WebSocket, and microservice calls — Guards and Filters use `host.getType()` to resolve tokens
explanation: `ExecutionContext.getType()` returns 'http', 'ws', or 'rpc', letting a single Guard work across all transports.

text: How does NestJS handle exceptions?
options: Via controller-level try/catch blocks — each handler must catch errors and serialize the response, since NestJS does not provide a centralized exception mechanism
Via Exception Filters — classes implementing `ExceptionFilter` that catch and format errors; `HttpException` is the base class
Via middleware — a global middleware layer intercepts thrown errors, converts them into HTTP responses, and replaces the framework's exception-handling pipeline
Via interceptors only — interceptors wrap every request, catch rejected promises, and are responsible for formatting all application and HTTP exceptions
explanation: `@Catch(HttpException)` creates a filter. `throw new NotFoundException()` returns a JSON 404 response automatically.

text: What is an availability zone in a troubleshooting context?
options: An isolated location within a cloud region
A programming language
A database table
A billing account
explanation: Availability zones are isolated infrastructure locations inside a region.

text: How do you implement JWT authentication in NestJS?
options: Build it manually — parse the Authorization header, verify and rotate tokens in custom guards, and attach the authenticated user without using NestJS JWT or Passport integrations
Using @nestjs/jwt for token signing/verification and @nestjs/passport with passport-jwt strategy, applied via a JwtAuthGuard
Using cookies only — store the JWT in an HTTP-only cookie and authenticate every request through cookie parsing, without bearer tokens, Passport strategies, or a JwtAuthGuard
Using BasicAuth only — send a username and password on every request and validate those credentials in a guard, rather than issuing or verifying signed JWTs
explanation: The standard stack: `PassportModule`, `JwtModule.register({ secret, signOptions })`, JwtStrategy, and JwtAuthGuard decorating protected endpoints.

text: What is CQRS in NestJS?
options: A routing pattern — @nestjs/cqrs maps URL paths to controller methods and separates route definitions from HTTP handlers through a dedicated router bus
Command Query Responsibility Segregation — @nestjs/cqrs separates write operations (commands) from read operations (queries) using handlers and a message bus
A testing pattern — @nestjs/cqrs organizes test fixtures and assertions into command and query suites, using handlers to execute isolated scenarios
A caching pattern — @nestjs/cqrs stores query results and invalidates them after commands, using the message bus as a cache coordination layer
explanation: CQRS improves scalability by separating reads and writes. Commands mutate state; queries return data. Events propagate side effects.

text: How does NestJS health checking work?
options: Via a custom `/health` controller that manually checks selected dependencies and returns HTTP 200, without using Terminus indicators or probe-specific semantics
Via @nestjs/terminus which provides a HealthCheckService with pre-built indicators (HTTP, database, Redis, microservice) for Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes
Via the load balancer, which determines application health from connection success and removes unhealthy Rails or NestJS instances from rotation
Via Prometheus metrics alone, with Kubernetes interpreting exported uptime and request counters as automatic liveness and readiness results
explanation: Terminus adds `/health` endpoints that return structured JSON, enabling K8s probes and uptime monitors to detect failures.

text: What does MVC stand for in Rails?
options: Model-View-Component — Models store application data, Views display components, and Components coordinate browser interactions instead of controllers
Model-View-Controller — Models handle data, Views render HTML, Controllers mediate between them
Multi-Value Cache — Models retain cached values, Views read cache entries, and Cache services mediate requests between the two layers
Module-Version-Controller — Modules define reusable features, Versions track releases, and Controllers select the correct package version for each request
explanation: Rails enforces MVC: controllers respond to routes, query models, and render views.

text: What is the Rails convention for RESTful resource routes?
options: resources :posts generates only the collection and member GET routes, leaving form, creation, update, and deletion actions to be declared separately
resources :posts generates 7 RESTful routes: index, show, new, create, edit, update, destroy
resources :posts generates routes only for reading posts, mapping GET requests to index and show without creating or modifying records
resources :posts generates 3 routes for create, read, and delete, while editing and updating are handled through a separate CRUD declaration
explanation: `resources :posts` auto-generates all 7 CRUD routes following REST conventions.

text: What is a Rails migration?
options: A data import tool that reads external CSV or JSON records, transforms their fields, and inserts the resulting rows into application tables
A Ruby class that describes incremental database schema changes in a version-controlled, reversible way
A deployment script that packages the current application, copies it to production servers, and restarts web and background worker processes
A backup file containing a point-in-time database dump, including table definitions and records that can be restored after an application failure
explanation: Migrations use `change`, `up`, and `down` methods. `create_table`, `add_column`, `add_index` are common helpers.

text: What is eager loading in Active Record?
options: Using CSS preloading directives to fetch stylesheets before the browser renders the page
Using `.includes(:association)` to load associated records in the same query, preventing N+1 queries
Caching instantiated model objects in memory so later requests can reuse them without querying the database
Defining associations that query related records only when the application first accesses them
explanation: `Post.includes(:comments)` fetches all comments in a second query (or JOIN), avoiding N+1 for `post.comments` in a loop.

text: What is a Rails concern?
options: An exception class under `app/errors` that represents a domain-specific failure and controls how Rails reports it to the application
A module in `app/models/concerns` or `app/controllers/concerns` that extracts shared model or controller functionality via `ActiveSupport::Concern`
A configuration object in `config/application.rb` that stores environment-specific settings and changes how Rails initializes the application
A Rack middleware component in `app/middleware` that intercepts requests and responses before controllers, rewriting headers or halting requests
explanation: Concerns use `included` and `class_methods` blocks to mix behaviour cleanly into multiple models.

text: What is the Rails asset pipeline?
options: An automated CI service that runs tests, builds the application, and publishes deployment artifacts after each commit
A framework (Sprockets/Propshaft) that concatenates, minifies, and fingerprints CSS/JS assets for production
A schema-change script that alters tables and indexes, then records its version in the database migrations table
A server-side cache that stores rendered pages and query results to reduce repeated work during production requests
explanation: The asset pipeline concatenates files for fewer HTTP requests and fingerprints them for long-term caching.

text: What is ActionMailer in Rails?
options: A logging library that formats application events, assigns severity levels, and writes structured messages to files or external services
A framework for composing and sending emails using mailer classes similar to controllers, with ERB email templates
A queue system that schedules background jobs, manages workers, and retries asynchronous tasks outside the web request cycle
An SMS adapter that formats text messages, selects a carrier gateway, and delivers notifications to mobile phone numbers
explanation: Mailers inherit from ActionMailer::Base, use `mail(to:, subject:)` to configure emails, and deliver with `.deliver_later`.

text: What is a core benefit of cloud computing?
options: On-demand scalable resources
Mandatory physical ownership
No networking
No automation
explanation: Cloud platforms provide elastic, on-demand infrastructure and services.

text: What is Action Cable in Rails?
options: A message queue that stores discrete work items for consumers to process later, typically supporting acknowledgments, retries, and durable delivery
Rails's WebSocket framework — channels handle real-time bidirectional communication, backed by Redis or the async adapter
A job queue that schedules background tasks for workers, allowing lengthy operations to run outside the request cycle and be retried
A Pub/Sub library for distributing published events to subscribed application processes, without providing Rails WebSocket channels or browser connections
explanation: Action Cable integrates WebSockets into Rails, enabling chat, notifications, and live updates with the same authentication stack.

text: What is ActiveJob in Rails?
options: A cron scheduler that triggers commands at fixed times or intervals, independently of Rails's adapter-based background job interface and worker processes
A framework providing a unified API for background job adapters (Sidekiq, Delayed::Job, Resque), with retry logic and callbacks
A Rake task runner that defines developer or deployment commands for the command line, rather than enqueuing application work for asynchronous execution
A database worker that polls tables for pending records and performs SQL operations directly, without providing a common interface for external job adapters
explanation: `MyJob.perform_later(args)` enqueues the job; Sidekiq or Resque workers process it asynchronously.

text: How does Rails caching work?
options: Rails provides no built-in caching facilities; applications must implement all response, fragment, and low-level caching through third-party gems and custom storage wrappers
Rails offers page caching, action caching, fragment caching (`cache` helper), and low-level caching (`Rails.cache.fetch`), backed by Redis or Memcached
Rails supports only HTTP caching through response headers such as `ETag` and `Cache-Control`, without fragment helpers or server-side cache stores
Rails supports only CDN caching for static assets and public responses, leaving database results and rendered view fragments uncached by the framework
explanation: Fragment caching wraps ERB with `<% cache @post do %>`. Russian Doll Caching nests caches for fine-grained invalidation.

text: How does Rails multi-database support work?
options: Rails supports only one database connection per application, so all models must use the same primary database
Rails 6+ supports multiple databases with separate `connects_to` configurations per model, enabling read/write splitting and sharding
Rails handles multiple databases only through manually written SQL queries and separate external connection scripts
Rails delegates multi-database configuration entirely to the Sequel gem rather than Active Record models
explanation: `connects_to database: { writing: :primary, reading: :replica }` routes writes to primary and reads to replica automatically.

text: What is the difference between `reload!` and code loading in Rails development vs production?
options: Development and production use identical loading behavior, with changed files remaining available until the process is restarted
Development uses Zeitwerk's reloading mode to reload changed files on each request; production eager-loads all code once at boot for performance
Production reloads modified application files before requests, while development loads the complete application only during boot
Development eager-loads every application constant at startup, while production reloads changed files after each request
explanation: `config.cache_classes = false` (development) triggers reloading. `config.eager_load = true` (production) loads all constants upfront.

text: What is the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR?
options: CHAR stores only the characters supplied, while VARCHAR always pads values to the declared maximum length with spaces
CHAR is fixed-length (padded with spaces); VARCHAR is variable-length (stores actual length + 1-2 bytes)
VARCHAR is a fixed-width type optimized for uniform values, while CHAR dynamically allocates storage for each individual value
CHAR and VARCHAR have identical storage behavior, with the distinction applying only to how client libraries display strings
explanation: CHAR(10) always uses 10 bytes. VARCHAR(255) uses only as many bytes as the stored string requires.

text: What is the Rack interface?
options: A hardware specification for arranging servers in a rack and defining how their network interfaces exchange HTTP requests with external clients
A minimal Ruby web server interface: an object responding to `call(env)` returning `[status, headers, body]`, which Rails apps implement
A Ruby routing framework that converts URL patterns into controller actions and bypasses the Rack middleware stack during normal application requests
A Rails testing framework that supplies browser simulators, request stubs, and assertions without implementing the application server interface
explanation: All Ruby web frameworks (Rails, Sinatra) are Rack apps. Middleware stacks are Rack middleware chains.

text: Your Auto Scaling Group has EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). You want to scale based on request count per target and CPU. Which scaling policy type should you use as of 2024?
options: Scheduled Scaling with calendar-based capacity changes and no metric-driven response to request count or CPU utilization
Target Tracking Scaling policies (e.g., ALBRequestCountPerTarget, CPU) and Predictive Scaling
Manual Scaling through administrator changes to the Auto Scaling Group desired capacity whenever traffic or CPU increases
Simple Scaling using one fixed adjustment and cooldown period, without target tracking or predictive capacity planning
explanation: Target Tracking is recommended. You can combine CPU, RequestCountPerTarget. Predictive Scaling uses ML to forecast.

text: A company must encrypt EBS volumes with centralized key management and audit trail, with ability to auto-rotate keys. Which service?
options: Self-managed encryption keys stored on EC2 and copied between instances, with application-controlled rotation and no centralized KMS audit trail
AWS KMS (Key Management Service) with KMS-managed keys for EBS encryption + automatic rotation
AWS Secrets Manager storing encryption material and rotating database credentials, but not providing native EBS volume encryption-key management
Amazon S3 server-side encryption protecting objects with SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS, which does not encrypt attached EBS volumes
explanation: KMS provides CMKs, automatic yearly rotation (now supports automatic rotation for symmetric keys, ~1 year), audit via

text: What is MySQL replication?
options: A periodic export of table contents into a restorable file, typically created independently of binary logging and applied during disaster recovery
Asynchronous copying of changes from a primary server to one or more replica servers using the binary log
A coordinated execution mode in which several MySQL servers share workload and maintain synchronized ownership of the same writable dataset
An in-memory store of recently executed SELECT results that avoids rerunning identical statements until the cached entries are invalidated
explanation: Replicas replay the primary's binlog events. Used for read scaling, high availability, and geographic distribution.

text: What is the slow query log?
options: A MySQL diagnostic file recording startup failures, crashes, and server warnings, used to investigate errors rather than measure query execution time
A MySQL log recording queries exceeding `long_query_time` seconds, used for performance analysis
A MySQL log recording client connections and disconnections, used to audit session activity rather than identify statements exceeding a time threshold
A MySQL log recording binary-log events sent to replicas, used to monitor replication progress rather than measure slow statement execution
explanation: Enable with `slow_query_log=1` and `long_query_time=1`. Use `mysqldumpslow` or pt-query-digest to analyse the log.

text: What is a composite index?
options: An index built from an expression such as LOWER(name) or a generated value, rather than from several ordinary table columns
An index on multiple columns that speeds up queries filtering on the index's leftmost prefix of columns
A specialized index that tokenizes natural-language text and ranks matching words, rather than ordering values across multiple columns
An index structure stored separately for each table partition, with entries restricted to individual partitions instead of using a multi-column key
explanation: Index `(last_name, first_name)` speeds `WHERE last_name=?` and `WHERE last_name=? AND first_name=?` but NOT `WHERE first_name=?` alone.

text: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking in MySQL?
options: There is no meaningful distinction: both approaches acquire the same row locks before an UPDATE and differ only in the terminology used by application developers
Optimistic locking checks a version column on UPDATE without locking rows (application-level); pessimistic uses SELECT FOR UPDATE to lock rows
Pessimistic locking is always better because it prevents conflicts before they occur, whereas optimistic locking cannot safely protect concurrent updates
Optimistic locking uses database transactions only, while pessimistic locking is limited to application checks and never issues row-locking statements
explanation: Optimistic: `UPDATE ... WHERE version=?` — fails if row changed. Pessimistic: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` — holds row lock until COMMIT.

text: What is Apache Spark?
options: A distributed message broker for publishing, buffering, and delivering records between producers and consumer applications
A unified analytics engine for large-scale distributed data processing, supporting batch and streaming with in-memory computation
A relational database system for storing structured records and executing transactional SQL queries on server nodes
A business intelligence platform for designing dashboards, reports, and interactive visualizations from enterprise data
explanation: Spark processes data 100× faster than Hadoop MapReduce by keeping data in memory and using a DAG execution engine.

text: What is a DataFrame in Spark?
options: A local Python data structure containing named fields, processed on one machine without distributed execution or Catalyst planning
A distributed Dataset organised into named columns, similar to a SQL table, with query optimisation via Catalyst
An alternative name for an RDD whose records have no schema, column expressions, or SQL-oriented query optimization
A streaming-only object representing unbounded events, unavailable for batch data or queries over stored files and tables
explanation: DataFrames provide a higher-level API than RDDs with schema awareness, enabling Spark SQL queries and Catalyst optimisation.

text: What is MySQL Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster?
options: A centralized backup and restore service that periodically copies database files, retains recovery points, and protects against server failure
A multi-primary, synchronous replication system providing automatic failover, conflict detection, and distributed consensus
An asynchronous replication mode that ships binary-log events from one source to replicas, providing eventual consistency without coordinated consensus
A read-replica feature that routes SELECT statements to secondary servers, reducing primary load without supporting coordinated failover
explanation: Group Replication uses Paxos-based consensus. InnoDB Cluster wraps it with MySQL Shell for orchestration.

text: What is a Spark Driver?
options: A JDBC connectivity library that translates database-specific SQL calls into network requests made by application clients
The process running the main() function, creating SparkContext, building the DAG, and coordinating executors
A worker-node process that receives partitions and executes tasks, while another coordinator builds the application execution plan
A file and table data source that provides schemas and records to Spark jobs without scheduling tasks or managing executors
explanation: The Driver breaks the job into stages/tasks and schedules them on Executors via the cluster manager.

text: What is a Spark Executor?
options: The application process that creates SparkContext, constructs the logical plan, and coordinates jobs submitted by the main program
A JVM process on a worker node that runs tasks and caches data in memory for the duration of the application
A cluster scheduling service that assigns applications to worker nodes and negotiates resources before any executor process starts
A columnar storage format used to serialize partitioned records, preserve schemas, and exchange data between Spark applications
explanation: Executors receive tasks from the Driver, execute them in parallel, and return results or write output.

text: What does few-shot prompting involve?
options: Providing a few examples before requesting a new answer
Asking the model to answer several unrelated questions
Using a prompt that contains only a few total words
Giving the model access to a small collection of documents
explanation: Few-shot prompting includes a small number of examples that demonstrate the desired task or format. The model can use those examples to guide its next response.

text: What causes deadlocks in MySQL and how do you handle them?
options: A single-user scenario where one transaction repeatedly updates its own rows, causing MySQL to detect a lock cycle and roll back the transaction
Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, causing a cycle. MySQL detects and rolls back one victim. Handle by catching error 1213 and retrying
Full table scans that make every query wait behind a global read lock, requiring the server to terminate the scan before other transactions proceed
Insufficient indexes that directly create circular lock dependencies, resolved by rebuilding every table with a clustered index before retrying
explanation: Prevent deadlocks by accessing rows in a consistent order, keeping transactions short, and using appropriate isolation levels.

text: What is ProxySQL and how is it used with MySQL?
options: A MySQL-compatible database fork that replaces the storage engine, SQL optimizer, and replication protocols while remaining wire-compatible with existing clients
An intelligent MySQL proxy providing connection pooling, query routing (writes to primary, reads to replicas), query rewriting, and caching
A backup tool that schedules full and incremental copies of MySQL data files, validates restore points, and archives them to remote storage
A monitoring tool that collects server metrics, detects slow queries, and displays dashboards, but does not sit between clients and database servers
explanation: ProxySQL sits between apps and MySQL, load-balancing read queries across replicas without application code changes.

text: What is the Catalyst Optimizer in Spark?
options: An execution-time component that allocates executors, assigns stages to worker nodes, and monitors task retries across a Spark application
Spark SQL's query optimizer that applies rule-based and cost-based transformations to logical plans, generating optimised physical plans
A catalog service that stores table metadata, resolves column names, and converts SQL statements directly into Parquet files
A storage-layer component that compresses shuffle blocks, manages spill files, and persists DataFrame results on distributed disks
explanation: Catalyst rewrites queries (predicate pushdown, constant folding, join reordering) before execution, making DataFrames faster than RDDs.

text: What is `persist()` vs `cache()` in Spark?
options: `persist()` and `cache()` are aliases that always keep a dataset in executor memory, with no way to select disk or serialized storage
`cache()` stores in memory (MEMORY_AND_DISK); `persist(StorageLevel)` lets you specify the storage level (disk, serialised, replicated)
`persist()` replaces `cache()` for modern Spark releases and is required whenever a DataFrame will be reused across multiple actions
`cache()` writes a durable disk copy by default, whereas `persist(StorageLevel)` only controls how long the cached data remains available
explanation: Cache intermediate DataFrames accessed multiple times to avoid recomputation. Unpersist when no longer needed to free memory.

text: What is `mapPartitions` vs `map` in Spark?
options: `map` opens a separate database connection for every element, while `mapPartitions` processes only one representative element from each partition to reduce work
map applies a function to each element; mapPartitions applies a function to each partition iterator — useful for initialising expensive resources (DB connections) once per partition
`mapPartitions` is a SQL-only optimization that combines adjacent partitions, whereas `map` is the RDD operation used to create shuffle boundaries
`map` is preferred for expensive setup because Spark can reuse its function automatically; `mapPartitions` is mainly for preserving element order across the entire RDD
explanation: Opening a DB connection per element with `map` is slow. `mapPartitions` opens it once per partition, sharing across all rows.

text: How does Spark achieve fault tolerance?
options: Via checkpointing only — Spark periodically saves every intermediate RDD to reliable storage so lost partitions can be restored without recomputation
Via RDD lineage — Spark tracks the sequence of transformations to rebuild lost partitions from scratch without replication
Via data replication — each RDD partition is synchronously copied to several executors, allowing Spark to switch to a surviving replica after failure
Via HDFS snapshots — Spark captures filesystem snapshots after each stage and reloads those snapshots whenever an executor or partition is lost
explanation: RDD lineage means Spark re-executes only the lost partition's transformations from the last checkpoint, not the entire job.

text: What file format is recommended for Spark workloads?
options: CSV — a row-oriented text format with delimiter-based fields, limited compression, and no embedded schema for efficient column pruning
Parquet — a columnar format with compression and schema, enabling column pruning and predicate pushdown
Text files — a simple line-oriented format with minimal metadata, requiring parsing and full scans when Spark reads distributed datasets
JSON — a flexible row-oriented format with nested records, but comparatively expensive parsing and limited support for column pruning
explanation: Parquet's columnar storage means Spark only reads required columns, dramatically reducing I/O for analytical queries.

text: What is `SparkSession`?
options: A network connection — a client-side channel used to send jobs and receive results from a remote Spark cluster
The single entry point for Spark functionality — replaces SQLContext, HiveContext, and SparkContext in Spark 2+
A cluster manager — a service that allocates worker nodes and schedules executors across the resources available to Spark
A data source — a cataloged input provider that reads tables or files and exposes their contents as DataFrames
explanation: `SparkSession.builder.appName(...).getOrCreate()` is the first call in any Spark application.

text: What is a shuffle in Spark and why is it expensive?
options: A data compression operation that shrinks partitions before storage, reducing network traffic without repartitioning records between executors
Redistributing data across partitions (e.g., for groupBy/join) — requires writing data to disk and sending it over the network, causing high latency
A sorting algorithm that orders records within each existing partition, improving local access without exchanging data across the cluster
A cache eviction process that removes inactive DataFrames from executor memory when storage capacity becomes limited during a job
explanation: Shuffles are the most expensive Spark operation. Minimise them with broadcast joins, pre-partitioning, and avoiding unnecessary groupBy.

text: What is Spark Structured Streaming?
options: A legacy streaming API based on discretized micro-batches, using RDD transformations rather than the unified DataFrame query model
A high-level streaming API treating a live data stream as an unbounded table, enabling SQL queries and DataFrame operations on streams
A batch execution mode that processes finite input files through scheduled jobs, without maintaining streaming state or accepting new records continuously
A Kafka-specific API that exposes Kafka topics as streaming tables, but cannot process streams from files, sockets, or other supported sources
explanation: Structured Streaming integrates with Kafka, Kinesis, and files. It offers exactly-once semantics with checkpointing.

text: What is watermarking in Spark Structured Streaming?
options: A serialization format for streaming records that determines how events are encoded before they are written to storage or delivered to a sink
A threshold specifying how late data can arrive; events older than `eventTime - watermark` are dropped, enabling stateful aggregations with bounded state
A scheduling interval that controls when Structured Streaming launches micro-batches and checks for newly available input data
A checkpoint retention policy that controls how long offsets, state snapshots, and query progress information remain on durable storage
explanation: `withWatermark('eventTime', '10 minutes')` tells Spark to hold state for 10 minutes to handle late arrivals.

text: How do you tune `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`?
options: Always leave the setting at 200 because Spark's default is designed to provide the best shuffle parallelism for clusters of every size and workload
Set it based on data volume and cluster size — typically 2-4× number of cores. Spark 3 AQE can auto-tune this at runtime
Set the value to 1 so each shuffle uses a single partition, avoiding task scheduling overhead and guaranteeing the most efficient execution
Treat the setting as a fixed internal constant because Spark determines all shuffle parallelism automatically and does not allow users to change it
explanation: 200 is Spark's default. Too low for large datasets → large spills; too high for small datasets → excessive task overhead.

text: What is Project Photon in Databricks?
options: A JVM-based Spark SQL module that replaces the Catalyst optimizer and interprets DataFrame expressions before sending ordinary tasks to executors
A vectorised query engine written in C++ (not JVM) that replaces Tungsten for columnar Parquet/Delta processing, achieving 3-10× throughput
A streaming API for ingesting events from Kafka and other message brokers, providing specialized operators for low-latency continuous processing
A cluster-management service that provisions Databricks compute resources, assigns executors to workers, and monitors the health of running clusters
explanation: Photon uses SIMD CPU instructions and avoids JVM overhead for vectorised columnar processing, especially in Delta Lake scans.

text: What is the difference between `foreachBatch` and `foreach` in Structured Streaming?
options: There is no meaningful difference because both APIs process rows individually, and neither one can write a micro-batch to multiple destinations or perform an upsert
`foreachBatch(func)` processes each micro-batch as a DataFrame (enabling idempotent upserts, multiple sinks); `foreach` processes each row individually
`foreach` is faster because it bypasses DataFrame planning, automatically batches all records, and provides the same transactional behavior as `foreachBatch`
`foreachBatch` is deprecated in recent Structured Streaming releases because row-level `foreach` is now the required interface for processing every micro-batch
explanation: `foreachBatch` allows using batch DataFrame APIs (merge, JDBC, Cassandra) in streaming, making exactly-once semantics achievable.

text: How do you handle schema evolution in Spark with Delta Lake?
options: Drop and recreate the Delta table whenever a column is added or changed, because Delta cannot modify table metadata after the initial schema is committed
Delta supports `mergeSchema` on write and `overwriteSchema` with explicit schema changes; schema incompatibilities are rejected by default, preventing corruption
Spark automatically accepts all incoming schema changes during writes, silently converting incompatible columns and preserving existing data without configuration
JSON is required for schema evolution because Delta tables cannot add, remove, or widen columns when data is stored in Parquet files
explanation: `.option('mergeSchema', 'true')` adds new columns automatically. Delta's transaction log tracks schema history for time travel.

text: What is an XCom in Airflow?
options: An external command interface that lets a task invoke shell programs or remote services and capture their execution status
Cross-communication — a mechanism for tasks to share small values (keys/values stored in the metadata DB) between each other
A connection type that stores credentials and endpoint information used by operators when communicating with databases or APIs
A DAG parameter that defines run-level configuration values supplied when the scheduler creates a new workflow execution
explanation: XComs are for small metadata (IDs, file paths), not large datasets. Use `ti.xcom_push(key, value)` and `ti.xcom_pull(task_ids, key)`.

text: What is the difference between `LocalExecutor` and `CeleryExecutor`?
options: There is no meaningful difference: both executors always run tasks through Celery workers and require a distributed message broker for scheduling
LocalExecutor runs tasks as subprocesses on the Scheduler's machine (single node); CeleryExecutor distributes tasks to a pool of Celery workers across multiple nodes
CeleryExecutor is deprecated for production use, while LocalExecutor is the newer distributed executor intended for multi-node Airflow deployments
LocalExecutor requires Redis to submit subprocess work, whereas CeleryExecutor runs tasks directly on the scheduler without a broker or worker pool
explanation: For production scale-out, use CeleryExecutor (with Redis/RabbitMQ as broker) or KubernetesExecutor (one pod per task).

text: What is a TaskGroup in Airflow?
options: A statically defined list of task objects that executes as one indivisible unit and prevents Airflow from scheduling or retrying its member tasks independently
A visual grouping mechanism for organising related tasks in the Airflow UI without affecting execution semantics
A parallel execution component that allocates worker slots to several tasks and automatically balances their workloads across available executors
An operator that performs a grouped batch operation at runtime, containing downstream work internally rather than displaying individual tasks in the DAG graph
explanation: TaskGroups collapse in the Graph view for cleaner UI. Introduced in Airflow 2.0 to replace SubDAGs.

text: What are trigger rules in Airflow?
options: Cron expressions that determine the calendar intervals on which a DAG is scheduled, including timezone handling and the creation of logical run dates
Rules governing when a task runs based on its upstream tasks' states — e.g., ALL_SUCCESS (default), ONE_FAILED, ALL_DONE, NONE_FAILED
Retry policies that specify the delay, maximum attempts, and failure callbacks applied when an individual task instance exits unsuccessfully
Sensor modes that control whether a waiting sensor occupies a worker slot, reschedules itself, or polls repeatedly until its condition becomes true
explanation: Use `trigger_rule='all_done'` for cleanup tasks that should run even if upstream tasks fail.

text: What is a hallucination in a generative AI response?
options: A confident-sounding answer that contains unsupported information
A response that repeats the user's wording in a different format
A temporary delay that occurs while the model generates text
A system message that explains how the model should behave
explanation: A hallucination is inaccurate or fabricated content presented as if it were true. Checking sources and providing reliable context can help reduce this risk.

text: What is the KubernetesExecutor?
options: A Kubernetes monitoring tool that collects Pod health, node utilization, and container logs for Airflow deployments without launching or scheduling task workloads
An Airflow Executor that launches each task as an isolated Kubernetes Pod, providing perfect resource isolation and auto-scaling
A DAG format that serializes workflow definitions into Kubernetes resource manifests so the Kubernetes API can interpret dependencies between Airflow tasks
A scheduler upgrade that replaces Airflow's scheduling loop with Kubernetes-native cron processing while continuing to run every task on a shared worker node
explanation: KubernetesExecutor dynamically creates a pod per task, allowing different images, resource requests, and auto-cleanup.

text: What is an Operator in Airflow?
options: A Python class — a reusable implementation that can be instantiated directly, but does not itself represent a unit of work in a DAG
A template for a task — defines what work to do (e.g., BashOperator runs a bash command, PythonOperator calls a Python function)
A scheduler component — selects runnable tasks from registered DAGs and submits their executions to available workers
A sensor implementation — repeatedly polls an external condition and reports whether the expected event has occurred
explanation: Operators are the building blocks of DAGs. Popular ones: PythonOperator, BashOperator, SparkSubmitOperator, HttpSensor.

text: What is the Airflow Scheduler?
options: A cron replacement — a standalone time-based service that launches every DAG directly, without consulting task dependencies or an Executor
The component that reads DAG files, determines which tasks are due, and sends them to the Executor
The web UI — the browser-based component that displays DAG status, task logs, configuration, and execution history
A database component — the metadata storage service that records DAG definitions, task states, connections, and historical runs
explanation: The Scheduler continuously monitors DAGs, checks dependencies, and triggers task instances when their schedule is due.

text: What is a Connection in Airflow?
options: A DAG link — a named reference connecting one workflow to another, including the target DAG identifier, schedule, and dependency metadata
A named, encrypted credential (host, port, user, password, extras) stored in Airflow's metadata DB or Secrets Backend and referenced by operators
A Python import — a reusable module declaration that loads credentials and client libraries into an operator during DAG parsing
A network socket — a live communication channel containing the remote address, connection state, protocol, and worker process information
explanation: Connections separate credentials from code. Operators use `conn_id='my_postgres'` to look up the stored connection.

text: What is a `@dag` decorator in Airflow 2?
options: A Python class that subclasses the DAG object and provides methods for declaring tasks inside a decorated workflow
A decorator that converts a Python function into a DAG, enabling the TaskFlow API with cleaner Python-native DAG authoring
A connection decorator that registers credentials and injects them into Python callables during DAG parsing
A test helper that wraps a function so Airflow can execute it only during isolated unit-test runs
explanation: The TaskFlow API (`@dag`, `@task`) reduces boilerplate, handling XCom push/pull automatically via function arguments and return values.

text: What is the Airflow Scheduler HA setup?
options: Running multiple Celery workers as schedulers, using their task queues to elect one active scheduler and avoid duplicate DAG processing
Running multiple Scheduler instances using database-level row locking (via `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`) to coordinate without a single point of failure
Using ZooKeeper to coordinate scheduler leadership, maintain distributed locks, and select a replacement when the primary scheduler fails
Configuring one primary Scheduler with standby instances that remain passive until a health check promotes one after failure
explanation: Airflow 2.0+ supports multiple concurrent Schedulers. They compete for DAG ownership via database locks.

text: What is a calculated field in Tableau?
options: A spreadsheet formula written in Excel to calculate a result from cells on the current worksheet or workbook
A custom field created using Tableau's formula language to compute new values from existing data (e.g., [Sales] / [Quantity])
A physical database column stored in the source system that contains values loaded into Tableau without further calculation
A report-level filter control that removes selected records from worksheets without defining a new calculated value
explanation: Calculated fields appear as new dimensions or measures and can use LOD expressions, string, date, and aggregate functions.

text: What is a slicer in Power BI?
options: A set of Power Query steps that cleans, reshapes, and combines source data before it is loaded into the Power BI model
A visual filter control (dropdowns, buttons, sliders) that lets users interactively filter other visuals on the same report page
A calculated column evaluated separately for every row in a table when the data model is refreshed
A DAX measure that calculates an aggregate result dynamically according to the filter context of a visual
explanation: Slicers are page-level filters presented as interactive UI elements rather than the filter pane.

text: What is a filter context in Tableau?
options: A SQL WHERE clause written against a database table to eliminate rows before the query returns its result set
The set of filters (dimension filters, context filters, quick filters) that restrict which data is visible in a view
A saved connection definition containing the server, database, credentials, and metadata needed to access a Tableau data source
A calculated field formula that creates a derived value for each mark in a Tableau worksheet using existing fields
explanation: Filter order in Tableau: Extract → Data Source → Context → Dimension → Measure → Table Calc filters.

text: Which prompt is most specific for requesting a short technical summary?
options: Summarize this API in three bullet points for new developers
Tell me everything important about this API for the team
Explain this API clearly and include any useful information
Write a helpful overview of this API with appropriate details
explanation: The first prompt specifies the subject, audience, desired length, and output format. These details give the model clearer criteria for producing the response.

text: What is the Power Query Editor?
options: A formula authoring environment for writing and testing DAX measures, calculated columns, and calculated tables in a semantic model
A data transformation tool in Power BI Desktop (based on M language) for cleaning, shaping, and combining data before loading into the model
A report-design workspace for arranging visuals, configuring interactions, and formatting pages after the data model has been loaded
A connection object that identifies an external database, file, or service from which Power BI retrieves tables and records
explanation: Power Query handles ETL: remove nulls, pivot/unpivot, merge queries, filter rows, and rename columns without SQL.

text: What is an LOD (Level of Detail) expression in Tableau?
options: A geographic configuration that assigns fields to latitude, longitude, and map layers to control how locations are plotted in a view
A Tableau expression that controls the granularity of a calculation independently of the view's level of detail — using FIXED, INCLUDE, or EXCLUDE
A formatting property that changes the physical dimensions, padding, and display size of a chart or worksheet on the dashboard
A worksheet filtering mechanism that removes records according to selected field values before Tableau generates the displayed marks
explanation: `{ FIXED [Customer] : SUM([Sales]) }` computes total sales per customer regardless of what dimensions are in the view.

text: What is dynamic task mapping in Airflow 2.3+?
options: Creating a fixed set of task instances when the DAG is parsed, with no runtime expansion or per-item mapping
Creating a variable number of parallel task instances at runtime using `.expand()` — replacing complex manual fan-out patterns
