options: A network exploit that sends malformed directory packets to crash LDAP servers or bypass firewall rules protecting internal applications
An attack inserting malicious LDAP filter syntax into input fields to manipulate directory queries; prevented by input validation and parameterised LDAP APIs
An NTLM attack that captures challenge-response exchanges and replays them against domain services to impersonate authenticated users
A replication exploit that alters directory synchronization messages between domain controllers, prevented by disabling replication and restricting site links
explanation: Unsanitised input in LDAP filters can return all users. Always escape special characters in LDAP queries.

text: Which command pulls an image from Docker Hub?
options: docker fetch
docker pull
docker get
docker import
explanation: compose.yml — Defines multi-container setups.

text: What is Zero Trust and how does it apply to AD/Entra ID?
options: A network security architecture that blocks all inbound traffic at a central firewall before allowing approved corporate devices
A security model assuming breach — verify every access request using identity, device compliance, and context
An Active Directory trust relationship that automatically grants users access across separate forests after one identity check
A remote-access model that replaces repeated identity checks with a perimeter VPN once the device has connected
explanation: Microsoft Zero Trust pillars: Identity (Entra ID), Device (Intune), Network (Defender for Cloud Apps), Apps, and Data.

text: What is the difference between SAML, OAuth 2.0, and OpenID Connect in Entra ID?
options: A single sign-on protocol family in which SAML, OAuth 2.0, and OIDC use the same token format and serve identical authentication roles
SAML is XML-based federation for legacy apps; OAuth 2.0 is for API access; OIDC extends OAuth 2.0 for authentication with an ID token
SAML is a lightweight JSON protocol for modern APIs; OAuth 2.0 authenticates users directly; OIDC is used only for authorization
SAML is primarily for API authorization; OAuth 2.0 is XML federation for browser sign-in; OIDC is directory synchronization for Entra ID
explanation: Modern apps use OIDC (authentication) + OAuth 2.0 (authorisation). SAML remains for legacy SSO. Entra ID supports all three.

text: An enterprise has 50 AWS accounts and wants to deny all accounts from using non-Graviton (non-ARM) EC2 instances except for a sandbox OU, and require all S3 buckets have encryption. Which approach enforces this at scale?
options: Create matching IAM policies manually in all 50 accounts to deny selected EC2 instance types and require S3 encryption, then update each policy whenever accounts change

AWS Organizations with Service Control Policies (SCPs) - Deny ec2:RunInstances where instance architecture not ARM, plus require s3 bucket encryption, plus Tag Policies/Guardrails via AWS Control Tower
Use VPC security groups to block non-Graviton EC2 launches and configure bucket access rules, since network controls can enforce both compute architecture and storage encryption
Enable AWS Config rules in every account to detect non-ARM instances and unencrypted buckets, without organization policies or automatic remediation to prevent their creation
explanation: SCPs at OU level can DENY actions. Use condition: ec2:architecture != arm64, require s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption.

text: You need to decouple microservices and ensure an S3 upload event triggers multiple downstream Lambdas, Step Functions, and queues without tight coupling. Which service is best for event bus routing?
options: Direct S3-to-Lambda notifications with separate integrations for every downstream consumer
Amazon EventBridge (with S3 Event Notifications to EventBridge)
Amazon SNS with S3 notifications and fan-out subscriptions configured for each consumer
An SQS queue receiving S3 notifications, with each workflow polling for new events
explanation: EventBridge is serverless event bus, allows routing S3 Object Created events to 20+ targets with filtering, archive, replay. S3

text: Why use infrastructure as code?
options: To provision infrastructure consistently and repeatably
To provision resources manually through a documented console checklist
To manage infrastructure without declaring or tracking its desired state
To deploy applications while bypassing validation, testing, and review
explanation: IaC makes infrastructure declarative, versionable, and reproducible.

text: What does Amazon CloudFront provide?
options: A managed relational database service that stores structured application records and supports SQL queries
Content Delivery Network (CDN) with edge locations to cache and deliver content with low latency
An automated source-code build and deployment service that packages applications and releases them to production
Persistent block and file storage that attaches to EC2 instances for retaining application data
explanation: CloudFront is CDN with 600+ PoPs. Integrates with S3, ALB, EC2, Shield, WAF, Function URLs.

text: An application on EC2 needs to securely access S3 without storing AWS credentials on the instance. What is the best practice?
options: Embed long-term IAM access keys directly in the application code deployed on the EC2 instance
Place AWS access keys in a private S3 bucket and retrieve them from the instance when the application starts
Attach an IAM Role to the EC2 instance with S3 permissions
Configure the application to use the AWS account root credentials stored in an encrypted instance configuration file
explanation: Best practice: IAM Role via Instance Profile. Use Instance Metadata Service v2 (IMDSv2) to retrieve temporary credentials

text: Which feature, stable since K8s 1.29, allows in-place pod resource resizing without restart?
options: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes replica count from metrics but cannot resize an existing pod without replacing it
In-place Pod Vertical Scaling (alpha in 1.27, beta progress in 1.30+ / Pod resize with resize subresource)
kubectl set resources updates the workload template and causes new pods to receive requests after a rollout
Node auto-provisioning adds or removes nodes to fit pending pods, rather than changing resources of running pods
explanation: In-place Pod Vertical Scaling (alpha in 1.27, beta progress in 1.30+ / Pod resize with resize subresource)

text: Which property is most important when an API operation may be safely retried after a timeout?
options: The operation produces the same externally visible result when repeated with the same request.
The operation always completes within the client timeout configured for the request.
The operation routes every retry to the same application server instance.
The operation stores each response only in the caller's local memory cache.
explanation: An idempotent operation can be repeated without creating additional unintended effects. This is essential when clients retry requests after uncertain network failures or timeouts.

text: In a cache-aside design, what normally happens after a cache miss?
options: The service reads from the database, returns the value, and writes it into the cache.
The cache synchronously broadcasts an invalidation message before reading the database.
The database forwards the request to the cache and stores the returned value automatically.
The service rejects the request until a background process repopulates the missing cache entry.
explanation: With cache-aside, the application loads missing data from the system of record, returns it, and usually populates the cache for later requests. The application, rather than the cache, controls this workflow.

text: What is the primary purpose of a circuit breaker around a failing downstream service?
options: It prevents repeated calls temporarily and allows recovery checks after a threshold.
It guarantees that every downstream request completes successfully within a fixed deadline.
It increases downstream capacity by distributing each request across several network paths.
It stores all failed responses permanently so callers can avoid contacting the service again.
explanation: A circuit breaker stops sending requests to a dependency that is failing, reducing cascading load. After a recovery period, it permits limited trial requests before closing fully.

text: What is a common consequence of serving reads from an asynchronously replicated database replica?
options: A read may return stale data because replication has not yet applied the latest committed change.
A read is always serialized with writes because replicas share one transaction coordinator.
A read automatically repairs missing records by synchronously consulting the primary database.
A read becomes impossible whenever the primary accepts writes faster than the replica can process.
explanation: Asynchronous replication introduces lag between the primary and replicas. Therefore, a replica read can temporarily return an older state than the most recent primary write.

text: A consumer receives the same message twice from an at-least-once queue. What is the usual application-level solution?
options: Make message handling idempotent by recording processed identifiers before repeating side effects.
Increase the queue retention period so duplicate deliveries are delayed until processing stabilizes.
Disable acknowledgments so the broker removes messages immediately after the first delivery.
Route every message through a single consumer so concurrent processing cannot occur.
explanation: At-least-once delivery can produce duplicates, especially after consumer failures or acknowledgment timeouts. Consumers should deduplicate using stable message identifiers or make their side effects safely repeatable.

text: Why is consistent hashing often used when distributing cache keys across a changing server pool?
options: Adding or removing a node typically remaps only a limited portion of existing keys.
Adding a node guarantees that every key moves exactly once to the newest server.
Removing a node preserves all cached values without requiring fallback or reconstruction logic.
Changing the pool size keeps every key on its original server regardless of membership.
explanation: Consistent hashing limits key movement when membership changes, reducing cache churn and warm-up traffic. Some keys still move or need reconstruction, so it does not preserve every assignment.

text: Which statement correctly describes a token-bucket rate limiter?
options: It allows bursts up to the bucket capacity while replenishing tokens at a configured rate.
It permits exactly one request per fixed interval and discards all unused capacity.
It queues unlimited requests during overload and releases them after the service recovers.
It calculates limits only from response latency and does not track request consumption.
explanation: A token bucket accumulates tokens at a defined rate up to a maximum capacity. Requests consume tokens, allowing controlled bursts while enforcing a longer-term average rate.

text: What is a key operational benefit of a blue-green deployment?
options: Traffic can switch between two environments, enabling rapid rollback to the previous version.
The new version is gradually mixed into every server without maintaining a second environment.
Database schema changes become automatically reversible because both application versions share metadata.
Application deployments require no health checks because inactive capacity validates the release beforehand.
explanation: Blue-green deployment maintains separate current and new environments, then shifts traffic after validation. If problems appear, traffic can be redirected to the previous environment quickly.

text: Which practice best improves request tracing across multiple services?
options: Propagate a correlation identifier through service calls and include it in structured logs.
Assign a new unrelated identifier at every service so each component has independent log searches.
Write complete request bodies to every log entry so matching can occur without shared identifiers.
Rely on server timestamps alone because synchronized clocks uniquely identify distributed requests.
explanation: A propagated correlation or trace identifier lets operators connect logs and spans belonging to one request across service boundaries. Structured logging makes those identifiers efficient to search and analyze.

text: A service must remain available during a network partition. Which design choice reflects a deliberate CAP trade-off?
options: Return potentially stale data during the partition instead of rejecting reads until replicas agree.
Guarantee the newest value during the partition by requiring every replica to acknowledge each read.
Avoid defining behavior during partitions because CAP applies only to databases with multiple regions.
Preserve both strict consistency and full availability by retrying requests until the network recovers.
explanation: Under a partition, a distributed system must trade off consistency and availability. Serving stale data favors availability, while requiring agreement favors consistency and may reject or delay requests.

text: What does horizontal scaling mean in a system architecture?
options: Adding more server instances so requests can be handled in parallel
Adding more memory and CPU to one existing server for capacity
Reducing network distance by placing servers near every user
Replacing application code with a faster database query engine
explanation: Horizontal scaling increases capacity by adding more machines or service instances. It allows requests to be distributed across multiple servers.

text: Which description best matches a stateless service?
options: A service that stores each user's session only in local process memory
A service that keeps each request's needed context outside the service instance
A service that sends every request directly to the database without validation
A service that assigns one permanent server to each user for all requests
explanation: A stateless service does not depend on locally stored client session data between requests. Required state is kept in an external store or supplied with each request.

text: What is a common benefit of placing a message queue between two services?
options: Ensures every request immediately receives a response from the final processor
Replaces database replication by storing all application data in memory
Allows producers and consumers to work independently and absorb traffic bursts
Routes each user permanently to one server to preserve local session state
explanation: A queue decouples the producer from the consumer, allowing each to operate at its own pace. It can also temporarily buffer work during traffic spikes.

text: What is the primary purpose of a content delivery network, or CDN?
options: Executes all application business logic on the user's local device
Stores the primary database on every network edge for faster updates
Replaces authentication by allowing requests from nearby client networks
Serves cached content from geographically closer edge locations to users
explanation: A CDN caches and serves content from edge locations closer to users. This can reduce latency and decrease traffic to the origin server.

text: What does it mean for an operation to be idempotent?
options: Repeating the same request produces the same final system state
Repeating the request always creates a new resource with a different identifier
Repeating the request guarantees the server responds without any processing
Repeating the request sends data only after all users have approved it
explanation: An idempotent operation has the same intended result whether performed once or multiple times. This is useful when requests may be retried after network failures.

text: Which statement correctly describes microservices compared with a monolith?
options: Microservices require all application features to share one deployment package
Microservices split an application into independently deployable smaller services
Monoliths always run on one machine and cannot use multiple instances
Monoliths cannot communicate with databases or external services
explanation: Microservices organize an application into smaller services that can often be developed and deployed independently. A monolith generally packages most application functionality together.

text: What is a common purpose of a service health check?
options: Measures whether users have created enough accounts to scale capacity
Copies all incoming requests to clients so they can verify responses
Tests whether a service instance is healthy enough to receive requests
Encrypts service traffic by replacing certificates during each request
explanation: Health checks help determine whether an instance is operating correctly. Load balancers or orchestration systems can use the result to avoid sending traffic to unhealthy instances.

text: What usually happens when a language model's temperature is increased while top_p remains fixed?
options: It raises randomness while leaving the candidate token pool otherwise unchanged
It raises randomness by expanding the candidate token pool automatically
It reduces randomness while preserving the configured candidate token pool
It reduces randomness by shrinking the candidate token pool automatically
explanation: Temperature changes how sharply the model favors higher-probability tokens, generally increasing randomness when raised. The candidate pool is primarily controlled by settings such as top_p or top_k.

text: Which practice best reduces prompt-injection risk when using retrieved documents?
options: Treat retrieved text as untrusted data and keep final instructions outside it
Treat retrieved text as trusted instructions and place it before the system prompt
Encode retrieved text in base64 so the model cannot follow embedded instructions
Ask the model to obey retrieved text only when its wording matches the user request
explanation: Retrieved content can contain instructions that conflict with the application's goals, so it should be clearly delimited and treated as data. The application should keep authoritative instructions separate and explicit.

text: Which chunking approach is generally a strong starting point for a retrieval-augmented generation system?
options: Use moderate, overlapping chunks and evaluate retrieval on representative queries
Use one very large chunk per document to preserve every surrounding sentence
Use tiny nonoverlapping chunks and rely on generation to restore missing context
Use fixed chunks without overlap because overlap always creates duplicate evidence
explanation: Moderate chunks with limited overlap often preserve useful context while keeping retrieved passages focused. The best size and overlap still require evaluation against representative queries and documents.

text: Which practice most reliably improves the quality of structured JSON responses from a language model?
options: Define a schema, request it explicitly, and validate the returned object in code
Describe the desired fields in prose and trust the model to preserve valid syntax
Set temperature to zero and assume every response will match the intended schema
Ask for JSON after generation and repair malformed fields without validation
explanation: A clear schema gives the model a precise target, while programmatic validation catches missing fields, incorrect types, and malformed output. Lower temperature alone cannot guarantee schema compliance.

text: When using few-shot prompting, which practice is generally most effective?
options: Add unrelated examples so the model learns to handle every possible topic
Put all examples after the question so the latest content dominates attention
Use representative, consistently formatted examples that match the target task
Prefer examples with subtle errors so the model learns to correct them automatically
explanation: Examples work best when they resemble the intended inputs and demonstrate the desired output format consistently. Unrelated or intentionally flawed examples can introduce ambiguity and unwanted behavior.

text: Which approach best reduces unsupported claims in a retrieval-augmented generation answer?
options: Increase temperature slightly so the model explores more possible grounded answers
Retrieve more documents without checking relevance, then summarize all of them
Tell the model it is an expert and require confident answers when evidence is absent
Provide relevant citations and instruct the model to state uncertainty when evidence is missing
explanation: Relevant evidence, citations, and an explicit abstention or uncertainty policy help constrain generation. Confidence instructions without evidence can actually encourage unsupported claims.

text: What is IAM primarily used for?
options: Identity and access control
Database indexing
Container builds
DNS caching
explanation: IAM manages identities, authentication, authorization, and permissions.

text: If a prompt and requested output exceed the model's context window, what can happen?
options: The model always summarizes the prompt before generating the requested response
The request may be truncated or rejected, so token budgets should be managed explicitly
The model silently increases its context window to fit both prompt and response
The model prioritizes developer instructions and discards only retrieved documents
explanation: Depending on the API, an overlong request may be rejected or portions of the input or output may be truncated. Applications should budget tokens and truncate or summarize content deliberately.

text: Which prompt design best handles user-provided text that may contain embedded instructions?
options: Place user text in a system message so its embedded instructions gain clear priority
Repeat user text after the final answer so the model can verify its own compliance
Delimit user text as data and explicitly instruct the model not to follow its commands
Remove all punctuation from user text so imperative wording loses its influence
explanation: Delimiting untrusted content and labeling it as data helps separate it from the application's instructions. The model should be told explicitly how to use the content without obeying embedded commands.

text: Which statement about embeddings is correct?
options: They convert documents into exact summaries that can be shown directly to users
They map content to vectors where similarity often reflects meaning within the model's domain
They guarantee that the nearest passage contains the answer to every user query
They eliminate the need for chunking, metadata filters, or reranking in retrieval systems
explanation: Embeddings represent content as vectors, and similarity between vectors often correlates with semantic relatedness for the model's training domain. They do not guarantee answer quality or remove the need for retrieval design.

text: Which evaluation design best measures the impact of a production prompt change?
options: Compare a fixed test set with task-specific metrics and review a sample of failures
Ask the model author whether outputs feel better across a few convenient examples
Measure only average response length because concise answers are usually higher quality
Run the new prompt once and compare its most impressive answer with the old prompt
explanation: A fixed, representative test set supports a fair comparison, while task-specific metrics and failure review reveal regressions. Single examples and subjective impressions are too easy to bias.

text: In a Dynamo-style replicated store with N=5, which statement is correct when every operation uses W=3 and R=3, assuming no sloppy quorums and one version per key?
options: A read quorum always returns the newest value, even when writes are concurrent or replicas have clock skew
A completed write intersects every later read quorum, preventing a later quorum from missing all replicas containing that write
A write quorum guarantees linearizable reads because any two quorums overlap on at least one replica
A read quorum provides serializable behavior because replicas synchronously order all versions before responding
explanation: Because W+R>N, every read quorum intersects the replicas that acknowledged a completed write. This prevents missing the write entirely, although it does not by itself provide linearizability or resolve concurrent versions.

text: Which statement best characterizes leveled compaction in an LSM-tree compared with size-tiered compaction?
options: Leveled compaction usually reduces read amplification by limiting overlapping files, while increasing write amplification
Leveled compaction usually reduces write amplification by merging only similarly sized files, while increasing read amplification
Leveled compaction eliminates tombstones during every flush, while size-tiered compaction retains them until archival storage
Leveled compaction guarantees constant write latency by preventing multiple compactions from targeting one level concurrently
explanation: Leveled compaction keeps non-overlapping ranges within levels, so reads inspect fewer files. The repeated rewriting needed to maintain that structure generally increases write amplification compared with size-tiered approaches.

text: A service uses hedged requests after the 95th percentile latency. Which consequence is most important when the backend is already near saturation?
options: Hedging usually lowers tail latency while increasing offered load, potentially creating a positive feedback overload loop
Hedging usually raises tail latency while reducing offered load, because duplicate requests share existing backend capacity
Hedging guarantees lower median and tail latency because only the fastest response is returned to the caller
Hedging affects latency but not capacity, because canceled duplicate requests consume no meaningful backend resources
explanation: Hedged requests can reduce tail latency when a small fraction of requests are stragglers, but duplicates increase backend work. Near saturation, that additional load can worsen queueing and create a feedback loop.

text: In Raft, when may a leader safely consider a log entry from a previous term committed?
options: Immediately after replicating that entry to a majority, regardless of which term originally created the entry
After any follower acknowledges the entry, provided the leader has already persisted the entry locally
Once a client receives the result, because client visibility implies that a majority has durably accepted the entry
After a current-term entry is replicated to a majority, which also commits earlier entries preceding it
explanation: Raft leaders use the current-term commitment rule to avoid incorrectly committing entries from prior terms based only on replication. Once a current-term entry is committed, all preceding entries in the log are committed as well.

text: Which design most reliably prevents cache invalidation from being lost when a database transaction commits successfully?
options: Update the cache first, then commit the database transaction and retry cache writes when readers report stale values
Write the database and cache in one distributed transaction, accepting two-phase commit overhead for every request
Record an invalidation or update event in an outbox within the database transaction, then publish it asynchronously
Expire the cache entry before every database update, allowing subsequent readers to repopulate values from the database
explanation: A transactional outbox makes the database change and the corresponding event atomic. A durable publisher can later deliver the event, avoiding the gap where the database commits but an independent cache update is lost.

text: Which communication style allows a service to publish work without waiting for an immediate reply?
options: Asynchronous messaging through a queue or event broker
Synchronous HTTP communication through a request and response endpoint
Direct database access through a shared relational database connection
Local method invocation through a function in the same application process
explanation: With asynchronous messaging, a service sends a message to a queue or broker and can continue without waiting for a direct response. A consumer processes the message later.

text: A payment API must safely support client retries across timeouts and failovers. Which mechanism provides the strongest practical duplicate-prevention behavior?
options: Use a short request timeout and reject retries, because clients cannot safely determine whether the original payment completed
Assign an idempotency key, persist its result with the payment state, and return the same result for repeated requests
Deduplicate requests using source IP and timestamp, because retries from one client normally share network identity
Place payments behind a queue without deduplication, because durable ordering prevents a message from being processed twice
explanation: A durable idempotency key tied to the payment operation lets the server recognize retries after ambiguous failures and return the original outcome. IP addresses and timestamps are not stable operation identities, and queues can redeliver messages.

text: Which statement correctly describes Kafka-style exactly-once processing when consuming records, updating a database, and producing output records?
options: Kafka transactions alone make external database writes exactly once, even when the consumer crashes after committing the database
Exactly-once semantics require atomic coordination or an idempotent protocol spanning the database and the consumed or produced records
Producer idempotence alone guarantees exactly-once results because duplicate input records are removed before application processing
A consumer offset commit after processing guarantees exactly once, provided the broker replicates offsets to a majority
explanation: Kafka transactions can atomically coordinate Kafka offsets and Kafka output records, but they do not automatically include an external database. The database therefore needs an atomic integration pattern or durable idempotency handling.

text: A multi-region database must provide linearizable writes despite a regional partition. Which tradeoff follows directly from that requirement?
options: The system must reject or delay writes in partitioned regions, sacrificing availability there to preserve a single global order
The system can accept writes independently in every region, because later conflict resolution reconstructs linearizable ordering
The system preserves both availability and linearizability by routing writes to any region with the lowest network latency
The system avoids the tradeoff by replicating asynchronously, because linearizability concerns reads rather than write acknowledgment
explanation: Linearizability requires operations to appear in one order consistent with real-time ordering. During a partition, a region that cannot coordinate with the authority must refuse or delay writes, sacrificing availability under the CAP tradeoff.

text: For a read-heavy query filtering on tenant_id and status while returning only id, updated_at, and title, which index design is generally most appropriate?
options: Create an index on updated_at alone, then scan matching records and filter tenant and status in the application layer
Create a composite index beginning with tenant_id and status, with returned columns included when the engine supports covering indexes
Create separate indexes on every returned column, allowing the optimizer to combine them for all tenant and status predicates
Create a hash index on title, because returned columns provide enough selectivity to avoid filtering by tenant and status
explanation: The predicate columns should lead the composite index so the engine can narrow the search efficiently. Including projected columns can enable an index-only scan, reducing table lookups when supported by the database.

text: A bounded worker pool consumes requests from a queue whose arrival rate exceeds sustainable processing capacity. Which behavior is the soundest overload strategy?
options: Increase queue retention indefinitely, preserving every request while shifting the overload into unbounded memory and storage growth
Add unlimited workers dynamically, assuming downstream services will absorb the additional concurrency without increasing queueing delays
Apply backpressure through bounded queues, admission control, and explicit shedding or retry policies for excess work
Disable timeouts and retries, allowing every request to remain active until capacity eventually becomes available
explanation: When arrivals exceed service capacity, backlog cannot grow indefinitely without exhausting resources and worsening latency. Bounded buffering plus admission control and deliberate shedding keeps the system stable and makes overload behavior explicit.

text: What does a standard transformer KV cache store during autoregressive inference?
options: Keys and values for prior tokens, avoiding their repeated attention recomputation
Hidden states for prior tokens, replacing all future transformer-layer computations
Attention probability matrices for prior tokens, avoiding repeated softmax evaluations
Queries and residual streams for prior tokens, eliminating subsequent projection operations
explanation: The KV cache stores each layer's key and value vectors for previously processed tokens. New queries attend to those cached vectors, while only the newly generated token requires full layer computation.

text: How can speculative decoding preserve the target model's output distribution while accelerating generation?
options: Accepting draft tokens with target-based rejection sampling, then correcting rejected suffixes
Selecting draft tokens only when their logits exceed a fixed confidence threshold
Averaging draft and target logits before sampling the next sequence token
Running the target model only after the draft model completes an entire response
explanation: Speculative decoding evaluates a draft sequence with the target model and accepts tokens using a rejection-sampling rule based on both distributions. This can produce exact target-model samples under the appropriate algorithm.

text: Which approach is most defensible when extending RoPE-based models beyond their training context length?
options: Using frequency-aware positional scaling validated against long-context retrieval and generation tasks
Multiplying every position index by one constant without changing attention normalization
Appending learned position vectors after RoPE so the original frequencies remain completely unchanged
Truncating distant keys while retaining all recent queries to avoid positional extrapolation errors
explanation: Long-context RoPE methods rescale or modify frequencies to reduce phase distortion, but their effectiveness depends on empirical validation. Retrieval and generation tests reveal degradation that perplexity alone may miss.

text: For a retrieval-augmented generation system over heterogeneous technical documents, which chunking strategy is generally strongest?
options: Structure-aware chunks with metadata, bounded size, and parent-context expansion when retrieved
Uniform token windows with large overlap, regardless of headings, tables, or document boundaries
Sentence-only chunks indexed independently, with no neighboring context added at generation time
Whole-document embeddings paired with keyword filters to avoid fragmenting technical explanations
explanation: Structure-aware chunking preserves semantic boundaries while bounded sizes support precise retrieval. Parent-context expansion can restore surrounding definitions without forcing every indexed unit to be large.

text: Which design best mitigates prompt injection from retrieved documents in an agentic RAG application?
options: Treating retrieved text as untrusted data, delimiting it, and enforcing tools outside model instructions
Repeating the system prompt after retrieved text so the model is more likely to follow its hierarchy
Asking the model to identify malicious passages before allowing it to execute any requested tool
Removing imperative sentences from retrieved passages with a classifier before presenting the remaining content
explanation: Retrieved content should never gain authority merely because it appears in context. Clear data boundaries, least-privilege tool policies, and application-level authorization provide defense beyond relying on model obedience.

text: What is the defining optimization in standard LoRA fine-tuning?
options: Training low-rank weight updates while freezing the pretrained model's original parameters
Updating every pretrained weight with a low learning rate and periodically merging gradients
Replacing attention projections with smaller dense layers that are trained from random initialization
Quantizing the base model and training only embeddings that correspond to observed prompt tokens
explanation: LoRA represents the trainable update to selected weight matrices as a product of two low-rank matrices while leaving base weights frozen. This greatly reduces trainable parameters and optimizer-state memory.

text: Which practice most reliably improves post-training accuracy for a weight-only quantized language model?
options: Using representative calibration data and evaluating task-sensitive layers at the target deployment distribution
Choosing the lowest available bit width uniformly without calibration to maximize memory savings
Calibrating only on synthetic random tokens because real prompts can bias activation statistics
Quantizing embeddings exclusively while leaving transformer projections unchanged during deployment
explanation: Activation and weight statistics depend strongly on the input distribution, so representative calibration helps determine suitable scales and identify sensitive layers. Layer-wise evaluation can justify mixed precision where uniform quantization harms quality.

text: In a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer, what is the primary purpose of an auxiliary load-balancing objective?
options: Encouraging tokens and routing probability to spread across experts without removing learned specialization
Forcing every expert to process identical token counts so routing becomes deterministic across batches
Increasing the number of selected experts per token to improve quality without changing inference cost
Replacing router logits with a uniform distribution so expert utilization cannot become imbalanced
explanation: Load-balancing losses discourage router collapse and excessive expert hotspots while retaining token-dependent routing. Capacity limits and token dropping may still be needed because balancing objectives are imperfect.

text: How do robust structured-output decoders most directly enforce a JSON schema during generation?
options: Constraining each next-token choice to continuations permitted by a schema-derived parser or automaton
Adding a schema description to the prompt and rejecting malformed outputs only after completion
Sampling multiple unconstrained responses and selecting the one that passes a JSON validator
Fine-tuning on valid JSON examples while leaving decoding unrestricted at inference time
explanation: Constrained decoding integrates a parser, grammar, or automaton into token selection, masking continuations that cannot lead to valid schema-conforming output. Post-hoc validation can detect errors but cannot guarantee validity.

text: Which statement correctly describes safe prefix KV-cache reuse across requests?
options: Reuse is valid for an identical token prefix and compatible settings, while changes require invalidation
Reuse is valid whenever prompts share similar embeddings, even if their token sequences differ substantially
Reuse is valid for identical system messages despite changes to tokenizer, adapters, or attention configuration
Reuse is valid across users whenever temperature matches, because sampling settings determine cached states
explanation: KV states depend on the exact token sequence, model parameters, tokenizer behavior, and relevant attention configuration. A cache can safely reuse a matching prefix only when those dependencies remain compatible.

text: What best describes a microservice in a microservices architecture?
options: A small, independently deployable service focused on one business capability
A shared library that contains reusable code for every application service
A single database process that stores records for the entire business system
A user interface component that displays data from several application screens
explanation: A microservice is a small, independently deployable application component organized around a specific business capability. It usually communicates with other services through well-defined interfaces.

text: Which practice is commonly recommended for data ownership in microservices?
options: Each service owns its data and exposes access through defined interfaces
Every service writes directly to one shared database for simpler coordination
A central service approves and performs all database operations for the system
All services duplicate every record so queries never require remote communication
explanation: Giving each service ownership of its data helps preserve loose coupling and allows services to evolve independently. Other services should use APIs or messages rather than directly changing that data.

text: What is a common responsibility of an API gateway in a microservices system?
options: Routing client requests to services and handling shared edge concerns
Replacing every service database with one centralized storage component
Implementing all business rules so individual services remain logic-free
Compiling service source code into one application before each deployment
explanation: An API gateway can route requests and provide shared edge functions such as authentication, rate limiting, or response aggregation. It does not replace the business logic inside individual services.

text: What can happen when a service calls another service synchronously and that service is unavailable?
options: The calling request may wait, fail, or return an error from the dependency
The calling service automatically creates an identical replacement service locally
The dependency becomes available because synchronous calls retry without any limits
The calling service continues with complete data because unavailable calls are ignored
explanation: A synchronous caller normally depends on an immediate response, so an unavailable dependency can cause delays or failures. Timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers can limit the impact.

text: Which set of signals is most useful for monitoring a deployed ML model?
options: Only the number of lines written in the training script
Only the visual style of charts in the experiment notebook
Prediction quality, data drift, latency, and resource usage
Only the total size of the team's source code repository
explanation: Production monitoring should cover model behavior and system health. Accuracy or other quality measures, drift, response time, and resource use can reveal different types of problems.

text: What is service discovery used for in a microservices architecture?
options: Finding available service instances and their current network locations
Finding unused source files and removing them before a service deployment
Finding database records and copying them into every running service instance
Finding user interface defects and reporting them to the development team
explanation: Service discovery helps clients or routing infrastructure locate healthy instances of a service. This is useful when instances change addresses because of scaling or redeployment.

text: Why are bounded responsibilities important when designing microservices?
options: They keep each service focused and reduce unnecessary dependencies between services
They ensure every service contains all business features needed by every user
They require all services to use identical programming languages and deployment schedules
They allow one service to change another service's internal implementation without coordination
explanation: A clear responsibility keeps a service cohesive and limits the number of reasons it must change. This supports independent development, testing, and deployment.

text: Which set of capabilities is most associated with observability for microservices?
options: Logs, metrics, and distributed traces collected across service interactions
Compilers, editors, and source control tools used during application development
Schemas, indexes, and stored procedures used inside a service database
Screens, buttons, and style sheets used to build a service user interface
explanation: Logs, metrics, and distributed traces provide complementary views of system behavior. Together they help teams understand failures and performance across service boundaries.

text: What is a key advantage of independently deployable microservices?
options: A team can release one service without rebuilding and redeploying every service
A team can change shared data structures without considering other service consumers
A team can eliminate the need for testing because services have separate deployments
A team can guarantee that network failures never affect communication between services
explanation: Independent deployment allows a service to be released separately when its interface and dependencies remain compatible. It can reduce release scope and coordination compared with a single deployable application.

text: How does a microservices architecture generally differ from a traditional monolith?
options: Functionality is split across deployable services rather than one deployable application
Functionality is moved entirely into the database rather than application components
Functionality is placed only in client devices rather than server-side components
Functionality is combined into one larger process rather than several smaller services
explanation: A monolith is typically deployed as one application unit, while microservices split functionality into smaller services that can be developed and deployed separately. This also introduces communication and operational complexity.

text: Which statement best defines MLOps?
options: Practices for deploying, monitoring, and maintaining ML systems
Methods for designing neural network layers and activation functions
Techniques for collecting labeled data from external sources
Processes for tuning model hyperparameters during experimentation
explanation: MLOps applies software engineering and operations practices to machine learning systems. It helps teams deploy, monitor, update, and maintain models reliably.

text: What happens during inference in a machine learning system?
options: A pipeline removes duplicate records before creating a dataset
An optimizer updates model weights using a training data batch
An already trained model produces predictions from new input data
An evaluator compares predictions with known labels for scoring
explanation: Inference uses a trained model to generate predictions from new input data. Updating weights and comparing labels are typically part of training or evaluation.

text: Which practice best supports reproducible machine learning experiments?
options: Keep separate undocumented copies of datasets on individual machines
Store code, configurations, and data references in trackable versions
Change production settings manually without recording the updates
Store only final model files and delete intermediate experiment outputs
explanation: Versioning code, configurations, and data references allows others to identify and recreate the conditions of an experiment. It also makes changes easier to review and audit.

text: What is a feature store primarily used for?
options: Dashboard for displaying hardware utilization during model training
Repository that stores source code for application deployment
Service that automatically labels images for supervised learning
Central system for managing and serving reusable ML features
explanation: A feature store organizes reusable input features and can serve them consistently for training and inference. This reduces duplicated feature-generation work and helps prevent inconsistencies.

text: What can happen when a machine learning model experiences data drift?
options: Training becomes faster because incoming records are more consistent
Model performance may decline as real-world input patterns change
Model weights update automatically without any new training process
Prediction latency disappears because requests use cached outputs
explanation: Data drift occurs when the distribution of incoming data changes over time. Those changes can make a model's learned patterns less accurate, so monitoring and retraining may be needed.

text: Which statement best describes continuous integration for an ML project?
options: Manually retrains every model on a fixed calendar schedule
Stores all raw data in a database without applying validation rules
Automatically tests and validates code changes before integration
Replaces monitoring dashboards with a single final accuracy report
explanation: Continuous integration automatically checks changes by running tests and validation steps before they are merged. This helps detect problems early as teams modify shared code.

text: What is the main purpose of a model registry?
options: Converts unstructured documents into numerical training features
Allocates cloud servers and balances web traffic across them
Records individual user requests for later application debugging
Catalogs model versions, metadata, and deployment stages
explanation: A model registry provides a central catalog for model versions and related metadata. It commonly tracks whether a model is in development, testing, staging, or production.

text: Which condition most directly supports reproducibility in machine learning?
options: The same code, data versions, and settings can recreate a result
The model always achieves identical accuracy on every new dataset
Training requires no configuration files or environment specifications
Predictions remain correct even when input features are unavailable
explanation: Reproducibility means being able to recreate an experiment or result using the same relevant inputs and settings. Tracking code, data versions, environments, and parameters supports this goal.

text: Which statement correctly compares batch and real-time inference?
options: Real-time inference scores requests only after weekly aggregation
Batch inference scores many records together on a schedule
Batch inference always requires a user-facing response in milliseconds
Real-time inference cannot use a model trained on historical data
explanation: Batch inference processes groups of records at scheduled times, while real-time inference responds to individual requests as they arrive. The choice depends on latency and workload requirements.

text: Which practice best supports service autonomy in a microservices architecture?
options: Give each service ownership of its data and expose changes through APIs or events.
Allow all services to update shared tables while documenting the table relationships centrally.
Place business data in one database and let services query it through optimized database views.
Replicate every database table into each service and reconcile conflicting writes periodically.
explanation: A service should own its data and expose behavior through explicit interfaces. This reduces coupling and allows independent deployment, schema evolution, and scaling.

text: What typically happens when a circuit breaker enters the open state?
options: Calls are rejected or redirected temporarily without contacting the failing dependency.
Calls continue normally while the breaker records failures for later operational analysis.
Calls are queued indefinitely until the dependency confirms that its capacity has recovered.
Calls are retried continuously with increasing concurrency until a successful response arrives.
explanation: An open circuit breaker fails fast or uses a fallback instead of sending more traffic to an unhealthy dependency. After a delay, it usually enters a half-open state to test recovery.

text: Which approach makes a payment operation safer when clients may retry requests?
options: Use an idempotency key so repeated requests produce one effective payment operation.
Generate a new payment identifier for every retry and reconcile duplicate charges afterward.
Disable retries at clients and depend on the network to deliver each request exactly once.
Accept every request immediately and remove duplicates later with a scheduled cleanup job.
explanation: An idempotency key lets the payment service recognize repeated attempts and return the original result without charging twice. This is especially important when response delivery is uncertain.

text: What is a recommended approach for managing configuration across deployed services?
options: Externalize environment-specific settings and inject them through a controlled configuration mechanism.
Compile separate service binaries for each environment with values embedded in source-controlled files.
Store production credentials directly in container images so every instance receives identical settings.
Let services discover configuration by reading arbitrary files from whichever host runs them.
explanation: Externalized configuration separates deployable code from environment-specific values and supports safer changes. Secrets should also use an appropriate secret-management system rather than images or source code.

text: Which statement best describes a saga for coordinating a distributed business transaction?
options: It coordinates local transactions using events or commands and compensates completed steps when needed.
It locks every participating database until all services have committed one globally consistent transaction.
It copies all participating data into one temporary database and commits changes through one coordinator.
It retries failed operations forever so each service eventually reaches the original transaction outcome.
explanation: A saga avoids a long-running distributed transaction by using local commits and compensating actions. It provides business-level consistency rather than universal immediate atomicity.

text: A service publishes an event after changing its database, but the process crashes before publishing. Which pattern addresses this risk?
options: Use a transactional outbox that stores the event with the database change before publishing it.
Publish the event first and assume the database update will succeed during a later retry.
Send the event from memory after committing and accept occasional loss during process crashes.
Ask consumers to poll the service database directly whenever an expected event is missing.
explanation: The transactional outbox records the state change and event in one local database transaction. A separate publisher can then reliably deliver the stored event, typically with duplicate handling.

text: Which responsibility is most commonly associated with an API gateway?
options: Routing client requests while centralizing cross-cutting concerns such as authentication and rate limits.
Owning every service's business rules so downstream services only perform database persistence operations.
Replacing service databases with one gateway-managed data store for consistent cross-service transactions.
Guaranteeing exactly-once processing by synchronously retrying every downstream request until completion.
explanation: An API gateway commonly provides routing and cross-cutting edge capabilities such as authentication, throttling, and request aggregation. It should not become the owner of all domain logic.

text: Why are correlation IDs useful when diagnosing a request across multiple services?
options: They connect related logs and traces so one business request can be followed across service boundaries.
They guarantee that every downstream operation succeeds even when a dependency is unavailable.
They replace authentication tokens by proving that a request came from a trusted client.
They force asynchronous events to execute in the same order across all participating services.
explanation: A propagated correlation or trace identifier lets operators link logs, spans, and messages belonging to one request flow. It improves diagnosis but does not provide security or delivery guarantees.

text: What is the primary distinction between a readiness probe and a liveness probe?
options: Readiness controls traffic eligibility, while liveness indicates whether a process should be restarted.
Readiness triggers restarts, while liveness determines whether a service should receive production traffic.
Readiness measures dependency latency, while liveness verifies that every downstream service is healthy.
Readiness validates deployment metadata, while liveness confirms that configuration values are encrypted.
explanation: A readiness failure removes an instance from traffic while it starts or loses required capacity. A liveness failure signals that the process may be stuck and should be restarted.

text: Which statement correctly describes a PersistentVolumeClaim?
options: A PVC requests storage, and Kubernetes binds it to a suitable PV or provisioner.
A PVC stores container logs, and Kubernetes sends them to a selected Service.
A PVC exposes Pods externally, and Kubernetes assigns it a public IP address.
A PVC limits CPU usage, and Kubernetes uses it to calculate Pod replicas.
explanation: A PersistentVolumeClaim expresses a workload's storage requirements. Kubernetes can bind it to a matching PersistentVolume or provision storage dynamically through a configured provisioner.

text: What is the main purpose of consumer-driven contract testing between microservices?
options: Verify that a provider's responses satisfy the documented expectations of its consuming services.
Verify that all services share one database schema and deploy their migrations in identical versions.
Verify that network performance remains below a fixed latency threshold under maximum production load.
Verify that a consumer can access private provider implementation classes during integration testing.
explanation: Consumer-driven contracts capture the interactions a consumer depends on and test them against the provider. This detects incompatible interface changes earlier than full end-to-end testing alone.

text: Which design most reliably provides atomic persistence of a business change and publication of its integration event without requiring a distributed transaction?
options: Write the business row and an outbox event in one local transaction, then relay the event asynchronously.
Publish to the broker first, then commit the business row after the broker acknowledgment returns.
Commit the business row and event independently, relying on timestamps to reconcile any mismatch later.
Use a distributed transaction spanning the database and broker so both resources commit synchronously.
explanation: The transactional outbox commits the state change and event record atomically within one database transaction. A separate relay can retry publication, avoiding two-phase coordination while preserving eventual delivery.

text: Which statement most accurately describes the consistency limitation of a saga coordinating a multi-service business transaction?
options: Compensating actions restore business invariants semantically, but cannot generally undo externally visible side effects.
Compensating actions provide the same isolation guarantees as a database transaction across every participating service.
Compensating actions guarantee rollback ordering automatically, even when participants process messages asynchronously.
Compensating actions eliminate intermediate states because every service commits only after the saga completes.
explanation: A saga coordinates local transactions and uses semantic compensation when later steps fail. It does not provide global atomicity or isolation, and some effects such as emails or shipments cannot truly be undone.

text: A service receives overloaded traffic and experiences increasing tail latency. Which retry policy is most appropriate for protecting the system?
options: Use bounded retries with exponential backoff, jitter, deadlines, and retry budgets enforced at one layer.
Retry every failed request immediately at each client and proxy layer until one attempt eventually succeeds.
Use fixed-interval retries without deadlines so transient failures receive unlimited opportunities to recover.
Increase retry counts during saturation because additional attempts improve utilization of partially healthy instances.
explanation: Bounded, jittered retries limit synchronized retry storms and ensure requests stop consuming resources after their deadline. A retry budget and single responsible layer prevent multiplicative amplification across the call graph.

text: Which statement correctly characterizes an effectively-once processing design for messages delivered by an at-least-once broker?
options: A consumer deduplicates stable message identifiers and commits processing state atomically with the resulting side effect.
A consumer disables acknowledgments until the broker confirms that every downstream service processed the message.
A consumer relies on broker redelivery ordering to ensure repeated deliveries produce only one business outcome.
A consumer uses a unique transport connection for each message so the broker can suppress duplicate delivery attempts.
explanation: At-least-once delivery can produce duplicates, so consumers must make effects idempotent or deduplicate using durable identifiers. Atomic recording of the processing result and deduplication state prevents repeated business outcomes.

text: Which comparison between orchestration and choreography in saga implementations is most accurate?
options: Orchestration centralizes workflow decisions, while choreography distributes reactions and can make global flow harder to observe.
Orchestration removes service coupling entirely, while choreography requires every participant to share one transaction coordinator.
Orchestration guarantees atomic rollback, while choreography guarantees isolation through independently committed local transactions.
Orchestration requires synchronous calls, while choreography requires asynchronous messaging and cannot support request responses.
explanation: An orchestrator explicitly directs participants and makes workflow state visible in one place, at the cost of coordinator coupling. Choreography relies on events and local reactions, which can reduce central control but complicate reasoning and observability.

text: A service mesh automatically retries a failed request, while the application client also retries the same call. What is the primary risk?
options: Independent retry layers can multiply attempts, causing retry storms and worsening overload precisely when dependencies are unhealthy.
Independent retry layers serialize attempts, reducing throughput but preserving stable tail latency during dependency failures.
Independent retry layers bypass circuit breakers, so healthy instances become unreachable until all requests expire.
Independent retry layers prevent connection reuse, increasing handshake cost but leaving backend request volume unchanged.
explanation: Each layer may retry every attempt generated by the other, multiplying traffic and extending resource occupancy. Retry ownership should be explicit, bounded, and coordinated with deadlines, budgets, and circuit breaking.

text: Which approach best supports backward-compatible evolution of an event contract consumed by independently deployed microservices?
options: Add optional fields, preserve existing meanings, tolerate unknown fields, and reserve incompatible changes for a new version.
Rename existing fields when terminology improves, requiring consumers to deploy the updated schema before publication.
Remove deprecated fields immediately after producer deployment because consumers should always track the latest contract.
Change field types in place when the serialized representation remains readable by the original consumer implementation.
explanation: Adding optional data while preserving existing field semantics allows older consumers to continue operating. Incompatible changes should use explicit versioning or a separately governed contract rather than silently changing meanings.

text: Which technique most effectively reduces cache stampedes when a highly popular key expires under concurrent load?
options: Use single-flight refresh with jittered expiration, stale-while-revalidate behavior, and bounded fallback serving.
Expire all keys at identical times so workers coordinate naturally around one predictable refresh interval.
Allow every requesting worker to refresh independently so the fastest response repopulates the shared cache.
Disable expiration for popular keys and depend on manual invalidation whenever the underlying record changes.
explanation: Single-flight coordination permits one refresh while other requests reuse stale data or wait within a bound. Expiration jitter and stale-while-revalidate reduce synchronized misses without requiring indefinite cache retention.

text: A Kubernetes-hosted service is being terminated during a rolling deployment. Which shutdown sequence best minimizes failed requests?
options: Mark the instance unready, stop accepting new work, drain active requests, then exit before the termination deadline.
Exit immediately, allowing the load balancer and connection pool to discover termination through failed requests.
Sleep for a fixed interval, then exit without changing readiness because existing traffic should naturally drain away.
Continue accepting traffic until process termination, relying on the orchestrator to replay requests that fail during shutdown.
explanation: Readiness removal prevents new routing while graceful draining allows in-flight work to finish. The process must still honor a bounded termination deadline so shutdown cannot stall deployment progress indefinitely.

text: Which observability practice provides useful distributed-tracing detail while limiting telemetry cost and high-cardinality problems?
options: Propagate trace context consistently, sample intelligently, and keep unbounded identifiers out of metric labels.
Create a separate metric series for every user, request payload, and database key to preserve complete diagnostic detail.
Sample only successful requests because failed requests already contain enough information in application logs and alerts.
Generate independent trace identifiers at each service so local storage remains compact and cross-service joins stay optional.
explanation: Consistent context propagation connects spans across service boundaries, while tail or adaptive sampling preserves representative slow and failed traces. High-cardinality values belong in sampled logs or span attributes rather than metric dimensions.

text: Which distinction between a Deployment and a StatefulSet is correct?
options: Deployment manages interchangeable Pods, while StatefulSet preserves Pod identity.
Deployment provides node-level storage, while StatefulSet only runs stateless Pods.
Deployment schedules one Pod, while StatefulSet schedules all replicas on one node.
Deployment handles networking, while StatefulSet handles external load balancing.
explanation: Deployments manage interchangeable, usually stateless Pods. StatefulSets provide stable Pod identities and support ordered behavior and persistent storage patterns.

text: Which statement correctly compares Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps?
options: Secret stores sensitive values, while ConfigMap stores ordinary configuration data.
Secret stores ordinary settings, while ConfigMap stores encrypted credentials.
Secret assigns Pods to nodes, while ConfigMap exposes container ports.
Secret creates replicas, while ConfigMap controls their rolling replacement.
explanation: Secrets are intended for sensitive values such as tokens or passwords, while ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration data. Secret data is commonly encoded, but encoding alone is not encryption.

text: What usually happens when a Pod fails its readiness probe?
options: When readiness fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints.
When readiness fails, Kubernetes immediately restarts the container in the Pod.
When readiness fails, Kubernetes deletes the Pod and recreates its volume.
When readiness fails, Kubernetes marks the node unschedulable for new Pods.
explanation: A failed readiness probe means the Pod is not ready to receive traffic. Kubernetes generally removes it from matching Service endpoints without necessarily restarting it.

text: Which statement correctly describes a ClusterIP Service?
options: A ClusterIP Service provides stable internal access to a selected set of Pods.
A ClusterIP Service exposes selected Pods through a public cloud load balancer.
A ClusterIP Service stores container images on nodes for faster deployment.
A ClusterIP Service assigns persistent disks directly to each selected Pod.
explanation: ClusterIP is the default Service type and provides a stable virtual IP reachable inside the cluster. It routes traffic to Pods selected by its label selector.

text: What is a primary purpose of a Kubernetes namespace?
options: A namespace groups Kubernetes resources and helps separate names and access.
A namespace permanently reserves nodes and prevents their shared scheduling.
A namespace converts a Deployment into a StatefulSet with stable identities.
A namespace encrypts all configuration values before containers can read them.
explanation: Namespaces provide a logical scope for resources and can support separate names, quotas, and access policies. They do not create physical node boundaries.

text: What generally happens during a Deployment rolling update?
options: During a rolling update, Kubernetes gradually replaces old Pods with new ones.
During a rolling update, Kubernetes stops every old Pod before creating any new ones.
During a rolling update, Kubernetes changes only the Service port and selector.
During a rolling update, Kubernetes moves each container into a separate namespace.
explanation: A rolling update gradually creates new ReplicaSet Pods and removes old ones according to the Deployment strategy. This helps maintain application availability during updates.

text: Which statement correctly describes the kubectl apply command?
options: kubectl apply creates or updates resources from a declared configuration file.
kubectl apply only reads current status and never changes cluster resources.
kubectl apply deletes resources not mentioned in every configuration file.
kubectl apply builds container images before sending resource definitions.
explanation: kubectl apply uses a declarative configuration to create or update the specified Kubernetes resources. It does not build container images or automatically delete unrelated resources.

text: What does a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler commonly adjust?
options: An HPA adjusts Pod replicas using metrics such as CPU utilization or custom values.
An HPA adjusts node sizes using metrics such as disk capacity or image count.
An HPA changes container images using metrics such as restart count or age.
An HPA creates namespaces using metrics such as API latency or object count.
explanation: A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of Pod replicas based on observed metrics and configured targets. CPU, memory, and supported custom metrics are common inputs.

text: Which statement correctly describes a Kubernetes toleration?
options: A toleration lets a Pod be scheduled onto a node whose taint it matches.
A toleration forces a Pod to run on every node carrying the matching taint.
A toleration removes a matching taint from the node before scheduling the Pod.
A toleration automatically adds matching taints to all nodes in the cluster.
explanation: A toleration allows a Pod to be considered for a node with a matching taint. It does not force placement there or remove the taint.

text: What does Platform.OS provide in React Native?
options: Platform.OS returns the current operating system identifier
Platform.OS returns the device's current screen orientation
Platform.OS returns the installed React Native version number
Platform.OS returns the application's current network status
explanation: Platform.OS identifies the operating system running the app, such as ios or android. Developers can use it to apply platform-specific behavior.

text: Which preprocessing pattern best prevents data leakage during model evaluation?
options: Fit the scaler on training data, then reuse it for validation and test data.
Fit separate scalers on training, validation, and test data before evaluation.
Fit the scaler on all available data, then split the transformed dataset.
Fit the scaler on validation data, then apply it to training and test data.
explanation: Fitting preprocessing only on training data prevents information from validation or test samples influencing the learned transformation. The fitted scaler can then be applied consistently to all later splits.

text: Which pipeline design best supports safe, repeatable reruns when a job is retried?
options: Write outputs to deterministic locations and overwrite or safely upsert existing records.
Append a new output partition on every run, even when the input has not changed.
Use timestamps generated at runtime to create a unique output path for each run.
Delete all historical outputs before each run and rebuild every upstream artifact.
explanation: Deterministic paths and overwrite or upsert behavior make a pipeline idempotent. Retrying the same inputs should produce the same logical outputs without creating duplicates.

text: What is the most appropriate pattern for a production canary model deployment?
options: Route a small share to the new model, compare guardrails, then expand or roll back.
Replace the old model immediately, then inspect aggregate metrics after one full day.
Send all traffic to both models, returning whichever prediction arrives first.
Train the new model periodically, then deploy it broadly after offline accuracy improves.
explanation: A canary limits exposure while production metrics such as errors, latency, and business outcomes are evaluated. Traffic can then be increased gradually or reverted if guardrails fail.

text: Which practice best reduces training-serving skew for engineered features?
options: Package the same versioned feature transformation for both training and serving.
Reimplement transformations separately in each environment and compare outputs.
Let serving recompute transformations from current data without persisted parameters.
Apply a second normalization step at serving time to correct production variation.
explanation: Sharing versioned transformation code and fitted parameters keeps feature computation consistent across environments. Separate implementations often introduce subtle differences that degrade predictions.

text: Which capability is a primary purpose of a model registry in an MLOps workflow?
options: Store versioned model artifacts, metadata, lineage, metrics, and promotion status.
Store only the latest model binary so deployment always uses the newest artifact.
Store raw training data and omit evaluation metrics to keep registry records small.
Store application logs for services and route requests without tracking model versions.
explanation: A model registry provides traceability and controlled promotion across model versions. It commonly records artifacts, provenance, evaluation results, and lifecycle status.

text: Which approach is most suitable for detecting covariate drift in production?
options: Compare current feature distributions with a reference window using a selected statistical test.
Compare current prediction errors with labels from a reference window using a selected metric.
Compare current prediction distributions with a reference window using a selected threshold.
Compare current request volumes with capacity thresholds from the deployment environment.
explanation: Covariate drift concerns changes in input feature distributions, so current features should be compared with a trusted baseline. Error changes indicate performance drift, while prediction changes indicate output drift.

text: Which configuration practice is safest for credentials used by an ML service?
options: Keep nonsecret settings in versioned configuration and inject credentials through a secret manager.
Commit encrypted credentials beside code and decrypt them with a key stored in the repository.
Put credentials in environment variables defined directly inside the container image.
Store API tokens in a shared configuration file and restrict access with application logic.
explanation: Secret managers provide controlled access, rotation, auditing, and separation from source code and images. Nonsecret configuration can remain versioned for reproducibility.

text: Which CI practice provides useful early validation for an ML training change?
options: Run unit tests for feature logic, schema checks, and a small reproducible training smoke test.
Run only full-scale training jobs because small tests may miss distributed behavior.
Run dashboard checks manually after deployment, since training code changes rarely affect outputs.
Run inference benchmarks only, because data and model tests belong in offline notebooks.
explanation: Fast unit, schema, and smoke tests catch common failures before expensive training or deployment. Full-scale jobs and production checks remain useful later but are poor substitutes for rapid CI feedback.

text: When is batch inference generally a better choice than online inference?
options: Use batch inference when predictions can be precomputed and latency is not interactive.
Use online inference when predictions can be precomputed hours before requests arrive.
Use batch inference when each request needs a fresh response within milliseconds.
Use online inference when throughput matters more than request-level freshness.
explanation: Batch inference fits workloads where predictions can be generated ahead of time, such as daily recommendations or scoring files. Online inference is preferred when each request requires a timely, fresh response.

text: What is the safest rollback pattern for a model deployment?
options: Keep previous model and preprocessing artifacts, then switch traffic using a versioned deployment.
Retrain the current model in place and restart the service if the new version fails.
Roll back only model weights while retaining whichever preprocessing code is currently deployed.
Restore the latest container image without checking its model and feature artifact versions.
explanation: A reliable rollback restores the complete compatible model, preprocessing, and runtime bundle. Versioned traffic switching makes the reversal fast and avoids mismatches between artifacts.

text: Which design most reliably prevents training-serving skew for a feature whose value depends on event time?
options: Use point-in-time joins and shared transformation code, materializing training features with event-time semantics.
Compute training features in batch and recreate equivalent serving logic manually inside the prediction service.
