options: Returned entities are not added to the change tracker, reducing tracking overhead for read-only work.
Returned entities are detached and automatically written to the database when their properties are changed.
Returned entities bypass database transactions and therefore cannot be loaded with related navigation properties.
Returned entities are cached globally so later queries can reuse them without contacting the database.
explanation: AsNoTracking prevents EF Core from maintaining change-tracking state for the returned entities. It is useful for read-only queries, but changing those objects does not automatically produce updates.

text: What equality behavior is normally generated for a C# record compared with a typical class?
options: Records provide value-based equality using their relevant data, while classes normally use reference-based equality.
Records provide reference-based equality using object identity, while classes normally compare all public properties.
Records compare only their runtime types, while classes automatically compare every field declared in the object.
Records use hash codes as the sole equality test, while classes compare references before checking their contents.
explanation: Records are designed for value-oriented data and generate equality members based on their components or properties. Ordinary classes inherit reference-based equality unless they override it.

text: What is the primary purpose of calling ConfigureAwait(false) on an awaited task?
options: It prevents continuation code from requiring the synchronization context captured before the await.
It prevents the awaited operation from using thread-pool threads after the asynchronous work completes.
It forces the awaited operation to complete synchronously before the method continues executing its next statement.
It prevents exceptions from crossing the await boundary by converting failures into canceled task results.
explanation: ConfigureAwait(false) tells the awaiter not to marshal the continuation back to the captured context. This is commonly useful in reusable library code, although ASP.NET Core usually has no request synchronization context.

text: What do nullable reference type annotations primarily provide in a C# project?
options: They enable compiler analysis and warnings for possible null usage without adding automatic runtime checks.
They guarantee referenced objects can never contain null values after the compiler successfully builds the project.
They automatically insert null checks before every member access and throw consistent exceptions when needed.
They change the CLR representation of reference types so nullable and nonnullable values use different storage.
explanation: Nullable reference types are mainly a compile-time feature that improves flow analysis and produces warnings. They do not enforce non-null values at runtime or change the underlying CLR reference type.

text: Within which scope is a resource disposed when declared with the C# using declaration syntax?
options: It is disposed when execution leaves the enclosing scope that contains the using declaration.
It is disposed immediately after the declaration statement finishes before the next statement begins executing.
It is disposed only when the garbage collector determines that the resource is unreachable.
It is disposed when the containing method returns, even if the declaration appears inside a nested block.
explanation: A using declaration is compiled to disposal logic covering the remainder of its enclosing scope. If it appears in a nested block, disposal occurs when that block is exited, including during exception handling.

text: What is a key practical difference between querying through IEnumerable<T> and IQueryable<T>?
options: IEnumerable<T> generally runs delegates in process, while IQueryable<T> builds expressions for a query provider.
IEnumerable<T> always executes on a database server, while IQueryable<T> always materializes results before filtering.
IEnumerable<T> supports only synchronous methods, while IQueryable<T> automatically makes every operation asynchronous.
IEnumerable<T> tracks entity changes automatically, while IQueryable<T> disables tracking for every provider.
explanation: IEnumerable<T> typically applies delegates to objects in the current process. IQueryable<T> represents operations as expression trees that providers such as EF Core may translate into database queries.

text: Which Kubernetes feature enforces runtime security?
options: Falco
PodSecurityPolicy
ConfigMap
Secrets
explanation: Isolate namespaces.

text: In modern .NET with tiered compilation and dynamic PGO, what is the primary purpose of runtime profiling?
options: It recompiles frequently used methods with runtime profile data to improve generated machine code.
It compiles every method immediately with maximum optimization before the application starts.
It replaces managed calls with native calls only after assemblies are unloaded from the process.
It disables JIT compilation for methods whose first invocation completes without allocation.
explanation: Dynamic PGO collects runtime behavior such as type distributions and branch frequencies, then allows hot methods to be recompiled with better optimizations. Tiered compilation makes this staged optimization practical by initially favoring quick compilation.

text: What is the safest general guidance when a ValueTask may need multiple consumers or repeated awaits?
options: Treat it like a reusable Task and await it repeatedly without conversion or restrictions.
Await it once, or call AsTask when multiple consumers or repeated awaits are required.
Copy its result field before awaiting so the underlying operation can safely be restarted.
Use ConfigureAwait(false) to make repeated awaits safe even when the ValueTask wraps a source.
explanation: A ValueTask may be backed by a reusable or single-consumption source, so callers should normally await it once. Calling AsTask materializes a Task with the normal reusable-await and multi-consumer semantics.

text: Which statement correctly describes an important restriction imposed by Span<T> being a ref struct?
options: A Span<T> cannot be stored in heap objects or safely carried across await and yield boundaries.
A Span<T> is immutable and therefore safe to share concurrently without synchronization or copying.
A Span<T> always copies its referenced elements when passed to another method or returned by value.
A Span<T> can be boxed and stored in object fields when its element type is a blittable value.
explanation: Span<T> is stack-only and cannot be boxed, placed in ordinary object fields, or kept live across suspension points such as await and yield. These restrictions protect references that may point into movable or stack-managed memory.

text: What is the normal garbage-collection behavior for objects allocated on the Large Object Heap?
options: They are collected with generation two and normally remain uncompactable unless compaction is explicitly requested.
They are collected with generation one and compacted after every collection to minimize allocation gaps.
They are placed in the pinned object heap automatically and therefore never participate in garbage collection.
They are collected independently from generation two and compacted continuously during background collection.
explanation: The Large Object Heap is logically collected with generation two and is not compacted by default because moving large objects can be expensive. Applications can request a one-time LOH compaction through GCSettings when fragmentation warrants it.

text: What must generally be true for a collectible AssemblyLoadContext to become unloadable?
options: The context must be collectible, and no live references may remain to its assemblies, types, delegates, or loaded objects.
The context must contain only strong-named assemblies, and every loaded type must implement IDisposable before unloading.
The context must be unloaded from the default domain, and all assemblies must first be copied into a separate process.
The context must disable reflection, and its assemblies must use identical versions of every dependency loaded by the host.
explanation: A collectible AssemblyLoadContext can unload only when the runtime can no longer reach the context or objects associated with it. Strong references from host code, static fields, threads, delegates, or unresolved execution paths can keep it alive.

text: Which approach is most appropriate for many long-lived pinned buffers in current .NET implementations?
options: Allocate them on the pinned object heap so pinning does not fragment the ordinary movable managed heaps.
Pin ordinary small objects indefinitely because the garbage collector relocates pinned objects more efficiently over time.
Store every buffer inside a managed array and pin only its metadata so the contained elements remain movable.
Use stackalloc for persistent buffers because stack memory is automatically promoted when asynchronous work continues.
explanation: The pinned object heap is designed for objects that must remain pinned and helps avoid fragmentation in the normal generations. It does not make objects movable, so it should still be reserved for buffers whose lifetime and pinning requirements justify the tradeoff.

text: Which limitation is most relevant when migrating reflection-heavy code to .NET Native AOT?
options: Unbounded runtime code generation and metadata-dependent reflection may require source generation or explicit preservation.
Native AOT prohibits generics entirely, so all generic libraries must be rewritten using non-generic interfaces.
Native AOT requires every managed allocation to use stack memory, preventing ordinary object-oriented application design.
Native AOT removes asynchronous I/O support, so applications must replace Tasks with dedicated operating-system threads.
explanation: Native AOT performs closed-world analysis and may not include metadata or dynamically generated code that cannot be discovered statically. Reflection-heavy paths often need source generators, RD.XML-style preservation, or explicit code registration.

text: For a traditional C# lock whose operand is an ordinary reference-typed object, what does the compiler-level behavior fundamentally provide?
options: It uses Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit with exception-safe release, establishing mutual exclusion for that object.
It creates a new mutex for every entry, guaranteeing isolation even when different references contain equal values.
It performs an optimistic transaction and retries the body automatically when another thread changes shared state.
It uses a reader-writer protocol that allows concurrent readers while excluding writers from the protected region.
explanation: The traditional lock statement is implemented using monitor acquisition and release, with release placed in a finally-like path to handle exceptions. Mutual exclusion applies to threads using the same lock identity, not merely equal object contents.

text: Which configuration provides backpressure when producers outpace consumers using System.Threading.Channels?
options: Use a bounded channel with a full-mode policy of Wait so writes asynchronously wait for available capacity.
Use an unbounded channel with a full-mode policy of DropOldest so memory remains bounded during sustained overload.
Use a bounded channel with a full-mode policy of DropWrite so every producer naturally waits for consumer progress.
Use an unbounded channel with SingleWriter enabled so the channel automatically limits queued items under load.
explanation: A bounded channel limits queued items, and the Wait full mode causes asynchronous writers to pause until capacity becomes available. Drop modes discard data instead, while unbounded channels do not impose a memory-based queue limit.

text: What guarantee does ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue>.GetOrAdd provide about its value factory under contention?
options: The factory may run multiple times concurrently, but only one resulting value is published for the requested key.
The factory runs exactly once per key, because the dictionary holds its internal lock while evaluating the factory.
The factory runs only after the key is inserted, allowing every concurrent caller to observe its own produced value.
The factory is never invoked concurrently, although a previously published value may still be replaced by a later factory result.
explanation: GetOrAdd coordinates publication of the dictionary entry but does not guarantee single execution of the value factory. The factory can run outside the relevant synchronization, so it should be side-effect-free or tolerate duplicate evaluation.

text: In Oak, which index design best supports a query combining full-text search, a path restriction, and ordering by a property?
options: Use a Lucene index with included paths, evaluated path restrictions, and an ordered property rule.
Use only a property index, because it handles full-text predicates and sorting without additional configuration.
Use a node type index, because it automatically combines descendant filtering, full-text matching, and ordering.
Use repository traversal, because Oak optimizes path restrictions and sorting more reliably than custom indexes.
explanation: A Lucene index can support full-text predicates, path restrictions, and ordered properties when those capabilities are explicitly configured. Included paths also reduce index scope and maintenance cost.

text: What is the primary effect of setting statfileslevel on an AEM Dispatcher farm?
options: It controls where invalidation marker files are created, limiting the breadth of cache invalidation.
It determines how long every cached response remains valid before Dispatcher removes it automatically.
It enables stale-while-revalidate behavior, allowing cached responses to refresh asynchronously after expiration.
It changes the cache key to include repository paths, preventing collisions between similar requested URLs.
explanation: statfileslevel controls the directory depth at which .stat files are placed during invalidation. Dispatcher compares cached file timestamps with those markers rather than using the setting as a response TTL.

text: In AEM as a Cloud Service, what happens when application code attempts to write directly under an immutable repository area?
options: The write is rejected because immutable areas such as /apps are supplied through the deployment pipeline.
The write succeeds temporarily but is discarded only when the next author or publish pod is restarted.
The write is persisted on the local container and replicated later through the content distribution service.
The write is accepted on author but blocked on publish, allowing repository customization during development.
explanation: AEM as a Cloud Service separates immutable application code from mutable content. Code under areas such as /apps must be deployed through Cloud Manager, while runtime writes belong in supported mutable locations.

text: Which approach is appropriate when an OSGi service needs to access repository content using a service identity?
options: Obtain a service resource resolver with a mapped subservice name, use it briefly, and close it explicitly.
Obtain an administrative resolver from the factory, cache it in the component, and reuse it for efficiency.
Use the request resolver from an unrelated HTTP request, because its permissions reflect the active application user.
Create a system session through JCR APIs, retain it globally, and avoid repeated authentication overhead.
explanation: A service should use ResourceResolverFactory.getServiceResourceResolver with a configured service-user mapping and close the resolver after use. Administrative sessions, global sessions, and unrelated request resolvers create security and lifecycle problems.

text: What is the key behavior of a Multi Site Manager live copy when inheritance remains enabled for a component property?
options: Rollout can update the inherited property from the blueprint, while a local override prevents that specific update.
Rollout always overwrites the property, because inheritance affects structure but never component values.
The live copy permanently detaches from the blueprint after its first rollout, regardless of local modifications.
The property is synchronized only when an author manually copies the entire page into the live-copy location.
explanation: Inherited properties can be updated during rollout from the blueprint. A local modification typically creates an exception or cancellation of inheritance for that property, depending on the MSM action and configuration.

text: What is the expected effect of setting reindex=true on an Oak index definition?
options: Oak schedules a rebuild of that index, and queries may experience altered performance until asynchronous indexing completes.
Oak immediately deletes the index and permanently falls back to traversal until an administrator recreates its definition.
Oak changes only future index entries, leaving existing content unindexed until each affected node is edited again.
Oak synchronously rebuilds the index during the configuration request, blocking repository writes until completion.
explanation: The reindex flag requests a rebuild, usually performed by Oak's asynchronous indexing process. Reindexing can consume substantial resources and temporarily affect query performance, especially for large repositories.

text: Which strategy is generally preferred for high-volume AEM Content Fragment GraphQL traffic behind Dispatcher?
options: Use persisted GraphQL queries over GET, cache approved responses, and invalidate them through content-aware mechanisms.
Send arbitrary POST queries from clients, because Dispatcher caches POST bodies more safely than persisted GET requests.
Expose unrestricted schema queries and rely on browser caching, avoiding server-side cache invalidation complexity.
Render every fragment through HTL on publish, because GraphQL responses cannot be cached at the edge.
explanation: Persisted queries constrain query shape and permit cacheable GET requests, making them suitable for Dispatcher and CDN caching. Cache invalidation still needs to reflect changes to the referenced content.

text: Which statement correctly describes the preferred publication mechanism in AEM as a Cloud Service?
options: Content is distributed through the cloud content distribution service rather than customer-managed traditional replication agents.
Authors configure classic replication agents on publish instances, with transport credentials stored in repository content.
Each publish pod pulls author changes on a schedule, using reverse replication queues for all activated content.
The deployment pipeline replicates authored pages, so content activation is performed by application releases instead.
explanation: AEM as a Cloud Service uses the cloud content distribution architecture for author-to-publish content movement. Customers do not manage the traditional replication-agent topology used in many on-premises deployments.

text: What is a core benefit of cloud computing is the best choice?
options: On-demand scalable resources
Mandatory physical ownership
No networking
No automation
explanation: Cloud platforms provide elastic, on-demand infrastructure and services.

text: For reliable asynchronous processing triggered by repository changes, which AEM design is usually the strongest choice?
options: Convert the event into an idempotent Sling Job, allowing retries, persistence, and controlled processing across instances.
Perform all work directly in the event handler, because event delivery guarantees completion before the callback returns.
Store a static flag in component memory, because local state prevents duplicate processing across clustered publish instances.
Create a scheduled polling thread in each bundle, because independent polling avoids repository event ordering concerns.
explanation: Sling Jobs provide persisted, retryable asynchronous processing with queue and topology controls. Handlers should still be idempotent because retries and redelivery can occur.

text: Which Sling Models practice best improves maintainability and runtime behavior in a performance-sensitive component?
options: Use specific injectors such as @ValueMapValue and @OSGiService, with validation and optionality declared explicitly.
Use broad @Inject on every field, because Sling automatically selects the fastest injector for each adaptable object.
Resolve services manually from a static service registry, because annotations add reflection overhead during every request.
Inject the entire request and resource tree into each model, because downstream getters can then avoid repeated adaptations.
explanation: Specific injector annotations make dependencies explicit, reduce unintended injector searches, and clarify required versus optional values. Broad injection can introduce ambiguity, hidden coupling, and unnecessary resolution work.

text: Which AWS Region concept provides fault isolation within a Region?
options: Edge Location
Availability Zone (AZ)
Local Zone
Wavelength Zone
explanation: Each Region has 3+ Availability Zones (isolated data centers with independent power/cooling/network). Use Multi-AZ for high

text: You need to store 10 TB of static website images with millisecond access and 99.99% availability at lowest cost. Which S3 storage class is MOST appropriate for frequently accessed data?
options: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Standard
S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
explanation: For frequently accessed: S3 Standard is standard answer. In 2024+ best practice, S3 Intelligent-Tiering is often

text: Which EC2 pricing option gives you up to 72% discount for a 1 or 3-year commitment for steady-state workloads?
options: On-Demand
Spot Instances
Reserved Instances / Savings Plans
Dedicated Hosts
explanation: Reserved Instances and Compute Savings Plans provide up to 72% discount. Spot up to 90% but interruptible.

text: Which service provides a virtual firewall at the subnet level in a VPC?
options: Security Group
Network ACL (NACL)
AWS WAF
AWS Shield
explanation: NACL is stateless, operates at subnet level. Security Group is stateful, at instance/ENI level.

text: A company needs to run a web server that can be stopped and started without losing its root volume data. Which storage should be used for the root volume?
options: Instance Store (Ephemeral)
Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) - e.g., gp3 volume
S3
EFS

text: Go memory model and atomics: Why was atomic.Pointer[T] introduced in Go 1.19 and when to use sync/atomic vs mutex?

text: What is the difference between context.WithValue misuse vs proper use? Which causes memory leak in 2024+?

WithValue always leaks

text: Go 1.20+ introduced arena experiment and improved GC. How does Pacer and GOGC work since Go 1.19?

GC runs every second

No pacer **Answer: B **Explanation:** GC pacer redesigned in Go 1.19 to minimize assist time and pacing errors. GOGC=100 means heap can grow 100% before GC. Since Go 1.19, GOMEMLIMIT caps application memory, triggering GC more aggressively to stay within limit.

text: Subtle for range over integer added in Go 1.22 - and performance of defer in loop?

Defer in loop executes each iteration

Range over int panics **Answer: B **Explanation:** Go 1.22 added integer range: for i := range 10 equals 0..9, and for range 10 repeats 10 times. Defer inside loops is classic perf bug: defers don't run per iteration, they accumulate and run at return, holding resources longer than intended.

text: How does runtime.SetFinalizer interact with finalizers, and what is the pattern for io.Closer wrapper since Go 1.21 log/slog and context.AfterFunc?

Finalizer replaces defer

Go discourages them. Go 1.21 added context.AfterFunc and Go 1.23 improved slog resource cleanup; newer AddCleanup proposal formalizes explicit cleanup attachment.
explanation: Finalizers vs AfterFunc

Mutex only

explanation: Angular 17+ introduced new @for block; legacy *ngFor still valid.

text: How do you handle a computed property with a setter in Vue 3 Composition API?
options: Computed values are permanently read-only in the Composition API, so assigning a setter function inside computed() causes a compilation error and cannot update dependencies
const fullName = computed({ get: () => first.value + ' ' + last.value, set: (val) => { [first.value, last.value] = val.split(' ') } })
Use @computed set with a handler that receives the assigned value and splits it into first and last names before updating the underlying refs
Use watch only to observe first and last, then derive fullName from the watcher callback; computed() cannot define get and set functions together in Vue 3
explanation: computed can take object with get/set for writable computed.

text: Compare dependency injection in Vue vs Angular.
options: Both frameworks use essentially the same constructor-injected global container, with Vue services registered as providers and Angular relying mainly on composables for component-scoped dependencies

Angular has hierarchical, constructor-based DI container core to framework; Vue has Provide/Inject (provide() / inject()) which is simpler and not hierarchical in the same way, often supplemented by Pinia/composables
Vue provides no dependency-injection mechanism, so every dependency must be imported directly or placed in Pinia; Angular alone offers provide(), inject(), and hierarchical resolution
Angular DI is limited to injectable service classes created by the CLI, while Vue uses a mandatory constructor container that resolves components, directives, and composables automatically
explanation: Angular DI is central & hierarchical; Vue provide/inject is simpler.

text: In Vue 3, what is Pinia and why did it replace Vuex as official recommendation in 2022?

Pinia is the intuitive, type-safe, Composition API-friendly store with lighter API, no mutations, devtools support, and modular stores by design
Pinia is an Angular state-management adapter that exposes RxJS stores to Vue applications, allowing Angular services and dependency injection to be reused directly
Vuex remains the official Vue recommendation, while Pinia is a deprecated experimental store whose API is preserved only for migrating older Vuex projects
explanation: Pinia became official in Feb 2022, Vuex 4 in maintenance. Pinia works better with TS and Composition API.

text: How does Vue Router handle lazy loading vs Angular Router lazy loading (2024+)?

Both Vue Router and Angular Router use the same route configuration syntax, with component: () => import(...) for every lazy route and no framework-specific distinction between loading a component and loading child routes
Neither router supports native lazy loading in current versions; applications must import every view and route module eagerly, then hide unused components until navigation occurs
Vue Router uses Angular's loadChildren configuration for asynchronous views, while Angular Router loads Vue-style component functions directly and does not provide a separate loadComponent option
explanation: Both support dynamic import() for code splitting; Angular distinguishes loadComponent vs loadChildren.

explanation: Vapor mode announced 2023, progress in 2024-2025, alternative compile target for performance.

text: Architecturally, how would you design micro-frontends that need to mix Vue and Angular components?
options: Vue and Angular components cannot share a browser page because their renderers require one framework-owned component tree; the reliable architecture is to rewrite every feature in the framework used by the shell and expose only framework-native modules through the build system.

Use Module Federation (Webpack 5 / Vite plugin), Web Components (Angular Elements createCustomElement, Vue defineCustomElement), or single-spa, with shared dependency strategy and framework-agnostic design system. Isolate change detection zones and lifecycle.

The application should be rewritten entirely in one framework before deployment, because Module Federation and single-spa can coordinate only modules produced by the same compiler; Web Components cannot safely bridge Angular dependency injection with Vue component lifecycles.

Use iframes for every cross-framework feature so each application has an isolated document, runtime, and deployment boundary; custom elements, Module Federation, single-spa, and shared framework-agnostic design-system packages should be avoided because they introduce lifecycle conflicts.
explanation: Modern micro-frontend architectures enable framework interop via standards.

text: What is defineProps and defineEmits in Vue 3 <script setup>?
options: Runtime APIs imported from vue-router that register navigation properties and event handlers for a component, using route metadata to infer which values may be passed into or emitted from the view
Compiler macros (no import needed) to declare props and emits with type-based or runtime declaration, enabling type inference
Macros that must be explicitly imported from 'vue' before they can declare component inputs and outputs, with the import also enabling compiler-generated runtime validation and type inference
Options API helpers intended for data and methods objects, not <script setup>; they require a separate component configuration and cannot declare typed props or emitted events in setup code
explanation: Compiler macros are resolved at compile time, no explicit import required.

text: In Angular 17-18, what is Zoneless change detection and how do Signals enable it?
options: Removing zone.js by using provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection() - Signals can notify Angular of changes directly without zone.js patching async APIs, reducing bundle size and improving performance

Zone.js must always remain enabled for Angular applications because it patches browser APIs to discover asynchronous work; Signals can optimize rendering inside that zone but cannot notify Angular independently

Zoneless change detection means Angular stops checking templates after initialization, so updates from events, HTTP requests, and Signals are not rendered unless the application manually calls detectChanges() everywhere

Signals disable Angular's change-detection mechanism by isolating state from the component tree; enabling them requires Zone.js to perform all scheduling and prevents Angular from reacting directly to signal writes
explanation: Zoneless is experimental but key to Angular's future, enabled by signals. Reduces bundle by ~10kb.

Components written in Rust that compile to WebAssembly on the server, replacing JavaScript components in production builds
Old name for class components that React keeps for compatibility, with lifecycle methods executed on the server by default

text: Consider this code: const [state, formAction] = useActionState(actionFn, initialState). What does this React 19 hook do?

Manages form action state: takes an action function and initial state, returns current state and callable action, integrates with useFormStatus for pending/error handling
Only works with Redux, where it creates a store-bound action and returns the reducer state without integrating with React form status
Creates animation state by combining a timing function with initial values, returning transition progress and controls for starting or stopping playback
explanation: useActionState (renamed from useFormState) is React 19 core for actions.

text: How does useDeferredValue differ from useTransition?
options: useDeferredValue schedules the state update itself for later, while useTransition immediately replaces the rendered value; neither affects update priority or urgency
useDeferredValue defers the *value* (useful for debouncing search input rendering), while useTransition defers the *state update*. Both mark updates as non-urgent
useDeferredValue debounces and cancels state updates internally, while useTransition delays only network requests; both require an explicit timeout configuration
useDeferredValue and useTransition are interchangeable APIs, except useDeferredValue is intended for event handlers and useTransition is restricted to rendering components
explanation: DeferredValue = value-based defer, Transition = update-based control.

text: What does this React 19 code do? const data = use(fetchPromise)?

use(fetchPromise) starts the request and returns its resolved data synchronously during the same render, without suspending or requiring a Suspense boundary
The use() API is restricted to useEffect callbacks and server actions, where it unwraps fetch results but cannot be called during component rendering or read Context
explanation: use() is React 19's new hook that can be called conditionally and unwraps promises/contexts.

text: How does Git's 3-way merge algorithm work, what are merge.ours, theirs, union, and recursive vs ort strategy? Give config to auto-resolve lockfiles.
options: 3-way uses common ancestor base + ours + theirs to compute changes. ort (Ostensibly Recursive's Twin) is default since Git 2.33, faster than recursive. Drivers: -X ours keeps our side, -X theirs keeps theirs. For lockfiles you can set echo 'package-lock.json merge=binary' >> .gitattributes or custom driver, but better set merge=ours or union driver; e.g., git config merge.unity.driver - is anti-pattern, use .gitattributes: pnpm-lock.yaml merge=binary

A 3-way merge compares the two branch tips and treats the common ancestor as a historical reference rather than as an input for calculating independent edits. The ours, theirs, and union options are global strategies that cannot be selected per path, recursive remains the preferred implementation in modern Git, and -X ours or -X theirs resolves every conflict in favor of one complete branch. Lockfiles should therefore be resolved by checking out the desired version after the merge rather than by configuring an attribute or custom driver.

Git’s merge engine performs a two-way comparison between the current and incoming branch and uses the common ancestor only to display additional conflict context. The ours, theirs, and union names refer to complete repository merge strategies, not file-level drivers, while .gitattributes can control line endings but cannot select binary or union behavior. Consequently, package lockfiles must be edited manually or replaced with a branch copy, and -X ours or -X theirs cannot be limited to those files.

The recursive strategy is still Git’s current default because ort was an experimental optimization that was removed after Git 2.33; both strategies compare only the two branch tips and do not calculate changes from a merge base. Since lockfiles are always treated as ordinary text, configure rerere to remember a previous manual resolution, increase merge conflict verbosity, and accept that .gitattributes cannot assign a path-specific merge driver or automatically choose a lockfile side.
explanation: 3-way merge with ort strategy and merge drivers

text: In Elasticsearch Query DSL, why would you use a bool query with filter clause instead of must when you don't need scoring?

A Kibana security role for combining permissions from multiple spaces, with the reciprocal term describing how privileges are inherited; administrators create it in Stack Management and reference it from role mappings for hybrid dashboards

A snapshot repository format that stores reciprocal copies of shard metadata and document segments for recovery, allowing Elasticsearch to fuse versions from several repositories; it is selected in the snapshot lifecycle policy rather than during search

text: How does cross-cluster search (CCS) differ from cross-cluster replication (CCR)?

It is an Angular-specific replacement for ngModel that manages form fields and validation, but does not represent general component state or participate in change detection
It is a styling API for declaring reactive CSS variables and theme effects, intended for component appearance rather than state management or template updates
explanation: Signals introduced in Angular 16 as developer preview, stable in 17, enhance reactivity and future zoneless change detection.

text: In Angular, how do you implement SSR and hydration as of Angular 17-18?
options: Angular has no built-in SSR or hydration support in versions 17 and 18; applications must render HTML entirely in the browser, or adopt a separate Node server and community hydration library.

ng add @angular/ssr, enables server.ts with provideClientHydration() (and with withEventReplay() in Angular 18), and hydration reuses server-rendered DOM instead of re-rendering on client to avoid flickering

SSR is available only through third-party Angular Universal integrations, which generate static HTML but leave client-side DOM reconciliation, event attachment, and transfer state entirely to application code.

Hydration happens automatically after adding SSR: Angular always reuses server-rendered nodes without provideClientHydration(), event replay configuration, server setup, or any explicit client bootstrap changes.
explanation: Angular SSR improved drastically in v17-18, hydration with event replay is major feature.

text: Performance: Compare Vue's Virtual DOM optimization (Block & PatchFlag) vs Angular's new control flow and deferred loading.
options: Vue and Angular use essentially the same optimization mechanism: both maintain a complete virtual DOM tree, compare every node during updates, and defer JavaScript only through ordinary lazy-loaded routes rather than compiler-level block analysis.

Vue 3 compiler flags dynamic nodes with PatchFlag and creates Blocks to skip static subtrees, reducing diff cost. Angular 17+ uses new control flow that generates more efficient instructions and @defer to reduce initial bundle and JS execution.

Vue's compiler performs no meaningful runtime optimization because every component update walks the entire virtual DOM tree; PatchFlag and Block metadata are limited to development diagnostics and do not affect production diffing.

Angular still relies on the legacy View Engine for template compilation and change detection, so its newer control-flow syntax is cosmetic and @defer cannot split dependencies or reduce initial JavaScript execution.
explanation: Both frameworks heavily optimized compiler output for runtime performance.

text: Testing: What are the recommended testing utilities in 2024-2026 for Vue and Angular?
options: Vue: Vue Test Utils + Vitest (Vite-native, fast), Angular: TestBed + Karma replaced by Vitest/Jest via jest-preset-angular or new experimental Vitest support, and Angular Testing Library; For E2E both recommend Playwright/Cypress

The recommended approach is manual browser testing for Vue and Angular, supplemented by production smoke tests; framework-specific unit-test utilities are discouraged because component behavior should be validated only through full user workflows.
Vue applications are tested with Angular's TestBed and Jasmine because Vue Test Utils targets legacy Vue versions; Vitest cannot mount components or integrate with Vite-based Vue projects.

Angular applications use Vue Test Utils for component mounting and Vue's reactivity assertions, while Angular-specific TestBed and Angular Testing Library are intended only for old View Engine projects.
explanation: Vitest dominance for Vue via Vite, Angular transitioning away from Karma (deprecated) in 2024.

text: In Angular 17+, what is the purpose of defer block?
options: A rendering mode that eagerly loads and displays every block during initial navigation, ensuring deferred content is compiled before the application becomes interactive
Deferrable views: @defer { ... } lazily loads and renders content based on triggers (viewport, idle, interaction, hover, timer), improving performance
A build-time compiler option that postpones TypeScript compilation until a user visits the associated route, without changing when the template renders
A legacy template feature removed in Angular 17, retained only for compatibility with applications that still use older structural directives
explanation: @defer is major performance feature in Angular 17 for lazy rendering.

text: In Angular, what is the difference between Observable and Signal as of Angular 17-18?
options: Observable and Signal are two interchangeable names for the same RxJS abstraction: both represent asynchronous event streams, use pipeable operators, and require subscriptions before Angular can observe changes; neither is intended for ordinary synchronous state

Observable is async stream (RxJS) great for events, HTTP streams, operators; Signal is synchronous reactive value with automatic dependency tracking, great for local component state. Signals can be created from observables via toSignal(), and vice versa via toObservable().

Observable is a synchronous reactive value that always contains the latest result, while Signal is an asynchronous RxJS stream for events and HTTP requests; Signals require subscriptions and are converted with subscribeToSignal()

Observables were removed from Angular 18 in favor of Signals, so HTTP clients, event streams, and RxJS operators must be rewritten as synchronous signal values; toSignal() and toObservable() are obsolete compatibility helpers
explanation: Interop functions in @angular/core/rxjs-interop bridge them.

text: In Angular, what is Control Flow new syntax @if, @for, @switch vs legacy *ngIf, *ngFor, *ngSwitch?
options: A cosmetic renaming of the legacy structural directives: @if, @for, and @switch still require CommonModule, create embedded views through the same directive machinery, and provide no additional @empty or @else block support
New built-in control flow (Angular 17+) has better type narrowing, no need for CommonModule, better performance (no structural directive overhead), and supports @empty, @else blocks directly

The legacy *ngIf and *ngFor implementation is generally faster because it is compiled directly by the browser, whereas the new syntax adds runtime parsing and requires extra structural directive instances for each block

The new control-flow syntax is available only inside NgModule-declared components and requires importing a control-flow module; standalone components must continue using *ngIf, *ngFor, and *ngSwitch instead
explanation: New control flow is recommended from Angular 17+ docs, improved DX.

text: In Vue 3.4+ (2024), what major reactivity improvement was introduced with defineModel()?
options: defineModel() was removed before the stable Vue 3.4 release because automatic component binding caused ambiguous event names; current components must continue declaring a modelValue prop and update:modelValue emit manually

defineModel() is a compiler macro that simplifies two-way binding for component v-model, replacing manual prop + emit pattern: const model = defineModel() returns a ref linked to prop and emits update:modelValue automatically
defineModel() is a compiler macro dedicated to styling component elements and synchronizing CSS custom properties through v-model; it does not create refs or participate in parent-child data binding

defineModel() replaces ref() throughout Vue applications by creating ordinary reactive state for local variables, but it does not declare props, emit update:modelValue events, or provide any special support for component v-model
explanation: defineModel() stable in Vue 3.4 (Jan 2024) greatly simplifies custom v-model components.

useLayoutEffect is intended only for server components, where it replaces useEffect during server rendering and hydration
useEffect was deprecated in React 19, so new components should use useLayoutEffect for all subscriptions and DOM work
explanation: useLayoutEffect blocks paint; use for measurements. useEffect is non-blocking.

forwardRef is required for all components now, including ordinary function components, because ref remains a special value that cannot be received as a regular prop

explanation: React 19 simplifies ref handling: ref is prop. forwardRef remains for compat but deprecated pattern.

text: What is git reflog and when would you use it?

A log of all moves of HEAD in local repo (commits, resets, rebases, merges) - crucial for recovering lost commits after reset --hard or deleted branches
A GitHub-hosted audit history of every repository event, including web edits, permission changes, and actions performed by collaborators
The same history shown by git log, listing only reachable commits and their messages while omitting ref updates, resets, and rebases

text: What does this GitHub Pull Request Merge Strategy do: "Squash and merge"?

Combines all PR commits into a single commit on base branch, producing linear history but losing granular PR commit history
Replays each PR commit onto the latest base branch in order, preserving separate commits and producing a rewritten linear history
Closes the pull request without applying its changes, leaving the base branch unchanged and retaining the branch for later review

text: What does .gitignore do, and where should you place a file named secrets.env to never track it?

It encrypts matching files before they are stored; place secrets.env in a .gitencrypt file at the repository root to enable that protection
It makes matching files commit more efficiently; place secrets.env in .gitinclude so Git will automatically omit it from the index

text: On GitHub, what is the difference between a Pull Request and an Issue?

text: Consider you accidentally ran git reset --hard HEAD~3 and lost 3 commits. They are not pushed. How to recover most reliably?

Run git clean -fd and git gc to clear the reset state, then recreate the three missing commits from the working tree
Use git reflog to find the hash before reset, then git reset --hard <hash> or git branch recovery <hash>
Create a new commit on the current branch and push it, since GitHub will reconstruct unreachable commits from the branch update

text: What are Git Submodules vs Git Subtree (2024-2026 best practice)?

Submodules link a specific commit of another repo inside parent (keeps separate history but complex), Subtree merges external repo code into parent repo history (simpler for contributors)
Submodules merge external commits into the parent history for simple updates, while Subtree keeps a separate repository link and records only the selected external commit
Submodules and Subtree both maintain independent histories outside the parent, differing only in whether updates use tags or branch names
explanation: 2024-2026: Many teams prefer Subtree or package manager over Submodules due to UX complexity. Monorepo tools often replace both.

text: You need to temporarily save your current changes without committing, then switch branches to hotfix, then return. Which sequence works and preserves untracked files too?

text: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase when integrating feature into main, and when should you avoid rebase?

Merge creates a linear sequence by copying feature commits onto main, while rebase adds a merge commit joining both histories. Avoid merge on public branches because it permanently rewrites their commit IDs.

Rebase permanently deletes the feature branch commits after applying their file changes, whereas merge preserves only the final snapshot. Avoid rebase only when the feature contains uncommitted files.
explanation: Merge preserves history vs rebase rewrites linear

text: Your repo has a large video.mp4 (400MB) accidentally committed. GitHub push fails. How do you remove it from history and prevent future large files for 2024-2026 best practice?

Use git filter-repo or git filter-branch / BFG to rewrite history removing the file, add it to .gitignore, and use Git LFS for large files going forward, then force push with team coordination
Add video.mp4 to .gitignore and run git clean -fd, then create a new commit and push; GitHub automatically purges the previously uploaded blob when the path becomes ignored.

Run git large-file remove video.mp4 --rewrite, commit the generated metadata, add the path to .gitignore, and push; the command converts the existing object to LFS without requiring rewritten remote history.
explanation: filter-repo + .gitignore + Git LFS

text: What does git reset --soft HEAD~1, --mixed (default), and --hard do differently?

--soft removes the commit and deletes its changes from the working tree, --mixed keeps the commit but stages all edits, and --hard only unstages files while preserving their contents for later recovery.
All three modes create a revert commit instead of moving HEAD: --soft affects only the message, --mixed affects the index, and --hard affects the remote branch after the next push.
--soft and --mixed both discard the selected commit and its file changes, while --hard preserves the working tree but removes only the index entries; none of them alter HEAD.
explanation: --soft vs --mixed vs --hard scope

text: What is GitHub's Pull Request workflow with forks and what does gh CLI do to streamline it?
options: Fork -> clone fork -> branch -> commit -> push to fork -> open PR via GitHub UI or gh pr create, then review, CI, and gh pr merge or squash merge. gh authenticates and automates PR creation from terminal.

Clone the upstream repository, create a branch, commit changes, and push directly to upstream before running gh pr create. Forks are only needed for private repositories, while gh pr merge sends the patch by email for review.

Forking copies only the current working tree, so clone the fork, create commits locally, and upload them with FTP. The gh CLI then converts the uploaded files into a pull request without requiring GitHub authentication.

Open a PR from the upstream main branch to the fork, then use gh pr sync to transfer commits back to the original repository. Reviews and CI run locally, while gh pr merge merely updates the fork's branch pointer.
explanation: Fork-based PR + gh CLI

text: Your team uses Conventional Commits and wants to auto-generate changelog and semantic versioning. A feature branch has 30 messy commits that must be cleaned into 3 logical commits before PR merge to main. options: Use git rebase -i main to squash/fixup 30 into 3, keep meaningful commit messages like feat: and fix:, force push to feature branch with --force-with-lease, open PR, then use Squash or Rebase merge strategy according to repo policy, with protected main requiring linear history

Use git merge --no-ff main to combine the entire feature branch, leave all 30 original commits visible for auditability, and rely on the pull request's default merge commit; do not rewrite the branch because preserving every intermediate commit is required for Conventional Commits or semantic-release

Delete the feature branch's 30 commits from the server, create three new commits directly from the final working tree, push the replacement branch, and let the PR use a normal merge without coordinating with authors or preserving the original commit metadata

text: Explain Git internal objects: blob, tree, commit, tag, and how HEAD, index, reflog, and .git/refs work. How would you recover a commit deleted by git reset --hard 2 days ago?
options: Blob stores file content, tree maps names to blobs/trees, commit points to tree + parents + metadata, annotated tag is object. HEAD is ref to current branch, index is staging area. Recover via git reflog which logs HEAD moves, find SHA, then git branch recovery <SHA> or git checkout

Git stores each version as a complete copy of every file in the repository, while branches and tags duplicate those files in separate directories; HEAD is the current file snapshot and the index is an optional cache, so object relationships are not needed for recovery

A hard reset permanently erases the abandoned commits and their objects immediately, so a commit deleted two days ago cannot be recovered unless another clone or remote branch still contains it; reflog only records successful pushes and cannot restore local history

Open the repository's GitHub page, select the deleted commit from the hosting service's recycle bin, and restore it as a new branch; GitHub retains every reset object indefinitely and provides the authoritative recovery mechanism instead of local reflogs or dangling objects
explanation: Objects blob/tree/commit/tag + HEAD/index/reflog

text: You have a large repo (5GB history). git clone is slow for CI. How do you optimize with partial clone, shallow clone, sparse-checkout, and GitHub's new features in 2024-2026?

Download the repository as a ZIP archive from GitHub for each CI run and unpack the entire source tree, then cache the archive between jobs; this removes Git negotiation but still retrieves the complete snapshot and cannot selectively fetch missing blobs or use sparse indexes

text: What is the result of String vs &str?

String and &str are equivalent representations, differing only in syntax and the functions used to construct them

text: You accidentally pushed secrets (AWS key AKIA...) to public GitHub repo main history 5 commits ago. GitHub push protection didn't block because bypass. Detail immediate mitigation steps including history rewrite, credential revocation, and GitHub security workflow 2024-2026.
options: Immediately revoke/rotate leaked key in AWS IAM, enable GitHub Secret Scanning alert, use git filter-repo or BFG to purge file from all history, force push with --force-with-lease after team warning, notify stakeholders, open GitHub Security advisory, add trufflehog/gitleaks pre-commit hook, enable push protection that blocks even admins

A routine pull request review and ordinary branch protection are sufficient, with no need for filter-repo, BFG, force-pushing, scanning alerts, or stakeholder notification.

Repository access controls will invalidate the key and GitHub will remove its public copies when visibility is restored. After a waiting period, make the repository public again; no IAM rotation, history rewrite, security advisory, secret-scanning configuration, or push-protection change is required.

text: Explain the nuance of Private Google Access vs Private Service Connect vs Private Services Access (PSA) vs Serverless VPC Access.
options: Private Google Access: VM in private subnet accesses Google APIs via private IP; PSA: allocates IP range in your VPC for managed services like Cloud SQL/Redis via VPC peering; Private Service Connect: consumer endpoint to producer services (service-oriented, no peering, supports consumer control); Serverless VPC Access Connector: legacy way for serverless (Cloud Run/Functions/App Engine) to connect to VPC, now largely replaced by direct VPC egress

Use Private Google Access mainly as an on-premises connectivity feature that lets data centers reach Google APIs through private addresses; configure Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect as its required transport, and reserve Private Services Access and Private Service Connect for VM-to-VM communication inside the VPC rather than managed-service or producer-consumer connectivity
explanation: This is classic confusion: PGA is for private subnet VMs -> Google APIs; PSA is peering-based private

text: You are managing 1000+ resources. terraform plan is slow. Which advanced optimization is valid as of Terraform 1.8+?

Delete or move the Terraform state file before running plan so Terraform does not need to compare existing objects, then allow apply to reconstruct state from provider queries while preserving the same resource addresses; this removes refresh overhead and keeps the infrastructure unchanged without requiring smaller state files, modules, or separate stacks

Run terraform plan only during weekend maintenance windows and permit production changes to accumulate between planning cycles, reducing the number of refresh and graph-building operations without altering provider behavior; rely on a larger final plan and emergency review rather than using parallelism, stack decomposition, refresh controls, or provider caching

Increase count or for_each on large resources so Terraform can group more instances into each graph operation, reducing provider API calls and causing repeated resources to be evaluated as one optimized unit; use larger collections and shared arguments to compress the dependency graph instead of separating state or tuning refresh and provider execution

text: A Jenkins controller shows high memory and CPS (Continuation Passing Style) issues with complex pipelines. What is the 2024-2026 best practice fix?
options: Increase the controller JVM heap substantially, retain the monolithic pipeline and its large Groovy loops, and tune garbage collection for longer pauses so CPS can serialize larger continuation graphs; keep computation inside the Jenkinsfile and use heap growth as the primary remedy for memory retention, checkpoint size, and pipeline responsiveness

Break pipeline into smaller stages, avoid excessive Groovy loops inside pipeline DSL, use @NonCPS only for pure non-pipeline logic, move heavy computation outside pipeline or into shared library src/ steps, and use Pipeline Graph View instead of Blue Ocean

Schedule a controller restart every night, terminate or discard running pipeline state, and rely on a fresh JVM to clear continuations, serialized programs, and retained objects; leave the complex CPS-heavy Jenkinsfile unchanged and treat regular process recycling as the supported long-term solution for controller memory pressure

Standardize every workload on Scripted Pipeline because unrestricted Groovy execution is assumed to avoid CPS transformation and serialization overhead; perform database queries, loops, and large computations directly on the controller, relying on the alternate syntax to eliminate continuation retention without externalizing work or separating shared-library logic
explanation: CPS serialization issues happen when non-serializable objects or large loops inside DSL; fix by extracting logic, using shared lib src/,

text: How do you implement a custom directive in Vue 3 vs Angular (advanced)?
options: Vue: app.directive('focus', { mounted(el) { el.focus() } }) with lifecycle hooks (created, mounted, updated, unmounted). Angular: @Directive({ selector: '[appHighlight]', standalone: true }) class with HostListener, ElementRef, etc.

Vue and Angular expose essentially the same directive API: register a directive by name, supply matching created, mounted, updated, and destroyed callbacks, and use a shared ElementRef-style abstraction to manipulate the host element in either framework.

Directives are an Angular-only feature; Vue 3 uses components and composables instead, so behavior such as autofocus must be implemented through a component wrapper, a composable, or an ordinary mounted lifecycle hook rather than app.directive().

Vue directives are class-based definitions decorated with a selector, constructor injection, and host listeners, while Angular directives are registered as plain callback objects on the application instance and receive mounted and updated hooks from Vue's runtime.
explanation: Vue directives are lightweight object with hooks; Angular directives are classes with full DI.

text: In Angular, explain input() signal-based inputs (Angular 17.1+) vs decorator @Input().
options: There is no meaningful difference between the APIs: input() is merely shorthand for @Input(), creates an ordinary mutable class property rather than a Signal, and has the same typing, required-input, transformation, and change-detection behavior as the decorator form.

name = input<string>('') or input.required<string>() creates Signal-based inputs: readonly signals, better type safety, input() is signal, integrates with computed/effect, supports transform functions. Replaces @Input() for new code.

input() is a deprecated compatibility spelling for Angular's older decorator API; Angular recommends @Input() for all components because signal-based inputs are being removed, cannot participate in computed or effect dependencies, and offer no improved type checking.

input() works only in NgModule-declared components and cannot be used by standalone components or combined with computed values, effects, required inputs, or transformation functions; those capabilities remain exclusive to decorator-based @Input() declarations.

text: What is the correct concurrent feature pattern for data fetching in 2024-2026 React?
options: Use an effect-style client pattern: fetch only inside useEffect after the initial render, place the response in local state, and let each component issue its own request independently; Suspense and a shared request cache are unnecessary because concurrent rendering does not coordinate network calls.

Fetch-then-render with Suspense: start fetch early (in Server Component or outside component/cache like fetch/react cache() or libraries like TanStack Query v5 + Suspense), wrap with <Suspense fallback>, use use(promise) or useSuspenseQuery, avoiding waterfall useEffect fetches

Create an XMLHttpRequest or fetch promise synchronously during component rendering, block until the response is available, and pass the immediately read result into JSX before React commits; this avoids Suspense boundaries, server caches, and asynchronous Server Components.

React applications should never fetch data during rendering or on the server, so all remote data must be loaded by client event handlers into local state and passed as props; Suspense, request caches, use(), and asynchronous Server Components are unsupported for production fetching.
explanation: Modern pattern is render-as-you-fetch with Suspense, not fetch-on-render useEffect waterfall.

text: In React 19.1 (May 2025) and Next.js 15, what is the behavior of "use cache" directive?
options: The "use cache" directive is not available in React 19.1 or Next.js 15; server rendering always performs a fresh request, so persistent caching must be implemented with browser storage, a database, or manually managed module-level variables rather than cacheLife or cacheTag.

New directive (React 19.1 canary) to enable per-component/request memoization caching for Server Components and Server Functions, complementing "use client" / "use server" - allows caching of async Server Component render with cacheLife and cacheTag

The "use cache" directive replaces state management across client and server components by synchronizing every useState value between requests; it therefore removes the need for reducers, context, server functions, and external data stores while automatically persisting component state.

The "use cache" directive is a Next.js asset-optimization feature for compiled CSS, fonts, and images used by Server Components; it cannot memoize asynchronous component rendering, does not affect server functions, and has no relationship to cacheLife or cacheTag metadata.

text: Complex reconciliation question: You render <>{items.map(i=><MyComponent key={i.id} id={i.id}/>)}</> where MyComponent is memoized with React.memo. If parent re-renders but items array reference is same (e.g., from cache), and prop id unchanged, will MyComponent re-render in React 19 without compiler and with compiler?
options: Without the compiler, Yes: a parent render invokes every mapped MyComponent even when React.memo receives the same id; with the compiler, No: automatic memoization recognizes the stable array reference and suppresses the child render, so only the parent work remains.

Without compiler: No, memo prevents re-render since props shallow-equal; With compiler: Also No, but compiler makes memo automatic even if you didn't wrap - both avoid re-render. If items array reference same but internal object mutated, still no re-render unless prop changes.

Both versions always re-render MyComponent whenever the parent renders, because keys identify list positions rather than props and React.memo cannot skip a child whose element was created inside map; stable item references do not affect reconciliation or memoization.

Without the compiler, No, because React.memo skips the unchanged id prop; with the compiler, Yes, because compiler optimization disables manual memoization and deliberately re-renders memoized children so reconciliation can verify their keys and array positions.
explanation: memo does shallow prop check. Same id -> no re-render. Compiler automates memo. Need stable reference & no mutation.

text: You need to keep a secret .env file that was committed and pushed 10 commits ago out of GitHub history completely (due to leaked API key). What is the correct modern approach (2024-2026)?
options: Add .env to .gitignore, delete the working-tree copy, commit the ignore rule, and push it; GitHub will then stop exposing the file automatically, including the ten earlier commits, because ignored paths are removed from repository history during subsequent pushes. Rotate the key only if misuse is confirmed.

Run git rm .env, commit the deletion, and push a new commit; once the file is absent from the latest tree, GitHub removes its earlier blobs and cached revisions automatically, so history rewriting, force-pushing, secret rotation, and push protection are unnecessary.

Use git filter-repo (or BFG Repo Cleaner) or GitHub's git filter-repo / git-filter-repo to rewrite history removing that file from all commits, then force push, and rotate the leaked secret immediately. Also use GitHub's secret push protection.

Delete the GitHub repository and recreate it from a clean checkout containing only current files, then push the same branches and tags; GitHub's backend will retain the old repository objects for comparison, so filter-repo is unnecessary but rotating the key can wait until cleanup finishes.
explanation: Simply deleting still leaves secret in history. Must rewrite history AND rotate keys. GitHub now has Push Protection that blocks secrets

text: How does Git internally store data?
options: As ordinary files plus patch records, where each version is represented mainly by line-based differences and identified using timestamps and sequential revision numbers; content-derived hashes are used only for optional integrity checks rather than as Git's primary object identifiers.

As a content-addressable filesystem with objects: blob (file content), tree (directory), commit (metadata + pointer to tree + parent), and tag - all identified by SHA-1 (and SHA-256 support from Git 2.29+ experimental)

As rows in a relational database containing paths, textual diffs, parent identifiers, and commit metadata, with MySQL or SQLite providing object lookup and history traversal while Git stores only a small working-tree cache outside that database.

As a compressed archive for every commit containing a complete repository snapshot, with directory names, author timestamps, and creation order serving as the identifiers; blobs and trees are reconstructed from archives instead of stored as independently addressable objects.
explanation: Git snapshots, not deltas (though packfiles use deltas for storage efficiency). Blobs store content, SHA-1 hashes content.

text: Explain git worktree vs git submodule vs git subtree vs git subrepo pattern. When would you use worktrees for parallel development in 2024?
options: git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix-branch creates linked working tree sharing same .git for parallel checkouts without switching; submodule links another repo at fixed SHA, requires separate commits; subtree merges external repo history into subdir. Worktrees are ideal for reviewing PR while continuing feature without stash.

Worktrees, submodules, subtrees, and subrepo are four interchangeable methods for duplicating project content into another directory. Each creates an independent repository with a separate object database and branch namespace, so changes in one copy never affect the others. A worktree is mainly a convenient name for a full clone, while submodules and subtree imports differ only in command syntax and packaging, not in history ownership or checkout behavior.

git worktree add moves the selected branch out of the original checkout and assigns it exclusively to a temporary directory, leaving the main working directory unable to use that branch. Removing the worktree deletes the branch and its commits unless they were pushed first. Because the linked checkout is disposable and cannot safely coexist with the original repository, worktrees are unsuitable for reviewing a PR while continuing feature development.

A submodule tracks a remote branch and automatically advances to its newest commit whenever the parent repository is fetched or pulled, so the parent does not record a specific external revision. Subtrees and subrepos instead preserve only a snapshot of imported files and discard the external repository's commit history. Updating any of these integrations requires no explicit revision selection or synchronization step.
explanation: worktree for parallel working trees vs submodule/subtree for nested repos

text: You need to enforce Signed Commits, verified by GitHub, and explain GPG vs SSH vs S/MIME signatures in 2024-2026. How do you set up commit signing for team?
options: Generate SSH key ssh-keygen -t ed25519, add signing key as allowed via GitHub Settings -> SSH and GPG keys -> Signing key, config git config --global gpg.format ssh, git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub and git config --global commit.gpgsign true; or GPG gpg --gen-key then git config gpg.format openpgp. GitHub verifies with Verified badge if email matches. Require via Branch protection -> Require signed commits and via Rulesets in 2024.

GitHub does not support signed ordinary commits from developers; only signed release tags can display a Verified badge. SSH keys authenticate Git transport but cannot be used for commit signatures, while GPG signatures are accepted only in private local repositories and S/MIME is limited to email. Branch protection and repository rulesets cannot require signed commits, so teams should use deploy keys, webhook checks, and manual review of author emails instead.

GPG is the only signature format GitHub accepts for commits, so every team member should generate an RSA OpenPGP key, upload its public key, and enable commit.gpgsign globally. SSH signing is restricted to local experiments and S/MIME signatures were removed from GitHub years ago. GitHub verifies only the commit author's email text, not key ownership, and neither branch protection nor rulesets can reject unsigned commits.

A signed commit encrypts its diff, parent references, author identity, and repository contents so that only holders of the signing key can inspect the change. GPG, SSH, and S/MIME therefore provide confidentiality as well as authenticity, and the signing key must be kept secret from GitHub. During a push, GitHub decrypts the commit payload and displays a Verified badge whenever the encrypted repository data can be opened successfully.
explanation: SSH signing (new in 2022) vs GPG vs S/MIME, enforced via Rulesets

text: What is the memory layout and optimization for enum with #[repr(u8)] vs niche optimization?
options: #[repr(u8)] only documents the preferred discriminant type and leaves layout optimization unrestricted; every Option<T> receives a separate tag, so pointer niches cannot reduce its size, and Option<Box<T>> must occupy more storage than a raw pointer

#[repr(u8)] forces discriminant to u8 and C-like layout; otherwise Rust can optimize Option<&T> and Option<NonZeroI32> to null-pointer / niche optimization, using invalid bit patterns to avoid extra discriminant storage, making Option<Box<T>> same size as *mut T

Rust disables niche optimization for enums containing references and NonZero integers, storing an explicit discriminant for Option<&T>, Option<NonZeroI32>, and Option<Box<T>> even when an invalid bit pattern is available for encoding the variant

Every enum stores a full machine-word discriminant in addition to its largest variant, so Option<Box<T>> is necessarily larger than a raw pointer, Option<&T> cannot use null as a niche, and repr(u8) cannot affect its layout

text: Which statement about materialized views vs regular views is accurate for 2024-2026?

Regular view is virtual query executed each time; Materialized view stores physical result, needs REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (CONCURRENTLY in PG), supports indexes, speeds analytical queries but is stale until refreshed

Materialized views cannot have indexes because their stored results are managed internally; only indexes on underlying base tables can improve queries against them, and refreshing one merely recompiles its query without replacing stored rows

Regular views and materialized views both store complete physical copies of their query results, differing mainly in permissions and whether users can update the copied rows directly; neither has meaningful freshness or refresh semantics

text: Consider unsafe Rust: What is correct about unsafe block?

It turns off the borrow checker for the surrounding function, allowing references to alias and outlive their data; safe statements elsewhere regain compiler checking only after the function returns, and all locals may be accessed without restrictions

Unsafe code cannot be wrapped in a safe abstraction, because any function containing an unsafe block must itself be marked unsafe and expose its unchecked operations to every caller; callers must therefore perform the same raw-pointer validation

text: Consider deadlocks. Two transactions: T1: locks A then wants B, T2: locks B then wants A. What is the database's typical resolution and best practice prevention?

Database detects deadlock graph and aborts one transaction as deadlock victim (e.g., SQL Server error 1205, Postgres: ERROR deadlock detected); prevention: consistent lock order, keep transactions short, low isolation if possible, retry logic in app

Both transactions can succeed because the database automatically reorders their pending lock requests and completes them in a safe order; applications should acquire locks in different orders to distribute contention across resources rather than standardizing the order

Deadlocks cannot occur under READ COMMITTED because locks are released after each statement; only SERIALIZABLE transactions can create circular waits, so applications do not need deadlock detection, victim handling, or retry logic for ordinary update transactions
explanation: Deadlock victim selection and retry is standard. Prevention via ordered access is interview favorite.

text: How would you implement a lock-free data structure with std::sync::atomic::AtomicPtr and what ordering is needed?

Must handle ABA problem, use AtomicPtr::compare_exchange, and ensure reclamation (e.g., via crossbeam-epoch or hazard pointers) to avoid use-after-free UAF.

Replace a Mutex with AtomicPtr and dereference the shared nodes through ordinary raw pointers, since atomic pointer operations serialize the pointed-to fields as well; Acquire and Release are therefore redundant, compare_exchange makes reclamation safe, and a node may be freed immediately after removal without risking a concurrent use-after-free.

AtomicPtr is not suitable for practical lock-free structures because Rust reliably supports atomic integers but not safe atomic updates of raw pointers; pointer-based stacks and queues therefore require a Mutex or channel, while compare_exchange cannot implement them safely unless ownership remains exclusive throughout every operation.

text: What is the ES|QL LOGSDB index mode introduced in 8.16+ and its benefit?

Use bpftool prog, grep Seccomp /proc/<pid>/status, cat /proc/<pid>/attr/current, check landlock via audit or strace of landlock rules, and dmesg for AppArmor implicit deny

Reinstall the operating system and refresh package metadata, then replace the binary from a trusted repository and rebuild its package database; intermittent EACCES indicates damaged executable headers or stale package ownership rather than a process-level sandbox, mount option, capability check, BPF policy, or IMA/EVM measurement, so inspect those only after reinstalling

Investigate storage hardware and inode corruption first with fsck, SMART, and filesystem repair, because unreadable sectors are the usual source of execve EACCES; container hardening mechanisms are expected to return only ENOENT or EPERM, so Landlock, seccomp, NoNewPrivs, BPF LSM, noexec mounts, and integrity policies cannot account for this failure
